three years after joining the european union, romanians and bulgarians do not enjoy full rights as european citizens. although the free movement of labour is a fundamental principle of the european construction, ten member states still maintain barriers for romanian and bulgarian citizens. the extension of restrictions on access to internal labour markets was decided despite the recommendation of the european commission that the mobility of eastern european workers had not disrupted labour markets and had driven economic growth. unfortunately, the economic crisis is now being used as an argument for keeping these restrictions in place, citing domestic unemployment and the pressure exerted by immigrants on labour markets. however, the reality is that the possible consequences of the influx of labour from the new member states are being exaggerated and that the persistence of barriers is also preventing the full potential of the labour force to emerge from the current crisis and to relaunch the european economy from being used. i therefore hope that the new european commission will take stronger action against these protectionist measures which discriminately restrict the free movement of labour within the european union.

member of the commission. − mr president, i appreciate very much the interest that you take in the second revision of the cotonou agreement. it is also with great interest that i read the report of the development committee, which provides a shrewd analysis on the matters at stake. throughout the whole process, it is a priority for us to keep parliament informed, as we have done over the last months. the negotiations have gained momentum and are now entering into the final phase, and the next joint ambassadorial meeting will prove the value of these discussions. we will be heading for an extraordinary joint ministerial meeting to conclude the negotiations in march, as foreseen by the cotonou agreement. let me now share with you some observations on the report. above all, the report has already proven helpful in upholding certain positions of the eu. just to name some of them: your position on strengthening national acp parliaments, on the international criminal court and on other human rights issues confirmed our negotiation position. likewise, the importance that you attach to climate change and food security is shared by us and will be reflected in the final outcome. i would like to focus on four items, starting with the importance of the parliamentary dimension as embodied in the joint parliamentary assembly, to which the report attaches great importance. the commission is committed to strengthening the parliamentary dimension in the cotonou agreement. therefore, our intention is not to weaken the jpa. on the contrary, the commission proposal must be seen in the broader context of growing parliamentary oversight functions, in particular with a view to existing and future economic partnership agreements (epas) and edf programmes. we should ensure maximum synergy between epa and cotonou institutions, including between regional jpa meetings and the epa parliamentary bodies. in this emerging setting, a reduction of plenary jpa meetings would make sense. the commission accepts, however, that this matter needs to be agreed with those who are most concerned, and is therefore open to reconsidering its position. at the same time, we would be interested to learn more from parliament how it sees the jpa’s role and functioning in a changing political and institutional environment. the establishment of epas does not only call for the need to ensure synergy between them and the cotonou institutions, but also requires an update of the cotonou trade provisions, since the cotonou trade regime has become obsolete. we have agreed with acp partners that we will continue the negotiations towards regional european partnership agreements. in this context, as development commissioner, i would stress that it is neither politically desirable nor legally feasible to incorporate eu unilateral trade regimes such as gsp or gsp+ in cotonou, as suggested in the draft report, since these depend on autonomous eu schemes. by contrast, the commission welcomes the call for cotonou to give more attention to the trade and development issues in general and to aid for trade in particular. in your report, you express the concern that the conclusion of epas and increased regionalisation might undermine the coherence of the acp group. the commission believes that regional differentiation within the framework of cotonou is more an opportunity than a threat. regional integration is crucial for the development of acp countries and we need to integrate this reality into cotonou to better support their own efforts towards this objective. this by no means signifies disrupting the acp group, and our acp partners largely share this approach. let me now briefly comment on sectoral policies which you are stressing in your report. we fully share the importance of climate change and renewable energies which are already included in the present revision exercise. likewise, we will address food security in the regional dimension. you also stress the importance of good governance in tax matters and in the fiscal area. good governance is a fundamental principle of the cotonou agreement. building on article 9 of the cotonou agreement, the commission is currently preparing a new policy on good governance in tax matters in the context of development cooperation. we are also seeking to address these aspects in the ongoing revision exercise. therefore, i can confirm that we share the same objective with you, which is to create fair, effective and growth-enhancing tax systems and effective tax administrations, as well as to strengthen the participation of developing countries in international tax processes. finally, i take note that you deplore that the commission has not consulted a wider variety of actors before launching the revision process – paragraphs 2 and 8 – and i fully agree that, for the future of the acp-eu relations post-2020, a comprehensive consultation process is needed, possibly in the form of a green paper. we will have to assess the results of the present revision exercise as a basis for this as a form of lessons learnt.
on behalf of the epp group. i would like to start by congratulating ms joly on the preparation of this report. the themes addressed are very important to ensure that the cotonou agreement remains the basis of a solid partnership with the acp countries and also a relevant instrument in the context of the new challenges facing these countries. the negotiations are taking place in a context which is, as we know, difficult and complex. on the one hand, the acp countries are deeply affected by the economic and financial crisis, but also by food insecurity and the consequences of climate change, on the other hand, there is an institutional challenge for all parties to the negotiations to reflect adequately the tendencies towards regionalisation in the acp-eu relationship. we must now ensure that the revised text contains all the necessary ingredients for effective development cooperation, capable of contributing to the achievement of the millennium development goals in the acp countries. i also want to emphasize that i have tabled five amendments on behalf of the ppe. they allow, in my view, a more nuanced reading of some of the proposals in the report. for example, in paragraph 29, it's important to emphasize the concept of ownership, in relation to arable land. as regards the creation of a mechanism forcing transnational companies to declare their profits, i believe that this should be set up at international level. in paragraph 25, a clear reference to a coherent approach to food security in the framework of the union's development policy is important. finally, in paragraph 31, the position expressed on readmission agreements with third countries does not correspond to the view of the epp group.

acting president of the council. - i am grateful that this question has been put by mrs ludford, who has spoken before, by mrs antonescu, mrs romero and mrs hautala and mr tavares, because we are indeed dealing with a very important issue, namely procedural guarantees in criminal proceedings. in this respect, i would like to say that we agree with the assessment of the importance of this matter, which has been made by the honourable member, and we also agree that this must be harmonised at european level. in your question you first point out that the swedish presidency has made important progress. the swedish presidency has indeed made important progress in this respect. the council agreed on a general approach to the text on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings and a month later - in october - in november, the council adopted a plan to take further steps, as requested by the honourable member, in the field of procedural guarantees. some of them you have mentioned, mrs ludford, such as the right to information on the rights to 'overcome redundancy' and on the position of a person in criminal proceedings, on assistance, legal advice, on communication with relatives and with consular authorities or on the special safeguards to be had and the protection of accused persons who are vulnerable. this is the case with the council during the swedish presidency. you then say: 'well, is there an agreement with the european parliament to continue this work as a priority? we say to them: yes, it is a priority to continue along that line. how did you do that? what initiatives? the first thing the spanish presidency will do is to try to get the directive on interpretation and translation rights in criminal proceedings, which has been launched by 13 member states, adopted, working with the european parliament. it was not possible to continue with the initiative presented by the commission and thirteen member states have replaced it. we want this initiative to be adopted in collaboration, of course, with the european parliament. and we also expect the commission to take appropriate initiatives in the other areas of procedural guarantees. we are very keen to see that this is done as soon as possible so that we can once again go ahead with the council and the european parliament in approving them. i would like to conclude by saying that the spanish presidency is planning to organise a seminar in madrid next march, together with the commission and the european law academy, on the subject of common standards for procedural guarantees. this shows, mrs ludford, how much we share with you and with the people who have signed this question the urgency of regulating these matters, of harmonizing them at european level and, of course, of keeping the european parliament always informed of the progress of the work.
the commission's vice-president - thank you for asking. you know how much i value these procedural safeguards. it is true that the commission has been campaigning for many years for the minimum common standards on the rights of the defence to be truly generalized in all criminal proceedings in europe. this is necessary for judicial cooperation and is the condition for the indispensable mutual trust between the member states. the commission has worked hard to get european legislation in this area adopted. and it is true that, thanks to the swedish presidency, the roadmap was adopted by the council on 30 november 2009. this is a fundamental step in the creation of european legislation on minimum procedural rights. the member states reached agreement on the scope of this legislation and agreed on the need to adopt it as a matter of priority in full collaboration with the european parliament. i have just listened, as you have, to minister lópez garrido, who has explained very well how the spanish presidency is also converging on this desire to adopt these first measures which are leading us towards a set of minimum guarantees. it is true that the step-by-step approach to the road map has finally seemed to us a good solution. this approach is likely to achieve the objective pursued. the step-by-step approach means not only that each right can be analysed in greater depth in the context of the legislative proposal, but also that in the negotiation each right can be examined individually. this avoids the cross-purchase which sometimes characterizes legislation that is too general and which can allow some member states to take negotiation hostage in order to gain an advantage on a very specific point. so, mrs ludford, i am sure that the new commission will work as quickly as possible to bring forward all the legislative proposals set out in the road map and to get them adopted as soon as possible. as regards the right to interpretation and translation, which is the first measure provided for in the road map, the commission took note of the initiative put forward by a number of member states. this initiative, i should say, is based on the commission's proposal of july 2009 and on the negotiations in the council during the second half of 2009. but it is true that the initiative of the member states is not in full conformity with the european convention on human rights, with the case law of the court of strasbourg. the commission's previous proposal, which made interpretation of meetings between the accused and his counsel compulsory, is not fully followed by the member states' initiative, which limits this right to communications taking place before the police authorities and during the trial. in addition, the commission's old proposal provided for a right to translation, a more complete right in the commission's text. of course, there will be work between the european parliament and the council and i think we can get an ambitious text on procedural rights. this is essential if we are to create a genuine european judicial area. and we will ensure that the text is in conformity with the standards laid down in the european convention on human rights and the case law of the strasbourg court as well as in the charter of fundamental rights. so i am sure that we can count on parliament's action in this area and, once again, i note that the spanish presidency will also help us.

defendant. the importance of common standards is an essential condition for mutual trust in the legal systems of the member states. the lack of balance between the rights of the accused and the in writing. the copenhagen summit on the environment was characterised by many as a resounding failure, as it resulted in a vague agreement with no clear assumptions or deadlines. however, if we look more closely at what happened in the danish capital, we see that here the foundations of a new world climate order have been laid, but it will take years and years of hard work and negotiations to get there. 115 heads of state and government met for the first time to discuss climate change. it's an important signal, and the fact that the summit was held under the un umbrella shows that even developing and under-industrialized countries are realizing that they need to play an active role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. the importance of bilateral talks between major industrialized and developing countries has increased, especially in the light of the upcoming environmental summit in mexico. the eu is well placed to play an important role in bilateral talks with countries such as china, india and brazil. it's time that no effort is too great when it comes to the future of the planet we all share.
in writing. for a month now, "failure" has been the most commonly used word to describe the copenhagen summit. the unsatisfactory outcome of the summit was due both to the reluctance of the major industrialized countries and to the complicated rules of the un consensus system. the european union's inability to act as a catalyst for global efforts to limit the effects of climate change should also be examined. by unilaterally announcing, a year before this conference, its intention to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 20% by 2020, the eu had the moral high ground to give impetus to the copenhagen negotiations. but we were unable to make our voices heard in a meeting dominated by the us and emerging countries. a smaller format is needed to hope for a negotiated outcome. the ministerial meetings in bonn and mexico in june and december must be used as effectively as possible to leave the way open for the adoption of a new treaty. member states need to coordinate so that we can speak with one voice internationally.
in writing. the european union must remain engaged in the international negotiations for the adoption of a post-kyoto agreement. it is clear that the conclusion of a new global post-kyoto agreement requires a thorough evaluation and preparation of the eu negotiating strategy, with a view to continuing the negotiations in 2010. although it cannot be considered a success and is far from what the european union wanted, the copenhagen conclusions represent a step towards the conclusion of a legally binding post-kyoto international agreement. the eu's efforts in the immediate period ahead must focus on diplomatic efforts to secure commitments from all relevant international partners, in particular the us, china and india, so that the global target of limiting temperature rise to 2 degrees celsius above pre-industrial levels can be met. we must be aware that the eu's commitment to increase the level of emission reductions by 30% by 2020 is conditional on comparable or proportionate commitments by third countries.

the commission has already taken the initiative of introducing a new procedure for the adoption of the directive on the protection of the environment by means of the use of biotechnology. the danube region is of particular importance to the european union, both for the large number of countries it crosses and for its direct access to the black sea. together with the rhine and the main canal, the danube links the north sea and the port of rotterdam, the largest port in the european union, to the black sea and the port of constanta, the tenth largest port in the european union. recognising the importance of the danube region, the european council of june 2009 requested the commission to develop, by the end of 2010, a european union strategy for the danube region. we call on the commission to start consultations with all the countries bordering the danube as soon as possible and, following the model of the baltic sea strategy, to accompany the danube strategy with an action plan and a multiannual operational programme drawn up together with the participating states. the development of transport infrastructure is essential for the development of the danube region. the modernisation of ports, the unification of navigation systems on the danube, the removal of bottlenecks on the rhine/meuse-main-danube river axis to improve navigation conditions, the provision of intermodality in the region and the increase of connectivity with the black sea through road and rail transport routes, i am referring to rail freight corridors and high-speed trains, are just some of the priorities for the development of transport in the region. the danube region plays an important role in diversifying the european union's energy supply sources. implementing joint projects in the field of energy efficiency and renewable energy, investing in new technologies and developing small and medium-sized enterprises will help to stimulate the green economy throughout the danube macro-region. tourism is also an important tool for promoting economic growth in the region. last but not least, the development of competitiveness poles, academic and cultural exchanges will contribute to territorial cohesion in the danube region. the danube region and in particular the danube delta comprises several special protection areas and special conservation areas within natura 2000, being a unique and fragile ecosystem. environmental protection in the danube basin will greatly influence agricultural and rural development in the region. the danube strategy will allow, through a coordinated approach, a more efficient use and absorption of european funds, but is not limited to this. to this end, we call on the commission and the member states to use the mid-term review of the financial perspective and the debate on the future financial perspective in 2010 to implement the objectives of the european union strategy for the danube region. the european parliament will be a constant partner in the process of developing and implementing the european union strategy for the danube region.
member of the commission. − madam president, i want to thank you for raising this very important issue on the danube regional strategy and also for your broader support for the macro-regional strategies in europe. the commission is working with the countries of the danube cooperation process in this context. this means the following member states: germany, austria, slovakia, the czech republic, hungary, slovenia, bulgaria and romania. in addition, the following third countries are participating: croatia, serbia, bosnia and herzegovina, montenegro, moldova and ukraine. concerning the state of play at this stage, we have established inside the commission an inter-service working group of more than 20 directorates-general to indicate the main policy priorities for this strategy. in parallel, the countries of the danube region have each nominated a national contact point, and the first meeting of these contact points has been held with the member states. a series of events has been planned between february and june this year to create momentum and trigger discussion with the relevant stakeholders. the first such event will be held in ulm in germany on 1 and 2 february. turning to the future content of the strategy, i would like to underline that we are, of course, only at the beginning of the process of elaboration and preparation. the content will be discussed in closer detail over the coming months among the countries concerned, the relevant stakeholders, the commission services and other eu institutions. nevertheless, it seems likely that the strategy will be based on three broad pillars or, in other words, broader policy priorities: firstly, to improve connectivity and environmentally sustainable communication systems; secondly, to protect the environment, preserve water resources and improve risk prevention activities; and thirdly, to reinforce socioeconomic human and institutional development. these three pillars will include a number of concrete actions based on the contributions received from the member states, stakeholders and from within the commission. finally, let me indicate the next steps. between now and june we shall continue to gather ideas and proposals from the member states, from stakeholders and from other interested parties through position papers, meetings, conferences and also a public consultation exercise via the internet. following that, by september the commission will prioritise and organise ideas in order to prepare the draft communication on the strategy and the accompanying action plan. then, finally, by december the commission will prepare the adoption of these documents. therefore, from next year – 2011 – on, we will start setting up the governance systems and concrete implementation of the actions and projects that will have been planned and decided by that time. thank you for your attention. i look forward to hearing the points you wish to raise in this debate.
on behalf of the epp group. the epp group attaches particular importance to the danube strategy. the rhine-main-danube axis is a bridge between east and west, between the north sea and the black sea, is directly linked to ensuring energy security, opens the way to asia through the black sea, and also links the mediterranean sea. we therefore support the development of the danube strategy this year, as the commission has committed itself to do, and i welcome the re-engagement of commissioner rehn and wish it to be adopted with a concrete action plan by the beginning of 2011 at the latest. among the major priorities to be pursued are: ensuring navigability along the entire axis, first of all the danube-rhine connection and the standardisation of navigation systems, modernising river ports and developing related infrastructure to become integrated multimodal systems, the efficient use of the danube's energy potential, developing irrigation systems to prevent desertification, implementing an integrated water monitoring system to increase the capacity to forecast, prevent and respond to floods, drought or pollution. concerted action is needed, as the failure of even one coastal state to get involved can lead to the entire process being blocked. financial resources are also needed, and i hope that the new european commission will take this into account and not avoid public-private partnership funding. of all the danube countries, romania has the largest sector. for this reason, romania supports the speedy development of this strategy to exploit the river's potential, which is essential for the whole of europe.
i believe that a well-founded strategy with the necessary financial resources could significantly improve the quality of life of the people in the danube basin. at present, financial instruments are available for infrastructure projects, economic development or environmental protection, but they can only be used by member states and their neighbouring countries. this is something that must be given special attention and we must not exclude the possibility of finding other sources of funding in the future besides the community. it is known that the other states do not have the necessary financial resources, and this makes cohesive development along the danube impossible, from an infrastructure and economic point of view, and therefore the regional authorities respond differently to the problems they have. the commission is, as far as we know, considering consulting local partners to ensure sustainable development. the question is whether the commission also envisages working with regional expert groups to develop the strategy. the question remains whether the objectives of this strategy should be to achieve cohesion, to exploit the economic and transport potential of the danube, to ensure the protection of the river, the ecosystem and the quality of the water. i would also recall that the danube is priority axis number 18 in the ten-t (trans-european network of transport) and the commission is currently initiating a broad review of the trans-european transport networks policy with a communication on this subject scheduled for may 2010. the question arises as to how the transport policy issues applicable in the eu member states are expected to be linked to this strategy, which naturally also takes into account the presence of non-eu states in the danube region.
i think we must express our support for a european strategy for the danube region, especially since the accession of romania and bulgaria to the union has brought the benefit that today most of the more than 2800 km of the river is in community territory. the baltic strategy has played a decisive role in opening up the macro-regions' perspective; the danube strategy marks a further step in the same direction. one of the priorities of the danube strategy should be economic, namely the development of the energy capacities of both the danube and its neighbouring area. following the january 2009 gas crisis, romania is already making a european-level effort to interconnect gas networks with neighbouring states through the arad-szeged, giurgiu-ruse, isaccea and negru vodă projects, but more efforts are needed towards alternative, renewable sources. i appreciate that the european danube strategy must take into account the analysis and the appropriateness of objectives such as the development of energy infrastructure, namely new transmission networks and new electricity generation capacity, the promotion of energy production from renewable sources, new hydroelectric power stations, wind power stations, biofuels, the continuation of nuclear power development programmes, such as the one in cernavoda. the protection of the environment in the danube basin must be a top priority. in this regard, it is necessary for the union, together with the riparian countries, to be involved in the conservation of the danube delta ecosystem, including by permanently stopping the works in the bastrop canal. we cannot allow misunderstood economic interests of a country in the eu's neighbourhood to produce an ecological disaster in the danube delta.
since i submitted my candidacy for the european parliament, i have considered the danube to be an important, untapped potential of the eu. the rhine-main-danube transport axis, which links the north sea via the port of rotterdam to the black sea via the port of constanta, could become the backbone of europe. the new danube strategy looks likely to be approved under the auspices of the hungarian presidency. it will focus on areas such as transport, economic development and environmental protection. one of the main barriers to the development of rhine-main-danube transport is the diversity of standards that navigators have to apply. unfortunately, it seems that the political will to harmonise these rules has so far been lacking. the ulm conference, which i will be attending on 1 and 2 february, is a first step in the consultation process. romania has offered to organise a number of conferences on this topic, including the ministerial conference in june 2010.
the danube is a life- and history-shaping element in central and south-eastern europe. in 1823, andrews and prichard were granted an exclusive patent to sail in the austrian provinces. they set up a joint stock company with its headquarters in vienna. the treaty of paris of 1856 made the al-duna section navigable, contributing to the economic prosperity of the region. today, the eu's lasting peace and prosperity is a guarantee that it will meet its challenges. given the historical precedent, we might ask why the first step was a bit of a stumble. i mean, the intergroup. perhaps because the interests of hungary, romania, germany and austria could not be reconciled. let's remember our history. the region has developed well when conflicting interests have been reconciled, but values have not suffered.

in writing. value added tax fraud is one of the criminal phenomena with very serious budgetary effects, with illegal reimbursement schemes being used in all member states, romania being no exception (e.g. the carousel of sales). reverse taxation, introduced by some member states, including romania, has worked very well, but it was also necessary to adapt the vat directive 112 to current realities so that the risk of implementing illegal vat refund schemes (such as fictitious exports) is as low as possible. the application of reverse charge to products with a high risk of tax fraud is therefore a safe method and, despite the deferral of payment of vat to the state budget in respect of transactions involving such a charge, the final effect on the budget is positive. in conclusion, given the choice between collecting vat only at the end of the business cycle, when the finished product or service reaches the end user, and avoiding fraud consisting in illegal vat refunds, the correct choice is the former. ideally, reverse taxation should be the rule rather than the exception, but this should be done after serious budgetary impact analysis.

statistics show that bluefin tuna is being fished far beyond the limits, with the bluefin tuna population declining every year. the proposal by the state of monaco to include bluefin tuna in cites appendix 1 may prove salutary, as this species is doomed to extinction unless radical and immediate measures are taken to protect it. in 1992, the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas adopted the recommendation to monitor the trade in bluefin tuna. unfortunately, it has proved to be a tool of more than limited effectiveness. in 2007, the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas adopted a much more complex programme, called the blue tuna catch documentation programme, which came into effect in the summer of 2008. although it represents a step forward, it is still premature to assess the effectiveness of this programme. i cannot therefore help asking: to what extent can the european union's position in favour of the inclusion of bluefin tuna in annex 1 counterbalance, in the context of the cites conference, the wish of certain bodies and non-eu countries to adopt a standby policy until the hypothetical fruits of the recent initiatives of the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas can be assessed?
mr president, all elements of this agreement are important but i want to focus on the bluefin tuna issue. it is vital that we act now to prevent a stock collapse and to allow the numbers of bluefin tuna to recover. in 2006 the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tuna agreed on an action plan designed to improve reporting and monitoring of stocks and inspection of vessels. but it is clear that it is not enough. the stocks, particularly the eastern stock in the mediterranean, remains critically low and there is a very real risk that we will soon witness the extinction of this endangered species. the conference of the parties to cites should therefore agree to place bluefin tuna in appendix i of the convention, and the member states and the commission must do more to combat illegal fishing and to enforce agreed restrictions and quotas.
i appreciate the report presented and congratulate mr van nistelrooij on the way he handled and completed it. i believe that the erdf regulation should be amended to allow the states to use this funding for the renovation and construction of housing for marginalised communities. the actions of states and local authorities must aim at the sustainable social inclusion of these communities in both urban and rural areas. i appreciate that the focused effort to support the roma community must involve all the member states of the union. this is because roma, the roma population, is the largest marginalised community in europe, a community with a high level of cross-border mobility in the european area. but we must also take into account the needs of other communities, in particular those of legal immigrants and the communities of workers temporarily working in other member states. for these reasons it is good to allow the use of erdf funding for housing in all eu countries. i believe in the success of the programme and hope that we will continue with a new phase in supporting families in marginalised communities through facilities and in terms of getting and keeping jobs, especially in the face of the crisis. i support this report which will also allow romania to access funding for the social inclusion of marginalised people, including roma in urban areas as well as in rural areas.
the eligibility of housing interventions to be financed by the erdf in favour of marginalised communities will help member states to improve their absorption of european funds. personally, i think that this eligibility should apply to all member states. regulation (ec) no 1080/2006 has recently been amended to allow all member states to improve energy efficiency in their homes. the new text provides for a 4% quota. perhaps, for the sake of consistency and to reduce red tape, it would have been better to keep the same percentage. the new provisions stipulate the need to develop urban development projects for areas threatened with physical deterioration or social exclusion, but also for marginalised communities. this includes areas affected by disasters such as floods or earthquakes. i would like to conclude, mr president, by asking the commission, together with the member states, to use 2010 to review the operational programmes in order to increase the absorption of european funds to improve the social housing stock.
the new eligibility rules for housing are an example of how the same funds, without being supplemented, can be used to a greater effect. the first step was taken last year by relaxing the rules on the use of eu funds to improve energy efficiency. in this respect, i would say that it was a small step and that the percentage allowed could be re-examined. the second step is today. in both cases, the adaptation of texts was involved, some of which date from very different periods than the present. i therefore wonder whether other aspects of the use of european funds should not be reviewed in order to change those criteria which no longer correspond to current needs.
the year 2010 is the european year against poverty and social exclusion. unfortunately, the number of those facing extreme poverty and marginalisation is very high, which is in contrast to the fundamental principles and values of the european union. the vulnerability of these communities has increased significantly in this period marked by the economic crisis. in this context, i welcome the initiative to extend the eligibility conditions for the european regional development fund, which is an important and indispensable instrument in the fight against poverty. because of the poor quality of the housing, i feel it is urgent to provide financial assistance. financial support must be provided for both urban and rural housing. the granting of such financial support should also not discriminate between the roma population and other social groups in similar situations.

mr president, i welcome all the efforts and the progress made by croatia towards its accession to the european union. this will certainly represent a major step forward in the direction of european integration for the entire western balkans region. i hope 2010 will be a very good year for croatia and for the western balkans too, but i would also like to underline the necessity of considering and adequately addressing the issue of refugees and the internally displaced persons. see the last report of the un high commissioner for refugees. as you know, in 2005 an agreement was signed in sarajevo by croatia, bosnia and herzegovina, serbia, and montenegro – the so-called sarajevo declaration. the agreement was aimed at sorting out the problem of the very large numbers of refugees and internally displaced people deriving from the conflict in the region. however, this is an issue that is still pending. i would very much like croatia to finally affirm its readiness to relaunch the sarajevo declaration and to bring to an end a situation that i consider highly sensitive, and this at least before its accession. i welcome very much the commitment of the commission to relaunch this spring the negotiations and i reiterate in front of you that this problem should be solved once and for all before croatia joins the eu. a final remark on turkey: when evaluating turkey i would invite you not to let our prejudgement based on religion, ethnicity and clichés to speak.
as the oomen ruijten report points out, turkey made a clear commitment to reform and good relations with its neighbours in 2009. moreover, the authorities have encouraged public debate on crucial areas of the reform process, such as the role of the judiciary, the rights of ethnic minorities, and the role of the military in the country's political life. the signing of the nabucco agreement also demonstrated turkey's commitment to creating security of gas supply in europe, as demonstrated by turkey's negotiations to join the european energy community. turkey has proven its key role as a regional actor by normalizing relations with armenia, as well as improving relations with iraq and the kurdish regional government. let us not forget, of course, the cooperation within the black sea synergy, launched three years ago with the aim of promoting stability and reform in the countries around the black sea. finally, i would like to mention a few of the main reasons for this country's accession to the union: turkey is clearly part of the european family and an important partner in the dialogue between civilisations. the approach of a secular, democratized and modern turkey to the union is certainly a plus for our community.
madam president, in its neighbourhood policy, the union’s objective has always been to export stability and not to import instability. this is why i appeal to member states and candidate countries not to promote bilateral conflicts to the level of the union. being a lawyer, i would like to recall that, through the interim accord between greece and fyrom signed in september 1995, greece agreed not to object to fyrom’s application to international or regional organisations if made under the name referred by the united nations, which is fyrom. the union’s institutions refer to this country as fyrom. these provisions are legally binding in terms of international law. therefore, there is no legal basis for greece to obstruct the country’s accession process. decisions must be taken on the performance of the applicant country. on this note, i support the debates on the progress made and the areas in which improvement is still needed. we need to talk about the merits and closely monitor the implementation of the reforms. based upon the progress made, the commission proposed that the country be given a date to start negotiations. i join the commission and call on the council to provide a starting date for accession negotiations at its summit in march 2010.
progress has been made in the protection of minorities in croatia and macedonia, but they are still far from excellent. what can we do? the eu could encourage these countries by setting an example in protecting minorities, but what is happening in the eu? it would be good if france and others ratified the charter for minority and regional languages, if slovakia abolished its measures discriminating against minorities, see the language act, and if greece also recognised that minorities live on its territory and guaranteed their individual and community rights. romania will hopefully have a minority law, but we are still far from having minorities in the leadership of the army, and they are more afraid of autonomy than the 14th russian army in transnistria. parliament could encourage the acceding countries to set a better example by making uniform standards for the protection of minorities across the union mandatory.
croatia continues to be the most advanced of the western balkan countries on the path to eu membership. it can serve as an example for the countries of the region on the prospects for accession in the context of compliance with the accession criteria and conditionalities. the progress made on internal reform is commendable, as also reflected in the 2009 progress report. the way in which the country meets the criteria for accession, in particular those deriving from chapter 23, justice and fundamental rights, is an important benchmark in the country's progress towards european standards. we support croatia's accession to the european union on the condition that it is based on strict compliance with the accession criteria, including full cooperation with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia. croatia will conclude its accession negotiations this year and so the report we are debating today is the latest progress report produced by the european parliament. we are confident that next year we will be in a position to vote on the treaty of accession of croatia to the european union, which will be a positive signal for the whole region.
the most effective external enlargement policy of the european union towards the western balkan states is that of enlargement in the region: this is the guarantee of peace and democratisation for a region whose recent history has unfortunately only reinforced its reputation as a 'powder-box of the european union'. in the mirror, the most effective foreign policy of the new western balkan states is that of belonging to the european union's area of stability and prosperity. in this process we need tools, so i welcome the country reports for croatia and macedonia, which are valuable tools. i also believe that economic instruments are needed, regional cooperation, economic, trade and investment instruments, which have already proven their effectiveness. i believe that these instruments should be considered by the european commission as well as by the governments of croatia and macedonia.
in writing. i believe that it is in the interest of both sides, the eu and turkey, that the enlargement process continues, and that turkey must therefore step up the reform process in order to meet its commitments. some examples: gender equality legislation is harmonised, but more effort is needed to implement it in order to close the gaps between men and women in labour market participation, in politics and decision-making, and in access to education. progress has been made in environmental protection, notably with the signing of the kyoto protocol, in this era of adapting to the effects of climate change, but much remains to be done in the fields of water quality, nature protection and gmos. i welcome the progress made by turkey but at the same time i support the call for ankara to make more efforts in the reform process to join the european club.
in writing. i hope that this year's evaluation report will encourage turkey to step up its foreign policy coordination with the eu. the black sea region should be a priority area where turkey, as a key eu partner, can contribute to the achievement of the european objectives set out in the black sea synergy. equally important is turkey's participation in ensuring the eu's energy security. last year, we welcomed turkey's participation in the nabucco project by signing the intergovernmental agreement. but i also expressed my deep concern about turkey's intention to cooperate with russia on the south stream project. i therefore insist on turkey's unequivocal commitment to the nabucco project. i welcome the rapporteur's call for the energy policies of turkey and the eu to be harmonised, in particular by opening accession negotiations on the energy chapter and by integrating turkey into the european energy community.

in writing. terrorism remains a high threat in the european union; therefore, all member states have stepped up their efforts to improve the tools used to prevent and combat it. the adoption of the lisbon treaty offers the possibility of reacting much more effectively in all areas directly or indirectly linked to the fight against terrorism. the issue of body scanners is a delicate one. i believe that these are important issues that need to be carefully considered before a decision is taken in this area. these concern the efficiency of scanners, the respect of the right to privacy, the economic impact of their use in view of the particularly high cost of their acquisition and, in particular, the way in which the use of these devices affects the health of those who will be monitored by them. the european commission is to develop three studies on the use and effects of body scanners; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the establishment of a european centre for the development of vocational training (ecvet) and the establishment of a european centre for vocational training (ecvet).
in writing. it is our duty as meps to get involved in solving the problems raised by the subject of body scanners, both in terms of the fight against terrorism and in terms of the civil and individual rights of europeans. i'm all for finding viable solutions to enhance the safety of our citizens. but we have an obligation to ensure that all the rights of our citizens are protected within the european union. this implies the right to privacy and the fundamental right to personal dignity, which must be balanced against the concept of security of airport facilities. the question that arises in this context is whether these body scanners are the most viable solution to solve airport security problems. i believe that europe must say yes to finding solutions to combat terrorism and organised crime and no to disregard for the right to privacy and personal dignity, which is a basic principle of democracy.

in writing. ukraine is a european state and shares all european cultural values. ukraine needs the honest and effective implementation of a political programme guaranteeing the rights of national minorities: russian, tatar, romanian, polish, hungarian, greek and others. the european charter for regional or minority languages, which guarantees their status as regional languages, needs to be implemented. i believe that the eu must support the implementation of such measures, insisting that no minority is left behind. for example, in ukraine there is a romanian-speaking minority of over 410,000 people. it is a traditional national community with deep historical roots, living in harmony with the majority and other minorities, especially in the chernivtsi region (northern bukovina, northern bessarabia and the herzegovina area), in the odessa region (the districts of southern bessarabia), in the transcarpathian region (historical maramureș). i believe that the eu should encourage the ukrainian authorities to develop romanian-language teaching units in vocational schools and high schools in the cities of the above-mentioned regions. the eu should also work with kiev to establish romanian-language departments at the state university of chernobyl in all existing profiles and specialisations.

the regulation of the gambling market in the european union is a delicate issue, whether we are talking about conventional or online gambling. the online gambling industry has grown in recent years and is a highly profitable industry. there are voices that support banning them and voices that, on the contrary, believe that banning them would lead to an increase in these activities in the context of a lack of regulation. both the european union and the member states share common objectives in the effort to better regulate gambling: to protect minors, to find solutions to addiction problems, to put in place appropriate supervision measures in terms of transparency and advertising rules, and to prevent addiction and excessive use of online gambling. in the absence of harmonisation of legislation, member states are free to set their policy objectives in this area and to define the level of protection sought. although the aims seem to be the same, the problem of regulating this area is not easy to solve. but we cannot deny the reality - gambling is an important economic activity which is not entirely subject to the rules of the internal market. unrestricted by technical barriers, they are accessible across borders and generate billions of euros in profits. the decisions of the european court of justice do not bring together those with differing views on the appropriate way to regulate. the commission continues to face a contradictory reality: the competence of member states to regulate this area and the complaints lodged by game providers against restrictions imposed at national level. i'm not a big fan of online gambling. i can say that i am rather against them, but i believe that we must start from the reality of the existence of these games and that is why we need to draw up harmonised legislation to regulate the activity of economic operators, but above all to provide for measures to support consumers. we need to ensure that online gambling is handled responsibly, ensure the protection of minors and vulnerable people, prevent addiction and avoid organised crime.

author. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, freedom of expression is not a virtual right on which we can agree without relating it to the political and social reality of a country. the freedom of the media to express critical opinions about a government or politicians, whether presidents, officials or the opposition, is the most important guarantee that a people can have - that is, access to a plurality of information - so that their right to vote is not a deception. unfortunately, the reality in venezuela is that, after many undemocratic acts by the government of president chávez against the opposition, it seems that the time has come to put an end to the press as well. this is not only the latest case of rctv international, which the venezuelan audiovisual authority imposed a retroactive law on, but also the closure of 34 of the most popular radio stations since july 2009 in venezuela. globovisión, on the other hand, which still maintains an independent editorial line from the government, is being pressured to change it. let's not forget that the most perverse way to eliminate the media is to provoke self-censorship. after the closure of the 34 radio stations, the government of hugo chávez formally announced that there is a list of other radio stations that are also about to be closed; a list that no one knows because there are no open procedures, but with which uncertainty is maintained with the sole purpose of provoking self-censorship. and all these abuses occur without the competent courts responding to the actions brought. in a country where a universal principle such as the non-retroactivity of the law is not respected, where the judiciary does not respond to any appeal until it receives instructions from the president, there is neither a rule of law nor a separation of powers. there is simply no such thing as democracy. sadly, that country is today's venezuela.

in writing. the economic crisis has had a profound negative impact on the growth potential of the countries of the union. i have followed the debate on this subject and i have noticed that the focus has been on measures to get out of the crisis and to recover economic growth in financial terms. while it is certainly good to approach problems in order of severity, it is important to realize that the situation is not the same as it was before the crisis. what needs to change is the economic model itself, which needs to be based more on innovation, clean energy and attention to the health of people. we can't have a performing economy if we don't have motivated workers, and we can't have a sustainable economy if we only support environmental protection halfway. recovering the growth potential i believe has to start with changing the economic model itself, which has to focus on what creates innovation and human motivation. the way out of the crisis is not primarily a matter of economic or fiscal policies.
in writing. the current economic crisis is the most serious in decades, with its effects in halving the growth potential at union level. the economic downturn is accompanied by an accelerating ageing of the population, which is hampering the recovery of the eu economies. in these circumstances, strategy 2020, which is intended to be a continuation of the lisbon strategy, must create the conditions for sustainable growth and fiscal consolidation. thus, lifelong learning needs to be much more accessible and universities need to be much more open to atypical students. better supply-demand matching and greater labour mobility will provide workers with more opportunities where their skills are most needed. to reduce poverty and exclusion, we need modern social security and pension systems. employment policy must focus on the flexibility of the labour market, with employees being responsible for their working lives through continuous training, adaptation to change and mobility. adjusting to the context of the crisis and the ageing of the european population is essential so that we are able to ensure an adequate level of support for people temporarily out of work.

i begin by recalling that when it was created as the sole human rights body within the united nations system, the human rights council marked a hope, namely the hope of increasing the protection of fundamental rights worldwide. the establishment of the universal periodic review mechanism, which is the most important innovation since the defunct commission on human rights, was intended to address the problem of excessive politicization and selectivity in dealing with cases of serious human rights violations. this mechanism is essential if the human rights council is to fulfil its mandate in any way. it should be stressed, however, that the old demons have not entirely disappeared and that excessive politicization continues to affect the work of this body. on the other hand, it must be said that the universal periodic review mechanism is not sufficient to ensure effective protection of human rights. when the council does not react quickly enough, as happened, to take one example, in guinea, in the case of the guinea crisis, this has very serious consequences: the perpetrators of human rights violations may simply feel that they have nothing to worry about. the council's credibility thus depends on its ability to act firmly and swiftly when serious human rights violations occur. in this connection, it is important that the european union promote the creation of mechanisms at the level of the human rights council dedicated to responding to crises such as those in, to take recent examples, afghanistan, guinea-conakry, iran, yemen or iraq. it is, i believe, in the european parliament's interest that this body, the human rights council, should be as strong and effective as possible, because, i say, we need a credible partner in the human rights dialogue.
i would like to refer to the situation in the gaza strip, which, as you know, is a constant concern for human rights, especially after the worsening of the situation following the clashes last winter. i don't think we can measure who has suffered more in this conflict, the military actions of both sides have made, unfortunately, mostly civilians suffer, but in the context of the situation on the ground, it is very difficult to differentiate between military and civilians, as far as the palestinians are concerned, and on the other hand, hamas's rocket attacks were aimed at terrorizing israeli civilians. i visited the area during the conflict, i saw the problems and fears on both sides, and i think any attempt to blame only one side for what happened is inconsistent with reality. the bloody clashes in gaza and their dramatic humanitarian consequences are a painful plea for concerted action in all sensitive areas of the world, in particular against the causes of suffering of defenceless civilians, and for the deeper and more effective involvement of international structures in order to promote dialogue for peace. it is an area where the european union has both the capacity and the credibility to act more strongly on the world stage.
in the context of today's debate, i would like to bring to your attention the case of israeli soldier ghilad shalit, abducted from kerem shalom in june 2006, a soldier aged just 19. last week i was part of the official delegation of the european parliament to israel, and one of the meetings was with ghilad shalit's father, noam shalit. despite the provisions of articles 13, 23 and 126 of the geneva convention on the rights of prisoners of war, ghilad, who is also a french citizen, is denied the right to be visited by his family and the international red cross, the right to humane treatment, the right to know precisely where he is being held. i should point out that even article 77 of the goldstone commission report, which is critical of israel, recommends that ghilad shalit enjoy the rights guaranteed by the geneva convention. on the other hand, israel respects the rights of its prisoners.
the eu should make clear to the un human rights council in march its conviction that the international community will not ignore human rights abuses in the developing world or the backsliding in developed countries. the declaration by the un general assembly on the rights of persons belonging to national, ethnic, religious and linguistic minorities of 18 december 1992 applies to both developing and developed countries, as well as to eu member states. the first paragraph of the second article of the declaration states that persons belonging to national minorities may use their language in both the private and public spheres without any interference or discrimination. this article is currently in trouble in eu member states. the eu can only be credible if it finds a solution that sets an example for the rest of the world in dealing with the backlog of human rights violations by minorities in the union.

equality of opportunity between men and women is a fundamental principle of the european union, enshrined in community law. in 2009, women represented 24% of the members of national parliaments, 26% of the members of national governments and 33% of the leaders of european companies, as well as 18% of the professors at european public universities. i would like to mention that 81.3% of young women have completed at least secondary education and 59% of university graduates in the european union are women. the european union's strategy for growth and jobs has set a target of 60% female employment by 2010. the risk of poverty among women, however, is primarily due to the situation of single-parent families headed by women. i think it is important to ensure that women have equal opportunities for career development and planning, conditions for reconciling personal, professional and family life; and here i want to stress the importance of childcare facilities. we've set a goal that 30 percent of children under three years old can be enrolled, can be in child care services under three years old.
one of the areas of action defined by the beijing platform in 1995 was the fight against violence against women. fifteen years after that historic un conference, the record of efforts to improve the status of women worldwide is disappointing. many of the programmes adopted over the years remain woefully out of touch, such as the millennium development goals, which promoted gender equality. sadly, domestic violence, rape as a weapon of war, female genital mutilation, forced marriage, human trafficking, and sexual slavery remain the nightmare that destroys the lives of millions of women worldwide. i believe that without the european union's stronger involvement we cannot speak of success. we need a comprehensive strategy that addresses poverty, lack of education and information, impunity, armed conflict, human trafficking for the purpose of prostitution. i think it is important to remember that, before being a cause of harm, violence against women is the effect of a complex of factors whose root must be tackled more unitedly and more firmly.
in writing. the united nations has established the international day for the elimination of violence against women, which the entire planet celebrates every year on 25 november. this is a widespread phenomenon, with 45% of european women being victims of various forms of violence, and globally one in three women has been beaten, forced into sexual intercourse or otherwise abused. this manifestation includes not only domestic violence against women and girls, but also exploitation, sexual violence, trafficking in human beings, honour killings, dangerous traditional practices such as bride burning or early marriage, and other forms of violence against their bodies, minds and dignity. in most cases, the abuser is the spouse or intimate friend or someone known to the victim. i believe that violence against women is one of the most serious violations of human rights and is an even more serious phenomenon because it exists on every continent, in every country and culture, regardless of the level of economic development. the perpetrators of these acts must be severely punished, and in the case of large-scale crimes the international criminal court must play an important role and in close correlation with the decisions of national courts.
in writing. i believe that gender equality should be one of the central objectives of any democracy. although much has been done in the european union to achieve the objectives of the beijing platform for action, they have not yet been fully achieved. in europe, we still face strong stereotypes about women, with significant gender pay gaps, and progress towards attracting more women to decision-making positions is very slow. in general, however, equal opportunities unfortunately remains only a wish, especially in the case of the eastern european countries, new members of the eu. in order to achieve better results in the member states in achieving the objectives of the beijing platform for action, it is essential to have reliable and comparable data at both european and national level on the situation of women, as well as a regular review of progress in the critical areas identified by the platform. i am glad, however, that the spanish presidency has included gender equality issues in its list of priorities and has paid particular attention to women in agriculture, and i congratulate it on this initiative.

the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon is giving the european union more competence in the field of energy policy. i believe this is an area where, if member states work together, europe can market more transparent and efficient. europe has set this priority very high on its agenda. last year we adopted a third energy package which aims to ensure a more competitive and efficient energy to making the market more transparent and more predictable. in this context, i think it would be a pity to waste the opportunity this new instrument offers, by not applying the correct legal basis member of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i have raised the question of how the commission intends to evaluate the information it receives from the member states under this regulation. our analysis will first compare the foreseeable development of the infrastructure with the expected development of demand. we will see whether the new capacity expected corresponds to future demand forecasts or whether gaps are to be expected. it is essential that, in contrast to the current regulation, an institutional dialogue on these issues be introduced. the commission therefore proposes, firstly, to publish a report every two years on the structural development of energy infrastructure. this should help to improve transparency for all market participants. secondly, we want to have a political discussion with parliament and the member states to draw conclusions. i would like to emphasize the latter. the regulation itself is an instrument for collecting and gathering information to make visible any need for action. the way in which these are addressed will be the subject of specific energy policy initiatives. i come now to the point which is of particular concern to you and to the house as a whole, madam president: the new article 194 of the treaty of lisbon and its application. this article is both an opportunity and an obligation for all of us - parliament, council and commission - to shape the eu's energy policy in close cooperation, that is, above all with the european parliament. as the new commissioner for energy, i therefore want to involve this house as early and as fully as possible in all future policy measures. the legal act to which today's debate refers, however, concerns only the collection and analysis of information in the energy sector and is therefore based, in the commission's view, on articles 337 and 187 euratom. the content of the regulation corresponds to these two articles of primary law and, in accordance with the case-law, the choice of the legal basis for secondary law must be based on measurable criteria of substance. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i ask for your understanding.
on behalf of the epp group. commissioner, you have tried to explain why we do not work in co-decision. i share the view of my colleague, mrs valean, the rapporteur of this report, that it would have been good if this regulation had been discussed in the codecision procedure. the new regulation is a very important legislative instrument for the european union's energy market. this analysis should complement national and regional strategies and contribute to strengthening energy security by identifying potential gaps and risks in infrastructure and investment, with a view to ensuring a balance between energy demand and supply. i think the commission's proposal includes some ambiguities which i think have been resolved by the amendments tabled, such as the issue of the publication of energy data sent by the member states, this data must be aggregated at national and regional level. this avoids the disclosure of commercially sensitive information. another problem is to clarify what is meant by a 'specific body', that is a body responsible for preparing and adopting multiannual plans for the development and investment of energy infrastructure at community level, the problem of avoiding duplication of the collection of these data and the problem of determining when a particular project must be reported, that is after the authorities have received the application for a building permit. another particularly important aspect is the issue of monitoring in third countries of european investments that have an impact on the european energy market. i believe that investments in third countries, both governmental and those made by national companies, which have a significant effect on the energy market, should be reported under this regulation.

in writing. in the context of the new energy policy aimed at securing supply, mitigating climate change and ensuring competitiveness, investment in energy infrastructure plays a key role. new policy requirements, such as fuel mix targets, will lead to changes in member states' policies so that they benefit from new and modernised energy infrastructure. the commission proposal aims to review the current system for informing about investment projects in the energy sector: it aims to collect adequate information on planned investments, to enable the commission to monitor the infrastructure situation and anticipate possible problems. as current eu legislation already imposes reporting and notification obligations related to investments and infrastructure, it is necessary to ensure that the use of this information is better coordinated, avoiding duplication of reporting obligations, confidentiality and citizens' access to information. although the proposal is rather administrative in nature, it gives an idea of the nature and expected qualities of future investments. it is therefore important to put a stronger focus on the environmental impact of projects in order to provide additional guarantees and incentives for the construction and decommissioning of energy infrastructure in a sustainable manner and with appropriate environmental protection. congratulations to the reporter!

in writing. − the launch of a new strategy to tackle fisheries problems in the european union is welcome. overfishing, illegal fishing, pollution, climate change, all of these are factors that threaten marine ecosystems. therefore, the pursuit of quality aquaculture in europe will bring economic benefits and at the same time environmental benefits. it is essential to maintain the right balance between economic growth, the fishing tradition of some regional communities and best fishing practices, and, most importantly, to understand that sustainable and economically efficient aquaculture in the long term depends first and foremost on how environmentally friendly we are.
in writing. − a key element in the reform of fisheries policy is the co-interest of producer organisations in respecting the principles promoted by the european community. the european union cannot wait for the natural, economically driven downsizing of europe's fishing fleets. their overcapacity, almost eight years after the world summit on sustainable development, and the continuing decline in fish stocks are further reasons for a substantial reform of the common fisheries policy. but it must not forget that there are entire communities in the coastal regions of the european union whose existence revolves around fishing. as the fisheries reform report also states, this activity is part of the cultural heritage and traditions that no one wants lost. a rethinking of the common fisheries policy is in the interest of each member state so that the main objective of the 2012 summit to achieve the maximum sustainable yield of fish stocks by 2015 can be achieved and the european community is no longer obliged to import half of its fish needs from other markets.
in writing. − i believe that long-term management and recovery plans for all fisheries and geographical fishing areas within the european union need to be drawn up. the first thing to do is to take account of the enormous differences in european fishing, to give more responsibility to fishing areas and to improve the traditional quota system. europe needs a strong, common approach to fisheries management, including both the continental and market dimension of the sector and the catch and aquaculture sector, in line with the new integrated maritime policy of the european union and its interest in sustainable growth in coastal regions.
in writing. − the commission’s green paper on this issue was a damning indictment and an honest recognition that the common fisheries policy has not worked. on the contrary, it has contributed to a variety of problems which continue to have economic, social and environmental impacts. only two weeks ago, this house voted in favour of suspending international trade in bluefin tuna because of the critically low stocks – a situation which is yet another sign that our current levels of fishing are unsustainable and have serious consequences for biodiversity and the future of the fishing sector. we must recognise that a new approach is needed. a decentralised policy with more funding will allow different regions to adapt and respond to their own circumstances – something that the previous ‘top-down’ policy prevented. this should lead to better management of stocks and have a positive effect on the marine environment. i fully support the commission’s commitment to whole-scale and fundamental reform, which has been rightly backed by the committee on fisheries. it is vital that we act to ensure that the european union implements a truly sustainable fishing policy in order to protect stocks, the environment, and european jobs in the long term.
