madam president, commissioner, the treaty of lisbon is new in the process of delegating executive powers to the commission, and article 290 is precisely what it is about. delegated acts are thus acts of a general nature which may amend non-essential elements of a basic legislative act which gives a mandate for the delegation of executive powers to the commission. in practice, this sets out a mandate, the duration of the delegation, the time limit within which parliament and the council may raise objections and the conditions for the revocation of the mandate. the parliament and the council shall carry out a review, but after the adoption of the delegated acts. delegated acts can also be published during the period during which the european parliament and the council can raise objections, but i would ask you, commissioner, to ensure greater transparency during the process of drafting delegated acts as well.
deputising for the author. − madam president, the question was submitted by brian simpson on behalf of parliament’s committee on transport and tourism, following the commission’s report looking into the effectiveness of the eu blacklist. the eu blacklist was established in 2006 to name, shame and ban airlines which are not complying with international safety rules. it was established in response to concerns over the level of enforcement of international safety standards and on the back of several fatal air crashes over a short space of time in 2004 and 2005. four years on, we know that the blacklist has proved an effective and valuable tool in promoting enforcement of icao safety standards and in protecting eu citizens. how we can now build on this is the question facing us today. in other words, how can we extend the protection beyond our own borders and further work towards the goal of improving global aviation security? the blacklist has a responsibility not only to identify where the safety risks lie but also to ensure that this information is effectively communicated to eu citizens. in line with this, how can we ensure that eu citizens taking flights outside europe are aware of banned air carriers that continue operating in other regions of the world? in cases where the air carrier’s licence has been revoked and therefore the air carrier does not appear on the blacklist, how can we be sure that passengers are aware of this situation? we have seen how effective the bringing together of different national blacklists into one comprehensive eu-wide list has been. however, the blacklist is only as good as the access we have to information relating to the safety of air carriers. how can we build on the information which forms the basis of the blacklist by improving the access to verifiable and reliable information? this means not only looking at strengthening the checks made in eu member states but also approving the data information received from non-eu member states. would the commission consider establishing harmonised and standardised ramp checks and reporting? in terms of improving the data information received from third countries, would the commission consider establishing an effective system of international exchange of reliable data, bringing us closer to a kind of worldwide blacklist which i know has been mooted in the past? furthermore, it is worth pointing out that the blacklist has proved an effective tool in incentivising airlines to meet international safety standards. but how can we work more proactively towards the ultimate goal of improving global aviation safety? by this i mean, how does the commission intend to support national civil aviation authorities in meeting safety deficits based on icao audits and improving their oversight capability? it is crucial that we ensure effective communication channels with the public, but it is also vitally important that, in the long term, we continue to work on promoting the enforcement of international aviation safety standards around the world. this will ultimately be the most effective way of improving safety for all passengers. the committee on transport and tourism of the european parliament looks forward to working with the commission to try and build on the eu’s blacklist achievements.
the blacklisting of unsafe air carriers is a welcome protection measure for european passengers. the list should be well publicised by the european commission and the member states, and especially by the travel agencies. it is really all about the good faith and the goodwill of the tour operators and the travel agencies. on the other hand, a solution is needed for a situation where a certain destination is served only by unreliable air carriers. a good number of the blacklisted carriers serve destinations in the third world, africa, south-east asia, central asia, developing or underdeveloped countries. the question is, to what extent can fair competition be maintained between the large european, american and far eastern airlines and the small carriers established in these developing countries? in this connection, i think we need to consider how the european union could support not their removal from the market by banning them, but their development by strengthening the safety and security of their flights. in this way, the european union would make it its duty to support the sustainable development of the air transport sector in these less-favoured countries as well.
the blacklist, updated on march 30 this year, contains 278 companies from 17 countries. the union must develop its technical and administrative capacity to ensure that the necessary rules are met in civil aviation, so that only airlines that comply with international safety rules fly into the european union, but at the same time we must also help third countries to improve their safety standards in civil aviation. the competent authorities of third countries need to strengthen their capacity to ensure oversight of the air carriers to which they grant licences. the analysis of the safety of flights of third country operators will be carried out in the european union and through ground checks of aircraft of these companies, taking into account evidence of incidents and serious accidents suffered by carriers in the last year. however, passengers must be informed of the entire route travelled and of all the companies they use to make the journey. this information should be provided at the latest at the time of purchase of the ticket.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank mr dorfmann for an excellent report on the commission communication entitled ‘towards a better targeting of the aid to farmers in areas with natural handicaps’. i would like to address a couple of issues. the overall objective of the natural handicap payments is to ensure continued land use and, through agricultural land management, maintain the countryside as well as to promote sustainable farming systems. the payments to farmers in these areas compensate farmers’ additional costs and income forgone, which occur due to the existing natural handicap. the council has decided to remove the socioeconomic criteria from the objectives of natural handicap payments. the removal of socioeconomic criteria should be seen in the context of the whole suite of measures available to member states in the rural development regulation – the diversification into non-agricultural activities, the development of micro- and small and medium-sized enterprises and tourism activities, as well as the provision of basic services. so the natural handicap payments are not the intervention lever that aims to tackle this issue of depopulation. compensating farmers in areas where production is not hampered by natural handicaps and where there is no additional cost or income forgone would distort competition with farmers in other areas. furthermore, socioeconomic indicators change over time and would, therefore, require a continual follow-up and revision process of each area concerned. the proposal to take remoteness into account is not practical against the agreed framework set down by the council, which relates to natural handicaps. in terms of their peripherality, there are other levels of delimitation possible, for example the specific handicap article of the regulation. at the different stages of the process, the commission invited member states to submit alternative proposals for biophysical criteria and their thresholds. these proposals will be analysed by scientists for their validity and, above all, for their transparency and possible community-wide applicability. the alternative thresholds, however, must lead to the conclusion that an area in question is affected by a significant handicap, as desired by the council. once the exercise of testing a delimitation based on biophysical criteria is completed, the commission proposal for the common agricultural policy after 2013 will take the results of this exercise into account. any legal proposal will also aim for a smooth transition for those areas which may lose their status of areas with a natural handicap.
in writing. the aid scheme for areas affected by natural handicaps has effectively contributed to maintaining the exploitation of agricultural land in these regions and the importance of providing adequate compensation for less-favoured areas is indisputable. the delimitation and classification of the zones was carried out by the member states on the basis of several criteria, according to their own system of indices. even comparing these systems is very difficult, as they use different methods of classification and weighting. establishing a common set of classification criteria would increase the transparency, reliability and efficiency of the system across europe. in this connection, i support the need to review the aid system for farmers in areas with natural handicaps and to draw up a comprehensive strategy for less-favoured areas, thus reducing the discrepancies between member states in the allocation of financial support.

vice-president of the commission. − in a world that is moving fast into a new digital age, europe needs to be prepared with the state of the art broadband infrastructure that will indeed drive the growth of tomorrow. the council of march 2009 fixed an indicative target of achieving 100% coverage by 2013. the europe 2020 strategy has taken the challenge one step further by setting the 2020 high-speed broadband targets as 30 megabits per second for all europeans, including people living in rural regions, and as 100 megabits per second for 50% of households subscribing to internet. the digital agenda for europe, which is one of the seven flagship initiatives under eu 2020, sets out a strategy to promote high-speed internet in europe and is scheduled for adoption not that long from now. the agenda will be followed by three documents on broadband: firstly, broadband communication, which details the implementation of the agenda with respect to broadband; secondly, the recommendation on new generation access (nga), which aims to clarify the basis to encourage investment in high-speed internet; and thirdly, the first radio spectrum policy programme, which will form the basis of the commission’s strategy to generate enough spectrum for wireless broadband. the actions to promote high-speed broadband in the digital agenda comprise not only the commission commitment but also suggestions to the member states. those suggestions will bring into focus the development of national broadband strategies covering the promotion of private investment using town-planning rules, mapping of infrastructure and clearing of rights of way; and by doing that the member sates can substantially cut investment costs and make them more viable. they will also focus on bridging the financial gap by fully using the available structural funds to fund high-speed broadband and, where there are no incentives for private funding, direct public financing. the commission for its part is looking at the options available to increase private and public investment in nga to reach the agreed targets. financial engineering will be among the considered options to reduce the gap between what is required and what the market is prepared to invest.

in writing. the new swift mandate for the eu-us agreement on the terrorist financing tracking programme is all the more welcome as the council and the commission have learned from the past and have included in the negotiations parliament's strong demand that data protection be held to a higher standard. this transfer of financial messaging data from the eu to the us must however be firmly negotiated with the us authorities. the transfer of collective data must be avoided and the technical means must be insisted on to allow the transfer of individual data, only of suspects. i hope that this agreement will not surprise the eu in the future and that it will be made clear before the agreement is signed that the eu has the right to obtain information from the us database and that the possibility of transferring data to third countries is excluded. this transfer must also guarantee the protection and rights of the citizen, in particular with regard to access and rectification of data, as they appear in national and european legislation. last but not least, the right of european citizens to object should personal data be misused needs to be clarified.
the protection of personal data is one of the fundamental rights of european citizens. the treaty of lisbon reinforces previously existing provisions by giving the european charter of fundamental rights legal and binding force. any processing of personal data must be carried out in compliance with directives 46/1995, 58/2002 and 24/2006. the european parliament therefore calls for any international agreement concerning personal data to be concluded under conditions where the signatory parties have in force provisions similar to those in the abovementioned directives. in the information society, and especially in the context of the development of broadband communications infrastructure, the data storage and processing centre may be located in different locations or even countries. we therefore ask that any agreement concerning personal data require that both the storage and the processing of personal data take place only in locations where there are legal provisions similar to those in european legislation. and one last thing, madam president, how do european citizens give their consent and, above all, under what conditions?
we must agree that the ban on cyanide in mining should become a priority in the environmental problem in romania, but also in europe. with more than 25 major accidents and spills worldwide between 1998 and 2006, it is becoming increasingly clear that cyanide poses a continuing environmental hazard for decades to come. these mining accidents raise a number of questions about the practices and enforcement of cyanide management regulations, even if there are good intentions at the corporate level. moreover, the difficulty of managing the transport, storage and use of cyanide, associated with the deficiencies in the operation and maintenance of the settling ponds, as well as bad weather can lead to explosive situations, devastating the environment. alternatives to cyanide mining exist but are not promoted by the mining industry, although eu-wide regulations are used to actively promote new emerging technologies that are safe. in november 2005, members of the european parliament and member states adopted the so-called mining waste directive. this directive is an ineffective legislative instrument and is the result of strong pressure from the mining industry and concerns expressed by central and eastern european countries about the elimination of any requirement and responsibility to clean up old and abandoned mining sites. some of the shortcomings of the directive become apparent when we consider that, for example, it does not deal with emissions of cyanide into the air. take the mining development at red montana, alba county. if the mine opens, it's estimated that it will release 134.2 kilograms of cyanide into the air per day, and that's every day of normal operation. this means an annual emission volume of 48 983 kg or 783 728 kg for the mine's 16-year life. there is also no european air quality legislation for such emissions. in this context, it is our moral duty to future generations and in the spirit of the global trend to ban cyanide mining, to support this legislative proposal.
first of all, i would like to thank the commissioner for the balanced position she has taken in opening this debate. technologies that use cyanide are dangerous. but other technologies, such as the production of nuclear technology, are equally dangerous. to prevent accidents there are regulations, standards and rules. we don't have to ban, we have to follow the rules. the resolution mentions 30 accidents in the last 25 years, avoiding specifying how many of these occurred in europe, because they were extremely few, in countries that were not members of the union at the time of the accident. moreover, following the unfortunate accident in 2000, the commission tightened up the regulations. cyanide technology is used to make a variety of products, including pharmaceuticals and vitamins. the resolution only discusses mining and, in particular, gold production. why would you do that? because the problem isn't really cyanide, it's gold. it calls not only for the technology to be banned, but for any ongoing projects to be halted until the alleged ban is imposed. i don't know of any other prospective gold mining project in europe other than the one in romania. ladies and gentlemen, i would ask you to read the text of the resolution carefully. references such as 'large future rainfall increases the risk of leakage' or 'mining offers few and low-prospect jobs - only 16 years' or 'human negligence may occur because some member states lack the skills to enforce the law'. i do not think that such references have a place in a text of the european parliament. i therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to assess both the reasons and the consequences and to vote against a resolution which undermines our credibility with the commission and reduces the chances of taking account, not only in this case but in general, of the proposals contained in the resolutions voted in the european parliament.
in my opinion, the initiative to ban the use of cyanide-based technology in gold mining is unjustified. there are several european legislative acts in this area, as mentioned earlier, which have regulated the conditions of use of cyanide more and more strictly, starting precisely from the unfortunate accident mentioned earlier, at baia mare, which led to a regrettable contamination. our efforts should therefore focus on the rigorous application of this legislative framework at national level in each member state that is in this situation. the use of cyanide in gold mining is a technology that has been used for over 100 years in an environmentally safe and efficient gold mining process. in fact, 90 percent of the gold mined worldwide in the last 20 years has been mined using this technology and not some alternative. technical rules for the use and neutralisation of cyanide have led to the minimisation of risks to the environment and human health. it should also be stressed, i think, that a correct application of the precautionary principle does not mean an emotional reaction that would result in the banning of a technology that has proven its usefulness and whose risks are perfectly known and controllable. the environmental risks arising from the alternative use of cyanide-like agents should also be considered in the application of the precautionary principle. or, experts say that the use of such alternative agents presents greater risks than the use of cyanide.
the authorisation or prohibition of mining projects using cyanide raises sensitive issues in some member states. first of all, we must make it clear that the solution to the problem cannot be a captive of political intentions and interests. the risk of pollution is a matter for experts, and when there is a risk of pollution, it is the responsibility of political leaders to protect the interests of citizens. at this point, the issue goes beyond environmental considerations, since pollution can endanger the health of the population, which is contrary to the right of eu citizens to a high level of health protection (article 35 of the charter). in this respect, there is no such thing as a small risk or a big risk. when the health of citizens is at risk, political debate is futile and the authorities must act against the potential polluter. although the use of cyanide is prohibited in some member states and permitted in others, member states should consult each other and seek partnership. the commission should take a position on this issue and initiate legislation that excludes the possibility of harm to the health of eu citizens.
i agree that all measures must be taken at european union level to reduce the risks posed by the use of toxic and dangerous substances such as cyanide. banning them, however, need not be the only solution. toxic and dangerous substances are used in many other industrial processes, not just mining. in addition to the great bay accident in 2000, there were two other major accidents in the mining sector: one in spain in 1998 and the other in sweden in 2003, both of greater magnitude. the causes were similar, however: the collapse of the settlement ponds. over 90% of the world's gold and silver production is produced by cyanide metal extraction technology. the unconditional ban on this technology and its replacement by technologies based on substances with lower environmental risks but extremely costly and low yields means that the country in question will virtually give up the production of these metals, with the associated economic and social effects.
one chemical that gets out of control and into the environment causes serious problems, but we have over 10 million chemicals. we have more places where they work with chemicals. we could discuss millions of potentially dangerous situations in the european parliament. sure, cyanide is toxic, too, but i'm a chemist, and i can tell you that we have a big problem in the world: less than 18% of cyanide is used in mining, with the rest being used to make pharmaceuticals, consumer goods in the cosmetics industry and many other fields. but the substances used on our planet are thousands of times more toxic than cyanide. in general, chemicals, if they get into the water, destroy life. we have many dead rivers around the globe that haven't been reached by cyanide. the dead sea is lifeless because it has a lot of sodium chloride, which is salt. all chemicals must be used in accordance with 2010 environmental protection technologies and standards. romania, as a european state, has definitely entered this path. all the countries of the world must do the same.
mr president, with all due respect can i say that this debate is largely misdirected. the subject before us is a very curious matter. it reignites an accident that took place 10 years ago. why? why has there been this long silence? and why now? why a debate now? if we follow this pattern we could and should ban anything and everything that can be linked to a past accident. i find the whole matter unjustified. i think it uses the environment as a screen and it is based on the mass fears so fashionable nowadays. in my opinion, and i think in truth, it is just a poor political plot.
member of the commission. − mr president, thank you for this debate. i will of course make sure that mr potočnik gets a full account of it. we share your concerns about cyanide. it is of course a very dangerous toxin and we are aware of that. but let me assure you that the commission has drawn conclusions from the terrible accident that happened 10 years ago in baia mare. the directive that we have very recently put in place includes a lot of limitations, requirements, restrictions and demands, in order to provide maximum protection as regards the effects on the environment and human health. the directive will also reduce the likelihood of such an accident happening again and, should there be an accident, will reduce the possible impact to a great extent. it is therefore extremely important that the directive is duly implemented. given the very stringent requirements of the mining waste directive and the absence of adequate alternatives today, a general ban on cyanide use for gold extraction does not, for the moment, seem appropriate. however we are following the issue, we are studying the latest technology development and there will be an evaluation in 2012. we must increase the recycling rates of the products containing precious metals in the eu, in order to reduce reliance on gold mining altogether. thank you for this debate. mr potočnik will of course be at your disposal to answer further questions on this. the commission is taking this very seriously. if you study the directive, you will see that many of your concerns are already there. let us help to push the member states to really implement it in full because that would considerably reduce the risks.
in writing. on january 30, 2000, the dam of the waste settling pond owned by the company aurul in baia mare, romania, ruptured, allowing the discharge of about 100,000 cubic meters of contaminated water containing 100 tons of cyanide as well as heavy metals. the spill has cut off drinking water to 2.5 million people, affecting three countries. the somes river had cyanide concentrations 700 times the legal limit. water life has been completely destroyed over a distance of several hundred kilometres. we must not forget the details of this disaster, which has become an international symbol of pollution. he demonstrates that despite the law and the controls, such accidents are possible at any time. dangerous substances have no place in mining if we want to prevent catastrophes. rosia montana is planning to build the largest surface gold mine in europe, based on the use of cyanide. the next one? the destruction of the environment, the disappearance of the village, the displacement of the inhabitants, the churches and cemeteries, the condemnation of precious relics dating back to the roman and pre-roman periods. history teaches us a lesson. we all have a duty to understand them. it is absolutely necessary to ban the use of cyanide in mining altogether in the eu to prevent human and environmental tragedies.

in writing. − i welcome the adoption of this report which will contribute to the development of a proposal for a comprehensive strategy for 2015 on information and communication technologies (ict). i believe that the way out of the economic crisis depends to a large extent on its ability to facilitate the widespread and effective application of information and communication technologies in the business environment. smes can be the catalyst for europe's economic recovery and the european commission needs to strengthen in the future the support measures for smes to use ict tools to increase their productivity. in today's vote, i support the proposal in this report to develop a digital plan to promote online businesses, with a focus on providing alternatives to those who have recently been made redundant in the context of the financial crisis. such an initiative could be implemented by providing free internet access and free consultation.

in writing. − the strengthening of the strategic bi-regional partnership between the european union and the countries of latin america and the caribbean, concluded in 1999, must be a priority of the european union's external agenda. while significant progress has been made in developing bilateral relations between the eu and latin america over the past decade, there is still more to be done, with the ultimate objective of the partnership being the creation in 2015 of a euro-latin american area of comprehensive interregional cooperation in the political, economic, commercial, social and cultural fields, guaranteeing the sustainable development of both regions. the european parliament voted today in favour of the future adoption of a euro-latin american charter for peace and security, which, on the basis of the united nations charter and related international law, should include strategies and guidelines for common political and security action. i also believe that the fight against climate change, which affects the poorest people in the world the most, must become the key element of the eu-latin america strategy, with both sides having to make considerable efforts to reach a common negotiating position in the debates leading up to the united nations climate change conference, which will take place at the end of the year in mexico.
in writing. − the resolution adopted today by the european parliament's plenary is an important signal that the union has a very good understanding of its global role. latin america is the favourite tourist destination of many europeans, but for europe it means much more. latin america may suffer from democracy, judging by european standards and principles. the european parliament recently debated a resolution on the flagrant human rights violations in cuba, resulting in the deaths of people exercising their right to freedom of expression. these are dramatic situations that must never happen again. but the european union's experience shows that a relationship built over time on friendly and diplomatic terms is far more productive in the long run. the european union will succeed in becoming the exporter of democratic principles it wants to be, if it takes a constructive approach. latin america is a huge continent that cannot be ignored economically or socially, and the fact that the european investment bank has already been present on the south american continent for a long time, offering the chance for long-term investment, is a significant signal. the resolution adopted today constitutes a clear mandate to the eu high representative in addressing relations with latin america.

in writing. − the european parliament, in its resolution adopted today, expresses its concern at the continued visa requirement by the canadian authorities for romanian, bulgarian and czech citizens and calls for the swift abolition of this requirement. the maintenance of visas for the citizens of these member states is contrary to the principle of free movement, creating unjustified disparities and inequalities, as citizens of the european union should enjoy equal and fair treatment. although the 2009 eu-canada summit in prague reaffirmed the partners' shared objective of ensuring the free and secure movement of people between the eu and canada, it is 2010 and nothing has changed. i am confident that in the near future the canadian authorities will make every effort to eliminate these visas. together with my colleagues in the european parliament, i will continue the work begun to allow romanian, bulgarian and czech citizens to move freely as soon as possible.
in writing. − citizens of three eu member states still need visas for canada. the czech republic is also among the countries that have introduced the visa requirement, due to the large influx of roma. in this context, there is a need for closer cooperation between the eu member states to solve the problems of the roma community and between the member states and canada to create a more efficient and transparent system of information on visa conditions in order to reduce the rejection rate. the canadian asylum system also needs to be reviewed and the merit of the resolution in this regard lies in its explicit request to the canadian side to take action to end the visa requirement.
in writing. − canada is one of the european union's longest-standing partners and this year's summit is important for continuing and strengthening this close bilateral cooperation in all areas. i voted for the joint resolution because it reflects, in a concise and objective way, the positive vision of our future cooperation. ensuring reciprocity in bilateral relations is a basic principle of the european union and i hope that in the near future canada will lift the visa requirement for romanian, czech and bulgarian citizens, thus ensuring equal and fair treatment for all european union citizens. i also welcome the progress made so far towards an eu-canada trade agreement and hope that this year's meeting will give impetus to its completion. given the current economic and climate context, i must stress the need for close collaboration to identify alternatives to traditional energy sources that respect the specificities of each country, as both the eu and canada are committed to the development and use of low-carbon technologies. at the same time, cooperation in the field of energy, climate and maritime affairs in the arctic must be promoted.
in writing. − by its vote today, the european parliament has shown its openness to a new agreement on the processing and transfer of financial messaging data under the terrorist finance tracking programme and reiterated that any new agreement in this area must respect the new legal framework established by the treaty of lisbon. the fight against terrorism remains a priority for the eu, and fruitful cooperation with the us, including, inter alia, the exchange of data and information, is an important prerequisite for preventing future terrorist attacks. i believe it is essential that this exchange of data be strictly limited to information required for the purpose of combating terrorism, since the collective transfer of data is a departure from the principles on which european legislation and practice are based. that is why, in today's resolution, i have explicitly called on the commission and the council to address this issue appropriately in the negotiations with the us that will take place in the near future and to examine with the us partners how to establish a legally viable and transparent procedure to authorise the transfer and extraction of relevant data.
in writing. − romania supported, as a nation state, the adoption of the swift agreement, but the european parliament considered that, in its first form negotiated by the representatives of the commission and the us administration, it infringed the rights of european citizens who were treated as bulk and not on a point of view, based on suspicions. it is important that the new agreement, negotiated in washington these days between representatives of the eu and the us congress, responds to the concerns of the european parliament. there is always the risk that the new version of the agreement will also be rejected if it continues to be at odds with the european charter of human rights. the european parliament is aware that this agreement is important for the security of europeans themselves. it is therefore clear that the objections of the meps are related to the substance and not to the form of the agreement. the european parliament has acquired greater decision-making powers with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. it is only right that this institution should use its powers and look after the interests of the citizens of the european community. but as long as the spirit of the positions expressed by the european legislator is preserved in the future form of the agreement, it will be adopted. the fight against terrorism and the swift identification of suspicious bank transfers remain as high as ever on the union's list of priorities.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this resolution and i would like to reiterate that eu-us cooperation in the fight against terrorism, as well as the conclusion of a specific eu-us agreement in this regard, is of major importance. this agreement must be kept permanently before parliament. the council and the commission must inform the european legislative body throughout all stages of its negotiation and conclusion. the ep's position on this subject has been expressed on several occasions. another key aspect of the resolution is that any request for data transfer must be approved by a european judicial authority. the transfer of data must be justified and transparent, and citizens must be guaranteed rights such as access, rectification, erasure, compensation and compensation for damage to their privacy. i want to emphasize the need to find a solution to limit the transfer of data, allowing only the exchange of data required for persons suspected of terrorism. it is important that the principles of reciprocity and proportionality in the agreement are respected, as well as that the agreement is terminated immediately in the event of non-compliance with the obligations assumed. i am confident that the jha council will take into account the recommendations contained in this resolution.
in writing. - i am not a hungarian mep to defend the interests of this country and therefore to support mr ader, nor an employee of an ngo. i am a romanian mep and i defend the interests of my country. as such, i have a duty to demand a study on the impact of using this technology before i can demand a ban on cyanide in mining. the initiators of the resolution had a duty to offer an alternative that was economically feasible and less toxic than the one they demanded to be completely banned. following the statement of the european commission representative cecilia malmström two weeks ago and the meeting with representatives of the local community (including mayors of the roşia montană area), i felt that before a complete ban on this technology, a detailed study should be carried out and all existing alternatives analysed. before making a decision, we must consider all the aspects involved: environmental protection, job creation, attracting investment, and the lack of alternatives to mining for the population of the entire area. in conclusion, i voted against this resolution and tabled two amendments because it reflects the view and interests of one party only.
in writing. - i am a signatory to the amendment to delete paragraph 4 of the draft resolution voted today. i therefore voted in favour of this amendment. i voted against the motion for a resolution on a number of grounds: we cannot ask the european commission to ban cyanide-based gold mining technology for some member states, such as romania, which has significant, untapped resources; the rosia montana project deserves support for its economic and social effects and in full agreement with the restrictions on the protection of the environment and archaeological sites. as a member of the european parliament, i support the opportunity of this troubled area and i am convinced that the responsible national government authorities will negotiate a level of royalties capable of ensuring the recovery and protection of the rosia montana goldfield. romania, as a member state, has the right to exploit its deposits under safe environmental conditions, but also with economic and social results in proportion to the natural results it has.
in writing. - there are times when ecological welfare, heritage protection and the welfare of people in general succeed in prevailing even over economic and partisan interests. this resolution proves that. the european parliament has succeeded today in demonstrating that it is primarily concerned with the general interest and the welfare of the people. cyanide mining is a risk we cannot afford to take; its effects are irreversible. i do, however, support the idea of encouraging the industrial conversion of areas where cyanide mining has been banned, through appropriate financial support for clean industrial sectors, renewable energy and tourism.
in writing. − i voted against the resolution on the ban on cyanide-based mining by the end of 2011 for several reasons: stopping ongoing cyanide mining projects would seriously affect both the member states using this technology (finland, sweden, spain, romania, bulgaria, greece) and the member states producing cyanide (belgium, the united kingdom, the czech republic and germany). europe would become 100% dependent on imports of gold, a metal used in europe's precious metals industry, but also in the electronics industry. approximately 87% of the production of cyanide is used in other industrial sectors, outside the mining industry, in the manufacture of vitamins, jewellery, adhesives, electronic components for computers, flame retardants, cosmetics, nylon, paints, medicines, etc. there are technologies in economic activity that are harmful to human health or the environment. cyanide technology is one of them. to prevent negative impact, there are regulations and standards that allow such activities to be carried out safely. this principle also applies to mining technology. there are laws, they must be followed. we don't have the right to ban, we have the right to protect.
in writing. - i voted against this resolution because the 2006 directive, which is in force, provides maximum protection for the environment and human health with regard to the use of cyanides in the mining industry. in view of the strict provisions of the mining waste directive and the absence of viable alternatives, a general ban on the use of cyanide in gold mining is not necessary.
sustainable economic growth also requires massive and coherent investment in the transport sector. the transport sector accounts for 10% of the eu's gross domestic product and represents over 10 million jobs. i therefore invite the european commission and the council to take into account, when finalising the eu 2020 strategy, the following highly relevant aspects in the field of transport: promoting research, development and innovation to achieve so-called green transport; strengthening the european objective of decarbonising transport through the use of alternative resources, electric cars, its, intelligent traffic management, including in the aviation sector; strengthening coordination in the field of infrastructure to strengthen the protection of the environment, the social conditions of workers and the safety and security of passengers. in specific areas, i would like to stress the following imperatives: urgent implementation of the single european sky in aviation; urgent achievement of interoperability in the railway sector; extension and improvement of road infrastructure and safety of european roads in road transport; achievement of convenience in inland ports and extension of motorways of the sea in maritime and inland waterway transport; urgent sustainable development of urban mobility. the european commission needs to take all these mobility issues into account, which must be one of the central elements of the eu 2020 strategy. the coordinated development of the transport sector is the key to sustainable development, the preservation and creation of stable jobs.
over the last two years, we have faced the worst economic crisis in the world. it is therefore vital that our efforts are better targeted to boost competitiveness, productivity and the potential for growth. the objectives of the strategy must be realistic and, for this reason, they must be defined in close correlation with the national objectives of the member states, which are themselves determined according to the priorities and specificities of each member state. i therefore welcome the idea of dividing the objectives set at community level into different national objectives. in a parliament resolution, i asked the commission to put forward new measures such as possible sanctions for member states that do not apply the strategy and incentives for those that do. the eu's funding should therefore be conditional on achieving results and being compatible with the objectives of the strategy, but we should not underestimate the importance of cohesion policy in achieving the eu's economic and development objectives. we must therefore examine the commission's proposals carefully, because a proposal such as the one to automatically suspend structural funds for member states with large budget deficits would be an unrealistic measure and totally at odds with the objectives of cohesion policy, namely to reduce disparities between member states.
today, in the european union, unemployment has reached 10 percent and among young people, 20 percent. this year, 1 may, the international workers' day, was a sad day, because there are 23 million unemployed in the european union. in order to secure jobs, we need to clearly define the areas in which the union must invest. only through education can we provide young people with the skills they need to have a job and a decent life. investment in agriculture will also enable the union to meet its basic needs for food and biofuels. investment in transport infrastructure is vital. this year we are revising the list of ten-t priority projects: the eu needs high-speed rail infrastructure to cover all eu capitals and major european cities, and to modernise its road, port and airport infrastructure. i believe it is a priority for the union to invest in the development of transport infrastructure in eastern europe. only then will we have a truly effective internal market. all these projects require billions of euros of financial resources, which will be returned to public budgets through taxes and, above all, through the jobs created and the economic development they generate. investments in energy infrastructure, energy efficiency and renewable energy will also reduce the eu's energy dependence and generate some 2.7 million new jobs by 2030. however, instead of investing in the smart cities initiative, we find that over €150 million of the european economic recovery plan has gone unspent. last but not least, the european union needs to invest in research and in the sustainable development of european industry. mr president, i would like to conclude by asking the commission and the council to set up an instrument similar to the european globalisation adjustment fund to support civil servants who have lost their jobs as a result of the economic crisis.
i am convinced that europe 2020 will be a stronger europe economically and more innovative. i am convinced that we will emerge from the current economic and financial crisis because we have enormous potential in terms of innovative human workforce and natural resources, and i appreciate the commission's effort in presenting this communication to us. but i cannot help but mention cohesion policy and express my dissatisfaction with the fact that the path towards the lisbon strategy seems to have been changed. achieving economic, social and territorial cohesion involves more than just smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. through us and our elected officials, citizens are saying that they still need investment in infrastructure, access to services and development in all areas, no matter how remote they are. the priorities set for the period 2007-2013 have demonstrated the need to improve infrastructure and support economic competitiveness in the convergence areas. the interdependence of economies requires cohesion and security [...] (the president interrupts)
in writing. it is imperative that both the common agricultural policy and cohesion policy support the european strategy for employment and growth. i believe that the cap must provide immediate responses to the effects of the economic crisis on agricultural enterprises, such as farmers' lack of access to credit, constraints on agricultural incomes and rising unemployment in rural areas; it must continue to provide solutions to the threat of land abandonment, depopulation of rural areas and the ageing of the rural population in the european union, in order to ensure the long-term sustainability of rural communities in the union. i would like to mention that in the light of these challenges, the cap post-2013 must send strong signals and respond to the concerns of both the rural community and society at large through a strong, sustainable, well-funded, credible and multifunctional food policy. i stress the urgent need to attract young generations to rural areas and to provide them with new and alternative economic opportunities to ensure a sustainable rural population and i believe that rural unemployment should be addressed by providing opportunities for diversification and new sources of income.
in writing. i want to thank the commission and the council for their statements on the new european strategy for jobs and growth. i consider that setting up the new energy targets will be a key factor in achieving a more resource efficient europe by 2020. i want to stress to the commission the fact that some member states will need special support in order to be able to develop and implement renewable technologies to achieve the 20% target of energy produced from renewable sources. i emphasise the positive impact of supporting the digital agenda initiatives in the flagship initiatives for new skills and jobs and i would like to see the commission coming forward with concrete legislative proposals to address the development of on-line environment by creating facilities, both financial and administrative, to promote on-line businesses and e-commerce. in terms of research and innovation in europe, i welcome the answer of commissioner quinn regarding the need to improve the research infrastructure in the new member states. research institutes and scientists are waiting for a fast and coordinated action from the commission and council in order to tackle this issue, as to allow them equal chances for participation in framework programmes.
in writing. the escalation of the economic crisis in greece, but also the stabilisation of the unemployment rate at the average level of 10% in the union, make the implementation of the europe 2020 strategy an immediate necessity. the pursuit of the objectives must be based on credible and strengthened action to overcome the crisis, with employment being one of the key points on this agenda. we all agree that to create a more competitive and sustainable economy, the union needs a highly skilled workforce capable of meeting current and future challenges. but statements are not enough to solve the existing problems, which is why i would like to remind you that urgent investment is required in the appropriate skills, but also in education systems, in order to align them with market demands. member states must be proactive, respect the commitments made in the european council and take the necessary measures to encourage the overcoming of the current crisis and economic growth.
in writing. i am a supporter of the europe 2020 strategy for smart (knowledge and innovation-based), green and social inclusive economic growth. i want this strategy to translate into the creation of well-paying jobs and the raising of people's living standards. in order to have a strong and balanced europe, we must pay close attention to the economic development of the regions in the new member states, in order to reduce the existing gaps. of course, building the right infrastructure must be a priority. i would like to emphasise the importance of implementing the flagship initiative 'youth on the move'. we need to increase funding for european programmes aimed at the continuous modernisation of education at all levels, as well as the mobility of teachers, students and researchers. the quality of education in european schools and universities must increase in line with the demands of the labour market. through appropriate policies and funding, we need to encourage language learning, multidisciplinarity, dual specialisations in universities, which are important for performance in scientific research and innovation, as well as for increasing the chances of young people in the labour market. it is also worth noting that strategy 2020 proposes a 'framework for youth employment' at european level.
in writing. the history of the lisbon agenda has shown that good principles and ideas are not enough, the most important step being the implementation of the proposed measures. unfortunately, the economic and financial crisis overlapped with the end of the lisbon agenda. however, i think it would be unfair to blame the crisis for the failure of this programme without trying to see where the european union went wrong in the implementation process. perhaps the lessons learned will serve us well in implementing the future eu 2020 strategy. i believe that we have important community instruments for putting the new strategy into practice, and i am referring in particular to cohesion policy. it should be stressed, however, that we cannot abandon the objectives of cohesion policy in order to reallocate funds to achieve the eu 2020 strategy. it would be a mistake with serious consequences for the member states which need these funds to overcome the development gaps which separate them from the other countries, it would mean the failure of the principle of cohesion at european level.
in writing. reducing the eu poverty level by at least 25% by 2020 is closely linked to raising the employment rate to 75%. a quantitative poverty reduction target is problematic. poverty includes economic, social, cultural and educational aspects, and qualitative rather than quantitative targets are needed to achieve the proposed objective. in romania, official data presented in march 2010 indicate an employment rate well below the minimum level set by the eu 2020 strategy (50% compared to 75%) and the downward trend continues, due to the current economic context. women, people over 45 and young people continue to have the greatest difficulties in finding employment. it's hard to believe that romania will be able to reach this target by 2020. we need to find answers to questions about the contribution of the full potential of work and knowledge of groups in society, women and men, young people, older people and migrants to the labour market, reducing youth unemployment or how to effectively increase women's participation in the labour market by diversifying their participation in all sectors of activity. without a clear answer to these questions, the twin goals of increasing employment and reducing poverty will end up in the same place as the lisbon agenda.
in writing. i am convinced that we must dream big, that the europe 2020 document must cover all areas of community cooperation and become a medium- and long-term european strategy. but the solidarity of european citizens is essential to its success. the new strategy is being drawn up with the contribution of the 27 member states of the enlarged european union, as defined by the treaty of lisbon, so that our citizens can feel that the common european effort is theirs. the hungarian electorate in romania expects the european union to find a solution to the rapid catch-up of the south and central-eastern european region as an expression of community solidarity. the strategy must address the long-term development of our countries, the internal market, agriculture and the development of smes, but also sensitive issues such as the social network, demographic challenges, equal opportunities in the labour market, interconnected european systems and networks in all areas of life. the europe 2020 strategy should be a strategy of catch-up and convergence.
i am pleased that by joining the most fundamental european human rights instrument, the union is taking another step towards a truly united europe and is reaffirming its credibility in addressing human rights problems in third countries. but let us not forget that in many respects the council of europe is ahead of the union in the protection of human rights. i therefore ask the commission to examine the possibility of acceding to other council of europe conventions and to draw up an inventory of international treaties concluded within the framework of the eec, which, by acceding to them, can further improve the quality of the human rights legislation in eu law. i am convinced that if europe is to become a true area of freedom, security and justice, it must also cooperate with the council of europe and adopt its existing human rights acquis. among these achievements, the european charter for regional or minority languages and the framework convention for the protection of national minorities should be highlighted, which set out the minimum requirements for responding to the problems of indigenous national minorities in the spirit of european integration, respect for diversity and the rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights. the member states of the european union are all members of the council of europe, and most of them have signed and ratified the said documents. it would be natural for such an extension of eu law to take place by means of such conventions, which have already been drawn up and widely accepted.
the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon ensures the accession of the european union to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. the court of justice in strasbourg will thus ensure that fundamental rights and freedoms are protected against the actions of the union. this is all the more important as member states have transferred important competences to the european union. i would stress that accession will not affect the principle of the autonomy of union law, as the court of justice in luxembourg will remain the sole supreme court for all matters relating to eu law. romania signed the convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in 1993. it is important to note that article 20 of the romanian constitution establishes that international regulations on fundamental human rights, to which romania is a party, take precedence over domestic laws.
in writing. as rapporteur for afet on the union's accession to the european convention on human rights, i have asked myself, as have other colleagues, what is new about such a decision. the answer, in my view, is that accession creates additional external control of compliance with rights at union level. in this way, the european public order, based, as we know, on human rights, democracy and the rule of law, is being consolidated. finally, accession means more credibility for the union in its external relations. on the other hand, we must be aware that there are a number of questions that need to be answered: what is the scope of accession? just the convention or the additional protocols? what will be the modalities of the union's representation in the convention bodies? what role will parliament play in the appointment of the union judge to the ecthr? i'm sure they'll all be answered soon.
road transport is responsible for 28% of pollutant emissions from non-ets sectors. under existing legislation, car manufacturers must produce only vehicles with emissions below 120g co2/km by 2020 at the latest. in addition, car manufacturers can offer customers discounts if they replace their older, less environmentally friendly vehicle with one that emits less pollutants. as a result, in the european union, there was a 7% increase in demand for hybrid or electric vehicles in 2009. these vehicles are specifically dedicated to urban mobility. the widespread use of electric or hybrid vehicles depends on the coverage of the infrastructure for their supply. in this regard, the standardisation of electric vehicles becomes crucial.
in writing. in the context of climate change, green vehicles are an effective way to reduce carbon emissions. their development must, however, be included in a future sustainable mobility policy. romania wishes to introduce electric cars gradually on the domestic market. in this regard, prime minister emil boc recently decided to set up an interministerial group to develop a national strategy for the manufacture of electric cars. countries such as denmark and israel are installing and testing charging stations that will be officially launched at the end of 2011. the governments of france, spain, and ireland also provide subsidies for the purchase of such vehicles. at this point, the cost of an electric car is high, and it's determined primarily by the cost of the battery. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's energy policy and its implementation in the member states. in this context, the commission should provide financial support to the member states. the benefits of 'green cars' are significant: they help to combat climate change, reduce europe's dependence on oil and contribute to the europe 2020 goals. that's why i think we need to encourage the use of electric cars.
in writing. the use of electric vehicles offers a number of major advantages for sustainable mobility. we can talk about reducing carbon dioxide emissions and improving air quality, reducing our dependence on imported fossil fuels and increasing the efficiency of electric cars compared to other transport technologies. globally, eu competitors are investing in research and development of new low-carbon technologies and launching programmes to shift to green road transport. to enable european industry to remain globally competitive and to ensure that it plays a leading role in green technologies, the european union needs to create an appropriate framework for promoting innovative technologies, encouraging research and developing the infrastructure needed to support the transition to a resource-efficient and low-carbon economy. i support the european commission's efforts in this regard and welcome the publication of the plan to promote the establishment of a european network of fast charging stations for electric cars and the establishment of common technical and safety standards for them by 2011.
in writing. the transition to a sustainable and energy-efficient transport system has become a priority for the eu in the context of climate change and volatile fuel prices. the development of electric vehicles at european level as a replacement for conventional vehicles is a viable solution with high market potential. to this end, member states need to coordinate so that a decision can be taken for european standardisation, for example, at the level of energy charging and storage systems, including smart grids and on-board integrated measurement and interoperability systems. the eu must also give more support to research and innovation, particularly in improving battery and motor technology, but also in incentives for the production of electric vehicles. i call on the european commission to take concrete action to anticipate changes in the automotive sector and supply chain and to support the coordination of national policies in this area. it is time for the eu to increase the competitiveness of the mobility industry by reducing development costs for manufacturers and by gradually reducing co2 emissions from road transport.
in writing. – i welcome the commission’s recent strategy on clean and energy-efficient vehicles, and especially the new focus on electric cars instead of biofuels as part of the shift to greener transport. however, just as biofuels are controversial and not without problems, there are significant challenges with electric cars which must be overcome before they become a realistic option for european citizens, and before they deliver real environmental benefits. the additional demand for electric power for transport must be met by low-carbon sources if these cars are to realise their full environmental potential. i am concerned that the eu’s development of these sources will not be sufficient to match the demand which will arise from increased use of electric transport. this needs to be considered as part of the eu’s energy strategy as we move towards a low-carbon economy and reduced dependence on oil supplies from third countries. a network of standardised charging points must also be put in place, and i encourage the commission and member states to work towards this standardised infrastructure to make electric cars viable for consumers and car manufacturers alike. if these key challenges can be overcome, we can look forward to low-carbon, low-pollutant transport and all the associated benefits to the environment and human health.
i have proposed a resolution to ban the use of cyanide in mining, because we have an obligation to take all safety precautions to protect people and the environment from environmental catastrophes. if we are making historic commitments to reduce emissions, if we are setting the tone for the world on environmental protection, why not make a basic clean-up gesture and eliminate this harmful practice from the european union? the baia mare accident in romania 10 years ago is considered a chernobyl of sorts, hitting three countries and destroying the ecosystems of affected rivers for hundreds of kilometers. now, in romania, at rosia montana, a new cyanide mine is being built. that's why today, more than ever, i thank you for voting no to cyanide in mining. the european union must help the regions affected to develop sustainably and to reach their full potential.
the very difficult situation in greece, and the very worrying information about other eu countries having serious problems, shows us that the economic crisis is not over and that, despite some progress in the older eu countries, there is still a risk of major imbalances. unfortunately, when some countries face declining budget revenues, the immediate temptation is to raise taxes and fees. this is about to happen in romania, where the government is currently discussing the increase of the single rate and vat. it is wrong to think that a sudden increase in taxes and fees will bring more money to the budget, and in the medium and long term the effects of such measures on the economy are very harmful. unfortunately, the european union is having difficulty developing a common strategy against the economic crisis. but i think that there needs to be better communication and cooperation between countries that have overcome the crisis with proactive, incentive measures, not by raising taxes, and countries with big problems, which are on the verge of, as a desperate measure, raising taxes and taxes, and risking to sink deeper into the crisis.
