deputising for the author. − mr president, the committee on economic and monetary affairs has put forward this question because it has followed with interest the review procedure of the motor vehicle block exemption regulation, and some careful thinking has to be done. as you know, block exemption regulations are very important instruments to the business community. this regulation was adopted in 2002. at that time the commission considered that there was an oligopolistic situation in the european car market, the six largest manufacturers in europe having together a market share of 75%. against this background, the commission considers that the motor vehicle sector should not be brought within the general vertical block exemption regulation, and therefore adopted a specific regulation. this regulation will expire on 31 may 2010. the commission now considers that the markets for new vehicles sales are highly competitive and that concentration levels have been declining. as a consequence of this assessment, the commission proposes that a specific block exemption is no longer needed for the sale of new cars and commercial vehicles. it proposes to adopt a special block exemption regulation only for repair and maintenance services, as well as for the spare-parts distribution. parliament is concerned about this reform. as you know, the eu is currently facing an exceptional financial and economic crisis, and unemployment rates are high. the european automotive industry is a key sector of the european economy, contributing to employment, innovation and the competitiveness of the whole economy. we believe that it is necessary to establish general conditions to make this sector sustainable and enable it to remain economically efficient and green. there is also a need to ensure that the small and medium-sized players in this market enjoy favourable conditions. we cannot forget the importance of smes as job providers and as suppliers of proximity. however, several motor vehicle dealers and repair businesses have expressed serious concerns about the new regulatory framework, arguing that it will lead to a further deterioration of the power balance between manufacturers and the rest of the automotive value chain. therefore, commissioner almunia, the committee on economic and monetary affairs would like to ask you, firstly: which results of market analysis led the commission to conclude that the primary market is currently competitive and the after-sales market is still problematic? secondly, how does the commission evaluate the balance of power between car manufacturers and car dealers under the current motor vehicle block exemption regulation, and under the proposed legislative framework? are there players with a simple or collective dominant position? thirdly, how does the commission intend to monitor the evolution of market power in the primary and after-sales markets? which measure does the commission envisage, should it appear that the competitive conditions, in particular in the primary market, have significantly worsened? fourthly, what is the expected impact of the new legislative framework on consumers, in particular as regards prices and conditions offered? fifthly, which comments received from stakeholders, namely during the consultation, does the commission intend to incorporate in the final legislative framework? finally, does the commission agree to consider proposing harmonising legislation in the area of distribution, for instance by amending the commercial agency directive, in order to ensure that all dealers benefit from the same high level of contractual protection in every eu member state?
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, the current motor vehicle block exemption regulation expires on 1 june this year, and we need to adopt a new regulation before that date. the college of commissioners has placed this issue on the agenda of our meeting of 26 may. the proposal that is now being discussed within our services and, in a few days, with our cabinets – preparing the collegial discussions – is the result of an in-depth analysis of the sector. the public consultation process started in june 2006. three and a half years later, in december last year, the commission published the draft block exemption and guidelines. throughout this process, stakeholders, the european parliament and the member states have all been closely involved, and a lot of arguments have been taken into consideration. a number of debates, workshops and initiatives have also taken place, including here in parliament. the latest took place on 12 april this year at the econ committee. what are the main conclusions of this long consultation process? first, we learned something positive: that consumers in europe enjoy vigorous competition in the car sales market. in our annual car price reports we have been reporting on 80 car models from around 25 manufacturers – and prices are not the only factor which tells us that competition is healthy. there is also more choice than there was 10 years ago, with more brands available for each type of car. in these circumstances it would be difficult to suggest that any carmaker would be able to exercise a dominant position, be it individually or collectively. the current regimes contain sector-specific rules that made sense at that time (in 2002) when a wave of consolidation was expected in the vehicle sector. this consolidation period did not materialise, and instead what we have today is a very competitive market. by allowing more flexibility for the distribution of vehicles, the proposed changes will restore manufacturers’ incentives to reduce the cost of selling cars. allow me to recall that distribution costs make up, on average, 30% of the price of a new car. by reducing those costs, manufacturers will improve their competitive position, with resulting benefits for consumers. i am perfectly aware that there are some concerns about proposed changes relating to multi-brand sales and contractual protection for dealers, and both of you have mentioned these concerns. let me stress that multi-branding exists – and will continue to exist – where market reality calls for it. this is the case in countries with very large dealers that have the capacity to distribute several brands – for example in the uk – and it is also the case in sparsely-populated areas, where it makes economic sense for the dealers to sell different brands from the same site. this was the reality before the current block exemption was adopted in 2002, and it remains the reality eight years later, but then, as now, single branding was the most common distribution model. what we have observed is that carmakers have increasingly resorted to other forms of distribution, including manufacturer-owned outlets. the evolution of distribution in germany, for instance, is symptomatic of this trend, with 67% of cars sold through dealer networks, as opposed to 90% before the regulation came into effect in 2002. nonetheless, we have responded to concerns expressed during the consultations, including the consultations that took place here in the parliament, and a number of safeguards have been introduced with regard to multi-brand dealerships. let me also underline that we propose a transitional phase, during which the current regulation will be in force until the end of 2013 for the car distribution market, to allow sufficient time for dealers who invested in multi-branding to amortise their investments. concerning the reason why we are proposing to do away with clauses granting contractual protection to dealers, it is simply because competition law is not the appropriate instrument to address eventual imbalances between contractual parties. these issues, as was discussed when we were preparing regulation (ec) no 1/2003, belong to the sphere of commercial law. in a competitive market such as the car market, competition law should not interfere with the balance of powers between the different contracting parties. to do so would be intrusive. we have to be proportionate when we interfere in how markets work. in the process of consultation we also learned some other, maybe less positive things: unlike car prices, the cost of the average repair job has actually risen over the past years. repair and maintenance is very important for consumers: not only for reasons of safety and reliability, but also because repair bills account for 40% of the total cost of owning a car. unfortunately, the ability of independent garages to compete with authorised repairers is still impaired by a number of restrictions, including limited access to spare parts and to technical information. therefore, our reform intends to allow independent garages better access to spare parts and technical information and to prevent them from being shut out of the market by other, newer practices. this will result in better-quality repair services and lower prices. to conclude, i strongly believe the new framework will be more favourable to consumers. our main priority is to increase competition in the after-sales market – in repairs and servicing – where it is most lacking. although vehicle manufacturers may be in a strong commercial position vis-à-vis dealers, they compete fiercely with each other, and today there is no need to deviate, to preserve competition on these kind of agreements, from the block exemption regulation for vertical agreements, which was adopted recently by the commission and will also come into force at the end of this month. indeed, the commission, and in particular my services, dg competition, will monitor the sector very carefully, and there should be no doubt about the commission’s determination to enforce competition rules and take necessary steps if any serious breaches or shortcomings are identified.
on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, the purchase and maintenance of a car is considered to be one of the most important costs for households. the very aim of competition policy is to ensure consumers’ freedom of choice and access to products at lower and more affordable prices. as a member of this house, and consequently a representative of eu citizens who are also consumers in the car market, i am deeply concerned about the review of the motor vehicle block exemption regulation and its impact on consumers. the commission – and i listened very carefully and attentively to the arguments from the commissioner – argues that this sector’s specific regulation is no longer needed for the sales market, since there is evidence that the competition objectives have been achieved and a proper level of competition has been reached. in principle i would not be against the removal of the specific sector block exemption if there were no risk for consumers. we should use the three-year transitional period to assess the impact of the decision to exclude sales from the motor vehicle block exemption regulation. there is an undeniable phenomenon of predominance of large car manufacturers. i would like to hear the views of the commission on the ways to ensure that they will not take advantage of their market share, and limit the choice that consumers should have on their market. i would also like to express my support for the proposal to maintain the specific block exemption for repair and maintenance, which proved to be less competitive than the sales market. my concern regarding the after-market is particularly related to those cases where consumers are unnecessarily tied to a specific operator for repairing their car. this can either be because independent repairers do not have proper access to the necessary technical information or because car manufacturers interpret warranty terms in an abusive way. this is an unacceptable limitation of the choice consumers ought to have, and i expect the commission to bring solutions to change this type of situation. i therefore invite the commission to bring some clarification concerning the measures it intends to take in order to avoid this situation, which is detrimental to consumers.
the european union's motor vehicle sector, including both vehicle manufacturers and vehicle parts manufacturers, needs to remain economically efficient and innovative. given that road safety is influenced by the competitive conditions on the spare parts market in the vehicle sector, we call on the commission to promote effective competition on the spare parts market so that prices for all types of spare parts are accessible. buyers should be able to purchase a vehicle at competitive prices and to choose the supplier for repair and maintenance services, regardless of the supplier's chosen distribution system. the future legislative framework should guarantee that smes in the automotive supply chain can benefit from favourable conditions and that their dependence on large manufacturers will not increase. the new provisions of the regulations, on the exemption of categories in the vehicle sector, should also be extended to include the definition of end-user to take account of leasing.
in writing. buying a car is often the most important expenditure of households in the european union, after buying a home. the commission is proposing to repeal the existing exemption in the motor vehicle sector and introduce general competition rules through the motor vehicle block exemption regulation. i consider that the removal of certain clauses of the current regulation in this field, in particular those relating to the freedom of up to 70% for intermediaries selling cars to sell several brands of cars, risks increasing the dependence of intermediaries on manufacturers, restricting competition and limiting consumer choice on the european car market. we are in a situation where a considerable number of automotive intermediaries, and in particular the more vulnerable smes in the sector, could disappear from the european market, thus weakening the entire european automotive industry. i therefore ask the commission to assess the consequences of its proposals, taking into account the structure of the european automotive sector, in which small and medium-sized enterprises play a fundamental role, and to present, if necessary, a new regulation at the end of the three-year extension of the current regulation.

president of the european investment bank. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i should like to thank you for the honour of inviting me to speak in plenary. it is a continuation of a tradition that was inaugurated a few years ago. i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr deutsch, for the high quality of his report. i particularly appreciated that mr deutsch, as well as other members of the committee, mr berman, mr kalfin, took the trouble to come to the premises of the european investment bank to ask very specific questions. i welcome this excellent cooperation with parliament. in reality, the european investment bank is the only international financial institution that is voluntarily accountable to a parliamentary institution. i think this is an excellent thing: the strengthening of the dialogue with the european parliament is, in my view, absolutely essential if we are to be able to fulfil our role, our specific mission, which is to be a bank - but not just an ordinary bank - at the service of the policies of the european union. as mr deutsch has already said, this is what we have tried to do in response to the crisis. as early as september 2008, after the lehman brothers bankruptcy, the ecofin council asked us to increase the volume of our lending to the real economy. we have responded to this council injunction and i think we can say that we have indeed fulfilled our commitments, since in 2009 our lending volume increased from 58 billion to 79 billion, an increase of 37% in the volume of our lending in the european union. this increase was mainly in the three areas which the council and parliament had indicated to us as being of priority. the first area was to make a special effort for the countries and regions that were hardest hit by the crisis. this increase is largely due to the so-called convergence regions and in particular to some countries that were experiencing particular difficulties in 2009. we have never lent so much to countries like hungary, lithuania, romania. this is also why we are making a special effort this year for greece: i was in athens last week and we agreed with the greek government that we would substantially increase the volume of our loans to greece as a sign of support and contribution to the overall effort to revive the greek economy. the second priority was to support small and mediumsized enterprises: we increased our lending to banks so that they could continue lending to small and mediumsized enterprises, with a new product that allows us to have better control over the actual use of the funds we lend. that's over 12 billion we lent to banks last year for small and medium-sized businesses. the third area we were asked to focus on is the fight against climate change. last year we spent almost 17 billion on projects that directly contribute to reducing the volume of greenhouse gas emissions. i think i can say that in 2009 we did what was expected of us, namely to make our contribution to the european economic recovery plan. we must of course continue along this path and i would like to mention very briefly the three major challenges that lie ahead of us in the months and years to come. the first is, of course, - and your rapporteur rightly emphasized this - to continue to be among the priorities of the european union. this means that we, as the eib, must contribute to the implementation of the europe 2020 strategy. you know that the commission has launched this new strategy, which is currently being discussed with the council and parliament. the eib is ready to contribute, in particular through innovative financial instruments, which would increase the leverage effect of certain funds in the european budget. we therefore want to set up joint instruments between the commission and the bank. the second major challenge we face is the renewal of the eib's external mandates. we shall have the opportunity to discuss this with parliament. the commission has just put forward a proposal which is entirely in line with the report of a committee of experts chaired by mr camdessus. the essential element of this proposal is to make the system even more efficient. you know that we have a guarantee from the european union for operations which are part of its external mandates. the commission proposes to simplify and harmonize our external mandates. the commission also proposes that the 2 billion which were set aside be allocated to projects contributing to the fight against climate change. this brings me to the third challenge i wanted to highlight: the need for the european investment bank, together with other institutions, to make its contribution, in particular, to meeting the commitment made by the european union in copenhagen. you know that the european union has made important commitments to support what is called fast track financing. in this context, we believe that the eib, which has developed undeniable expertise in these matters, can make an important contribution. that is why we have proposed that, together with other national financial institutions, a network be set up, a european platform, which could coordinate and thus make project financing in developing countries more efficient. the french development agency and the german kfw have already expressed interest in this initiative and i hope that in the coming weeks we will be able, together with the commission, to contribute to the development of this instrument. these are the three important challenges for the coming months and years to which i would like to draw your attention.

in writing. − switching to smart metering can reduce energy consumption by up to 10% at european level because it would allow for the bidirectional transfer of information between network operators, energy suppliers and consumers. analyses show that the intelligent use of ict can reduce energy consumption in buildings, which currently accounts for 40% of total energy consumption in europe, by up to 17%. all of these figures translate into reducing carbon emissions from transportation alone by up to 27 percent. all of these forecasts only encourage us to make the most of modern technology. even if they cannot be implemented at unitary level in the european union in the short term, it is important that all member states are aware of the alternative to using modern technologies to reduce carbon emissions, which is set with very ambitious targets in the europe 2020 agenda. the construction and transport industries are among the major energy consumers that can hasten the implementation of modern technological systems. similarly, the exploitation of natural resources can be made less environmentally aggressive and carbon-intensive with the help of new technologies.
in writing. − at the level of each member state, information and telecommunications technologies (ict) are ways of increasing energy efficiency, and provide new applications and technologies for improving the exploitation of natural resources, transforming production and industrial processes into an eco-efficient economy. ict-based systems can reduce energy consumption in buildings - currently accounting for 40% of total energy consumed in europe - by up to 17% and carbon emissions from transport by up to 27%. the ict sectors employ 6.6 million people in the 27 eu member states, boost the innovation capacity of all sectors and contribute more than 40% of overall productivity growth. the european commission and the committee of the regions must urgently develop a 'practical guide for local and regional authorities' on improving energy performance through the innovative use of ict. it will set out how authorities can exploit ict in their climate change plans and describe how cohesion funds can support business partnerships to create innovative ict applications, in order to encourage and support cities, municipalities in using ict to reduce emissions.
in writing. − i was rapporteur for the environment committee’s opinion for this report, and i am acutely aware of the potential for the ict sector to deliver considerable energy savings in the european union, particularly in buildings and the transport sector. but we must also bear in mind the effects of the so-called ‘digital divide’, which can be seen both within and between member states. it perpetuates social and economic inequality and it reduces the capacity of ict to deliver wide-reaching benefits in terms of energy efficiency. the importance of access to high-speed internet for everyone is paramount. member states, with the assistance of the commission, should make more efforts to roll out the necessary infrastructure to ensure that all european citizens and businesses can benefit from the available technologies. this would directly address the inequality and injustice created by the digital divide, and is the only way to ensure that the energy-efficient potential of ict is fully realised.

the reporter. − in 2008, the european union committed itself to reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020 and to having 20% of its energy come from renewable sources. at the european council of 25-26 march 2010, union leaders set a common target of increasing energy efficiency by 20% by 2020. the building sector is responsible for 40% of total energy consumption and 35% of pollutant emissions. improving the energy performance of buildings will have a significant impact on the lives of european citizens. at union level, the average household spends 33% of its income on water, electricity, gas and maintenance, and for very low-income households, this figure can be as high as 54%. investments in energy efficiency improvements will lead to lower energy bills and the creation of 2.7 million jobs in the union by 2030. in november 2008, the commission presented a legislative proposal to reform directive 91/2002 on the energy performance of buildings. in april 2009, the european parliament adopted its position at first reading under the co-decision procedure by a very large majority. subsequently, intense negotiations between parliament and the council took place during the swedish presidency of the council of the european union and political agreement was reached on the technical aspects of the legislative proposal in november 2009. the main achievements of this agreement are: introduction of a separate article and more recitals and provisions on financing issues. the commission is to identify existing financial instruments and fiscal measures and present new proposals by 30 june 2011. these provisions are also supplemented by a commission statement. by 31 december 2020, all new buildings must have a net energy consumption close to zero, and most of the energy must come from renewable sources. for the public sector, this period is two years earlier. for buildings with near net zero energy consumption, member states will define clear targets and action plans including supporting measures. the energy performance of buildings undergoing major renovation or of the renovated parts thereof shall meet minimum energy performance requirements applicable to technical building systems and components that have a significant impact on the energy performance of the building. new provisions on certificates. a minimum set of information, including funding opportunities to be specified in the certificate. provisions on the issuing and display of energy performance certificates. inclusion of the energy performance indicator from the energy performance certificate of the building in the announcements for the sale or lease of the building or part of it. more information and transparency on accreditation and training of experts, information for landlords and tenants. consulting local authorities and supporting them in implementing the recommendations, introducing new provisions for local planners and architects to take into account the energy efficiency of buildings. introduction of intelligent metering systems and active control systems such as automation, control and monitoring systems for energy saving. there will be no common methodology but by 30 june 2011 the commission shall establish a comparative methodological framework for calculating the cost-optimal level and minimum energy performance requirements. the directive will be reviewed by 1 january 2017. the council's common position is based on the agreement concluded in november 2009 between the european parliament and the council and i therefore recommend that it be adopted.
the energy performance of buildings directive will have a direct influence on new types of investment in the construction sector. investments in new technologies aimed at reducing energy consumption will have a significant impact on the national and regional labour market and improve the energy security of the european union. financial instruments are required. european citizens cannot afford to pay for the modernisation of energy systems on their own. the maximum amount that can be allocated to this end from the european regional development fund is not sufficient and must be increased to the highest possible level. the commission should provide complementary support by establishing, by 2014, the energy efficiency fund, which could be co-financed by the european union, the european investment bank and the member states. i encourage the european commission to continue developing the 'smart urban projects' initiative and to analyse the mechanisms in place in the member states with a view to disseminating best practice across the european union and sharing knowledge and technical assistance for the creation of new financial means to improve the energy efficiency of housing.

i congratulate the rapporteur on her work on this report and i fully agree with the need to simplify european public procurement legislation and increase transparency. i am concerned about the high number of public procurement litigation in many member states. for example, in romania, the particularly complex legislative framework leads to procedural errors and the incorrect application of public procurement regulations can be an obstacle to the use of structural funds. that is why we need a simpler and clearer legislative framework to make things easier for both sides. i would like to make one more comment on the problem of the lowest price. i agree that a public procurement contract should not be awarded simply because it has the lowest price and i agree with the rapporteur that the value for money and the economic interest of the tender should be paramount, and not exclusively the price. the revision of the legislation should therefore take this into account and introduce a little more flexibility for contracting authorities. but we must do so with great caution, because if we do not set clear criteria, we will open a real pandora's box, risking generating legal uncertainty and even corruption once again.
the value of the public procurement market at union level represents 16% of the union's gross domestic product. the internal market implies that any european company has access to purchases made in any member state. the services directive ensures that any european undertaking can provide services in any other member state, including by electronic means. the internal market needs to ensure interoperability between e-government systems and therefore also between electronic signature systems and electronic auction systems. i welcome the peppol pilot project on public procurement by electronic means launched by the commission, the decision on the list of accredited certification service providers, and the european plan to establish a european service for the validation of electronic signatures. i would point out that in 2005 member state governments committed themselves to having 50% of european public procurement by 2015 by electronic means. romania has implemented the electronic public procurement system since 2002, which has led to a reduction in public expenditure, greater transparency and increased access of smes to the public procurement market.
in the context of the global economic and financial crisis, my country's government was forced to cut budget salaries, pensions, unemployment benefits and cut subsidies. in view of these particularly tough measures, in order to ensure the correct and efficient spending of public money, public procurement needs to be carried out in the most transparent and timely manner possible. the use of electronic auction systems, which lead to the elimination of corruption and fraud in the public procurement system, should also be encouraged. the existing bureaucratic procedures, the confusing and complicated legal regime and the need to clarify the remedies for the award of procurement contracts have led to the blocking of important contracts. following consultations with the imf, the romanian government amended the public procurement law, which was to enter into force by 1 june.

in writing. − i voted in favour of the establishment of the european asylum support office because, in the case of member states whose national asylum systems are under pressure, the office supports the implementation of solidarity mechanisms designed to promote a better allocation of beneficiaries of international protection from the member states concerned to other member states, while ensuring that asylum systems are not abused. it is welcome that the european asylum support office will coordinate joint actions to assist member states facing specific situations, such as large flows of third-country nationals in need of international protection. it is essential to align both the laws and practices of asylum. the european asylum support office will identify good practices, organise training at european level and improve access to accurate information on countries of origin. i also believe that the activities of the european asylum support office should include the development of guidelines to facilitate a more accurate assessment of asylum applications and the monitoring of compliance with and application of the relevant community legislation.
in writing. − i consider this report to be beneficial for the energy future of the european union, as long as the objectives set are feasible and in line with the financial situation in all member states. the objectives adopted by the council on 14 april 2010 on the need to reduce the major differences between member states in the thermal efficiency of buildings, as well as the proposed target of achieving zero energy consumption in all buildings by 31 december 2020 by gradual steps by member states in 2015 and 2018, are welcome. the commission and the council must, however, take into account that many member states are still facing economic recession and will need financial and logistical support to achieve the proposed targets. the commission should consider in future the development of a financial intervention plan by allocating development funds to support member states which fail to allocate the necessary funds, in particular for rehabilitation works. this measure must be charged to the benefit of the citizen, since it is he who bears part of the costs of rehabilitation.
in writing. − the building sector is responsible for almost half of the co2 emissions not included in the eu emissions trading system and has a high potential to reduce these emissions at negative or low costs. the new energy performance of buildings directive sets out a set of minimum energy performance indicators/requirements for new buildings so that they reach near-zero energy consumption by 2020, with energy coming largely from renewable sources, and the application of these requirements to existing buildings. it is essential to inform citizens about these requirements and to encourage them to introduce smart metering systems (replacing hot water and air conditioning systems with energy efficient alternatives such as reversible heat pumps) when renovating buildings. partial funding from the union budget will be provided to stimulate energy efficiency-related measures. member states shall take appropriate measures to implement this directive swiftly. i voted for this report because the new legislation will help consumers to reduce their energy bills and thus enable the eu to achieve its target of reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020.
in writing. − the pressure of migration flows is increasing and there are a number of target countries for migration whose concern about this phenomenon must be understood. this is why it is important to have a resettlement programme that would allow for a fair sharing of responsibility for meeting international obligations to protect refugees, and to ease the burden on countries that are burdened by the large number of refugees they host. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the eu asylum acquis, in particular the implementation of the european asylum support office, which is a key instrument for the implementation of the eu asylum acquis. regardless of the country of resettlement, the most important thing is to provide refugees with immediate access to language and culture classes, as well as other spiritual facilities and, if necessary, psychological counseling. i believe that sustainability should be the main quality of such a programme, which is given a longer-term budgetary perspective by this decision. the beneficiaries are already traumatized by the break with the culture and traditions of their country of origin. they must build a new identity, a traumatic process that must not be accentuated by the precariousness and uncertainty of their future.
in writing. − corporate governance is an area which, although it has benefited from constant regulation, is raising new concerns, especially in the context of the current crisis. so, the accountability of managers and not just, i mean administrators, is absolutely necessary in the context of our aim to reduce systemic risk. in the case of corporations operating in strategic branches or having a large turnover or significant market share, the financial problems that such a corporation may have obviously go beyond the mere interest of the shareholders, entering the area known to 'interested parties', i.e. creditors, employees, consumers, the industry concerned or the state. in this context, the amendment of the undersigned concerning the accountability of the members of the board of directors of these corporations by requiring a fraction of its members to be professionals is in support of the reduction of systemic risks because, at present, the mere status of shareholder representative is no longer satisfactory as long as, as we have shown, the interest in the financial health and stability of certain corporations exceeds the strictly investment interest in the form of participation in the share capital. in order to encourage the social involvement of the shareholders of these corporations, which are often passive when the proportion of capital held is too small, electronic voting should also be regulated.
in writing. − the global economic crisis is just one of the factors contributing to changes in the behaviour and living conditions of young europeans, which should be a wake-up call for the member states and the union as a whole. for some time now, europe has been experiencing a demographic decline with dramatic consequences for its economies and social solidarity systems. it is worrying that young people are getting married later and having fewer children at an older age. at the same time, they are not provided with sufficient conditions for developing their skills and actively participating in society. education, employment, social inclusion and health are major concerns of younger generations, but also challenges for member states. that is why i voted in favour of the draft report drawn up by my colleague, mr papanikolaou. i am convinced that the amendments i have proposed will make a significant contribution to policy-making for young people, by ensuring their independence in decision-making, supporting their private initiatives, equal access to education for disadvantaged young people and, subsequently, their integration into the labour market. i believe that partnership with the media to promote european programmes and projects for young people is an essential element in achieving our objectives.
in writing. − educating young people is a crucial task because if mistakes are made, and they are not corrected in time, they tend to have generational consequences and are liable to be repeated, thus bringing about further degradation. the trouble with our ‘strategies’ is that, once elaborated, we become obsessed with implementation, thus neglecting the need to revisit and adjust them regularly. the current ‘strategy on youth’, essentially elaborated before the current crisis, is already facing a number of challenges: how to protect the young from the negative psychological impact of the current crisis; how to prepare them for tomorrow’s world, not today’s; how to ensure equal opportunity to education irrespective of income; how to separate ‘mobility’ from ‘brain drain’; and how to balance ‘virtual bonding’ through the net with actual bonding and team spirit through collective action. these are ‘strategic’ challenges, which need ‘strategic’ attention from decision makers in all eu countries.
in writing. - the 96 million young europeans aged 15-29 represent about 20% of the union's population. due to the economic crisis, the youth unemployment rate reached 20% at the beginning of the year, and the drop-out rate was 17%, mainly affecting young people in rural areas. young people are also increasingly exposed to temporary employment contracts, reducing their chances of financial stability and home ownership. young people are the future and we should involve them more in european decision-making. they are the ones who should be designing and acting, alongside us, for the development of the society in which we live. i call on the commission and the member states to adopt urgently a strategy and concrete measures for better involvement of young people in society. these measures should address non-discriminatory access to education to acquire the skills needed to find work that will ensure a decent living, the provision of affordable childcare services to reconcile family and working life, and support for youth employment and social housing for young people.

in writing. - i voted for this report because i considered that the adoption of the directive is of major importance at european union level, given the period of economic and financial crisis we are going through. given that in most member states, co-working spouses do not benefit from spousal social security, i argued that if a member state requires self-employed persons to join a social security scheme, it should also be mandatory for co-working spouses and life partners. it is regrettable that the council does not accept that the affiliation of spouses and life partners of selfemployed workers to social protection schemes should be compulsory where this status is recognised by national law. since the vast majority do not enroll, the benefits of social security systems that cover sickness, disability, and old age are ignored. as an alternative rapporteur on behalf of the s&d group, i argued that self-employed workers, wives and partners who decide to have children should be entitled to social protection and paid leave and not be cut from childcare allowance as the romanian government is doing.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the european union's financial assistance to ukraine because i believe that we must be united, including in overcoming the current economic crisis. as a neighbouring european country that wants to join the eu in the future, ukraine needs to receive a clear political signal to encourage the authorities to implement the reform measures agreed with the union. it is also important for us europeans to have prosperous neighbours with a stable internal policy in line with european standards and values. in this respect, we hope that the eu loan to this neighbouring country will help the whole of ukrainian society, including the more than half a million romanians in northern bukovina, northern maramureș and southern bessarabia. of course, the european commission must take all measures to ensure that this exceptional financial assistance is used judiciously, where it is needed, to produce the expected effects. the conditions for granting such assistance should be consistent with the major objectives of the eu-ukraine association agenda and the use of the funds should be subject to strict european control, with regular reporting to the european parliament.
in writing. − nobody disputes that ukraine is our “strategic partner” whose situation is of great interest to us. today, ukraine stands at a crossroads economically, given its difficult situation, and politically, with a new government that favours closer relations with russia. helping ukraine by making 500 million euro available is therefore the right decision strategically, which we will support. however, tactically, is there not a discrepancy between the level of financial support – a mere half billion compared to other schemes involving tens of billions in financial support – and the control over ukraine’s economic policy we want to achieve in exchange?! the eu does of course have strict rules that beneficiaries of its financial support have to respect, no matter the sums of money they receive, but sometimes, especially when the level of that support is relatively low, maintaining the same high conditionality reflects a political inflexibility which only diminishes the effectiveness of this instrument, especially at a time when others are much more flexible in their support.

in writing. - farmers have always been the most ardent and consistent supporters of the construction of the european union and they strongly believe that the cap remains a common policy in the true sense of the word. in a globalised world, the european union, with a single market, must act as one to guarantee food security and promote renewable resources, to combat climate change and to intensify research to make the most of the opportunities it offers. any cap budget cuts would cause considerable social and economic disruption and prevent agriculture from meeting future challenges. it is important to understand that farmers' incomes are dependent on direct payments, even if these alone do not ensure a decent standard of living for farmers. the average farm income in the eu, including all direct payments, is only half the average wage in the rest of the economy. i believe that reducing direct payments under the first pillar would have devastating consequences not only for farmers but equally for rural areas, for public services linked to agricultural production, for consumers and for the beneficiary society as a whole. direct payments are therefore essential and must be maintained.

in writing. − public procurement accounts for a significant share of the eu's gross domestic product. their goal is to purchase goods and services at the best value for money. european procurement directives slow down the award of contracts, make it more expensive and restrict the freedom of action of contracting authorities. unfortunately, more and more member states have been faced with such problems. that is why i voted in favour of the report, because i strongly support simplifying and modernising procedures. simplified and uniform legislation for all member states is needed. in this way we will eliminate the discrepancies between the rules applied by the member states, eliminate errors and make efficient use of public money.
in writing. − the european union is the world's largest aid donor, and this year development assistance to non-eu countries is expected to reach €69 billion, 20% more than in 2008. the european union has demonstrated that it is consistent with its commitments to international institutions. the clash between european development policies and its trade policies is a reality. however, the european union has committed itself to ensuring that all community policies with an impact on developing countries take account of the development objectives it has set itself. contrary to initial forecasts, the economic crisis is particularly affecting poor countries, many of which rely on development projects funded by the eu. on the other hand, the export and agricultural policies that the eu implements in these countries have a negative effect on their development. we are therefore dealing with an unintended effect: the eu builds at the macro level and has a negative impact at the micro level. in these circumstances, the objectives set out in the resolution voted yesterday by the european parliament in plenary are becoming very important and must be taken up by all the institutions of the union.
in writing. − the european commission's concern about the lack of a uniform system for regulating road fines in the member states is legitimate. applying similar sanctions, at least at the non-financial level, to all drivers in the member states would reduce the confusion experienced by many of the transport companies or individual drivers due to legislative differences between the home country and a third eu member state in which they travel. on the other hand, the european commission and the parliamentary committees are right when they say that it is too early to think about the uniform financial sanctions for traffic offences. the european union has significant disparities in the economic situation of firms and the population, and fines for the same traffic offence may not be the same in all member states. however, the standardisation of rules for passenger transport would lead to greater accountability for transport companies. harmonizing the rules across all member states and enforcing them firmly, without leaving the latitude to each member state to take up and break european recommendations, would also lead to greater safety on europe's roads.

acting president of the council. - madam president, as mr jáuregui said, the debate we are going to have next - together with the one we have just had in this house - is of extraordinary importance and i believe that it represents that historic step in humanity when the defence of human rights is not just a matter for the states - the traditional political agent, the traditional political subject of recent centuries - but becomes something that, in terms of defending humanity, goes beyond the borders of states and establishes a series of mechanisms and institutional guarantees for a better defence of its universal values. the european convention on human rights, which is probably one of the greatest treasures europe has, and the international criminal court, which extends beyond europe, are examples of the progress that is being made in our time towards the globalisation of human rights and the globalisation of the defence of human rights. as regards the european convention on human rights, i would just like to add to mr jáuregui's speech and to his excellent report - drawn up with the rapporteurs cristian dan preda and kinga gál - on this issue, the signing by the european union of the european convention on human rights. i would like to repeat many of the things that mr jauregui has said, and to stress that this accession is indeed an element of european integration - and therefore a strengthening of the european union - which will also join the great novelty of the lisbon treaty, which is the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which will work together, and that is one of the tasks - even technical, not just political but technical - of the strasbourg court and the luxembourg court, without any of the two being deprived of a millimetre of competence. and in addition, in this initiative which is provided for in the lisbon treaty, we also have an increase in the credibility of the european union in defending human rights, since we ask the countries, not of the european union, but of europe, to contribute to the strengthening of the european convention on human rights. in other words, they must ensure that the rights set out in that convention are respected and protected, and in this way the european union as such, and not just its individual members, will also be subject to the jurisdiction of the strasbourg court, and that increases our credibility, as mr jauregui's report very rightly points out. with regard to the international criminal court, i believe that we are at a moment which we can also describe as 'historic' and of very important political significance, because the rome statute review conference is due to meet in a few days' time, which is the only mandatory conference that should meet to review, if necessary, the rome statute and to take stock of this very important development which is an international criminal court. we are therefore also faced with a very important event which is being examined today in the european union in the political and security committee, which will be discussed tomorrow in coreper, and on which we hope that the council resolution will be adopted next week, so that we can join the very positive assessment of the international criminal court already made by other states, such as the latin american states within the unasur organization. we are facing an international criminal court which is in keeping with a commitment to defend human rights and therefore to prosecute crimes against humanity at the universal level, a commitment of the european union, of the member states of the european union. and i would like to remind you that there was a common position in 2003, an action plan in 2004 and an agreement on cooperation with the court by the european union in 2006. and that all the member states of the european union are now parties to the rome statute and are therefore subject to the international criminal court. and this seems to me to be extremely important in order to highlight the role of this international criminal court in the world and the commitment of the european union to its strengthening. an international criminal court which is currently working mainly on the african continent, but the kampala conference is here to tell the african peoples that we are not against africa, but on the contrary, we are with africa. that is why this review conference, which is open to all states, together with civil society and international and regional organisations, is also very important, and will allow us to assess the state of international justice at a time when this international criminal court is being established as the only permanent international criminal court.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, i agree with all the speakers and with all those members who have been working on the subject. the accession of the eu to the european convention on human rights is a step of constitutional importance. it will complete the system of protection of fundamental rights within the union, and you know perfectly well that the lisbon treaty does not make this an option but a destination. i therefore welcome the fact that parliament takes such a great interest in this file – and has from the very beginning, by the way – which is evidenced by the resolution which parliament has put on the table. in particular, i would like to thank the rapporteurs of the committee on constitutional rights and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs for their excellent cooperation on the file. i would like to thank them for the hearing which was organised and which was of real help and great use in bringing this file forward. the draft report presented by mr jáuregui atondo is, to a very large extent, in line with the position of the commission. let me just mention three points which, in my view, are very important. firstly, the commission shares the position that accession by the eu to the additional protocols of the european convention – which, by the way, have not been ratified by all member states – is also very desirable. indeed, many of these protocols are of potential relevance as regards the exercise of the union’s powers, and certain guarantees enshrined in these protocols are also reflected in the charter. the negotiation directives should therefore mandate the commission to negotiate a provision ensuring that the union may accede to any of the additional protocols. the decision then to which protocols we will de facto accede, on top of the convention itself, will have to be taken unanimously by the council after obtaining the consent of parliament. in the commission’s view, such decisions should preferably encompass all additional protocols and should be taken together with the decision concluding the accession agreement itself. secondly, it is important to deal with the specific situation of the union as a distinct legal entity vested with autonomous powers that is going to become a contracting party to a mechanism initially designed for states only. therefore, a number of limited and technical procedural adaptations to the convention are necessary with regard to the specific nature of union law. among those is the so-called ‘co-respondent mechanism’ to take account of the decentralised implementation of union law by member states. by that mechanism, the union will receive the right to join the proceedings as a co-respondent in cases brought against member states when union law is at stake. i am glad to see that parliament’s report also argues in favour of this. thirdly, i fully subscribe to the report which recommends participation by representatives of the union in the bodies of the convention on an equal footing with those of the contracting parties. such participation is indeed a key element in the smooth integration and insertion of the union into the system of the convention. you have understood this now to mean in particular the presence in the strasbourg court of a judge elected from each contracting party. the commission is therefore strongly in favour of having a permanent full-time judge elected for the union, who enjoys the same status and has the same duties as his peers. an ad hoc judge, who would intervene only in cases brought against the union or involving union law, would, in our opinion, not be sufficient. as for the method of electing a union judge, the normal procedure provided for in the convention should apply. this means that the parliamentary assembly of the council will elect a judge from a proposal for three candidates presented by the european union, and i agree with the draft report that an appropriate number of members of parliament should be allowed to participate in sessions of the assembly when it elects the judges of the european court. the procedure for drawing up the list of the three candidates is not a matter for the accession agreement: it is a matter for us. we have to do this by internal legal rules, and the idea that parliament should be involved in a way similar to that provided for by article 255 regarding the selection of candidates for the court of justice is a very interesting one which deserves close examination. honourable members, the spanish presidency attaches very high priority to this dossier, as you know, and the spanish presidency would like to reach an agreement before the end of june. if the council could reach an agreement by then – which i hope it will – this will allow us to then start accession negotiations after summer. as i already said two weeks ago in brussels, i will ensure that the commission – as the union’s negotiator – keeps parliament fully informed throughout the negotiation process. this all relates to european affairs, but we also have the question of international human rights on the agenda. as you know, 138 states took a step forward in 1998 when they adopted the rome statute creating for the first time in history a permanent international court to ensure that perpetrators of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes are brought to account. the court started to operate in 2003 and now, seven years later, we have the review conference in kampala, which invites us to conduct an early analysis of the court’s activities, of the challenges that lie ahead and of the effectiveness of eu support. as regards the activities of the court, we know that the court is fully operational, but is still in its infancy. no judicial cycle has been completed, but the icc is considering the situation in five countries: one trial has started, another trial is going to start on 5 july and one further case is in the pre-trial stage – all for dar and drc. let us not forget that this is only a court of last resort, so the primary responsibility lies with the states themselves. in most cases, the court acts as a catalyst for states to investigate and prosecute cases before national courts. at the same time, in its short life, the court has been a powerful deterrent for future atrocities because perpetrators now know that justice will prevail and, in this sense, the court faces challenges. the ratification by bangladesh brought the number of state parties to the rome statute to 111. however, it is very clear that we have to go for universal acceptance of the statute and of the court. the court needs the participation and the cooperation of all state parties and non-parties, as well as international and regional organisations. the court cannot perform its functions without the states arresting those for whom an arrest warrant has been issued by the icc; nor if the witnesses cannot be protected; nor if there are no prisons for those who have been condemned, and that is why the eu supported the court over the last ten years to help solve these problems. we, as the eu, have from the outset been staunch supporters of the establishment of the court as an essential mechanism in the new international order designed to end impunity which, as you know, has seen millions of people in recent history subjected to crimes but only a handful of those responsible brought to justice. the eu considers that an effective icc is an indispensable instrument for the international community to combat this impunity and to promote a rule-based international order. that is why we have been supporting the court using the various instruments at our disposal that the minister has already mentioned. the common position was translated into an action plan. we were the first organisation to enter into a cooperation and assistance agreement with the court in 2006, and we give the icc full political and diplomatic support with démarches, political dialogues and statements. the inclusion of icc clauses in international agreements is now standard practice for the european union. since 2000, the european initiative – later entitled the european instrument for democracy and human rights – has contributed eur 29 million to support the court directly or indirectly, notably through global civil society campaigns. the eu has also adopted several decisions in the justice, freedom and security area with a view to strengthening cooperation among member states in the investigation and prosecution of rome statute crimes at national level, so we do our best in order to advance the system. the system needs further perfection, but it needs strong engagement by all nations around the globe for this to happen.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on foreign affairs. - i will refer to the report of mr jáuregui atondo. i would first of all like to congratulate him on the preparation of this excellent report which, i believe, deals in an exhaustive manner with both the advantages and the challenges of the european union's accession to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. in the light of the opinion i drafted for the afet committee, i would like to emphasise the main contribution of the union's accession to the echr. it is something that may seem obvious today, in the post-lisbon period, but it is something that has been a periodically reiterated hope for the last thirty years. i consider that accession to the echr will enhance the union's credibility in the human rights dialogue with third countries, confirming once again to all that the union is, above all, a community based on the rule of law. the institutions of the union, like those of the council of europe member states, will thus be subject to the external and independent control of the court of strasbourg, in accordance with the formula 'one human rights standard, one court'. in view of the existence of a single human rights standard, i must stress that accession to the echr is also an opportunity for the union to accede to other treaties in the strasbourg system. i am, of course, referring to the additional protocols, the revised european social charter, which, as we know, complements and deepens this protection at the pan-european level. moreover, i believe that an increased participation of the european authorities in the council of europe bodies specialised in the protection of human rights is the logical consequence of this single standard of protection. as i also stressed in my opinion for afet, a balance must also be struck between preserving the specificity of the european legal order on the one hand and preserving the strasbourg judicial system, which has proved its usefulness for the protection of human rights at pan-european level, on the other.
madam president, i will speak on the union’s accession to the european convention on human rights. i want to underline that i am going to speak as a lawyer. i would like to draw attention to the role of the court of justice in the construction of the european union’s accession to the european convention. in particular the requirement in the european convention on human rights that the applicant must exhaust domestic remedies before applying to the european court of human rights must be transposed into a procedure which would give the court of justice in every case the opportunity to decide as the last domestic remedy before the strasbourg court looks into the matter. i mainly refer to the cases where member states apply eu law and member states are sued by individual applicants following the application of that eu law. the court in luxembourg must first be given the possibility to apply the convention in such cases. let us not forget that the court in luxembourg has been applying the convention for years. in relation to this, i would like to recall the european court of human rights’ finding in the case of bosphorus airlines vs. ireland in 2005. i quote, ‘the protection of fundamental rights by community law can be considered to be equivalent to that of the convention system’. along with my colleagues, i welcome the union’s accession to the convention, but at the same time i ask for a very careful analysis of the procedure we put in place, as we need to protect citizens’ interests and at the same time to preserve what is working well.
in writing. the entry into force of the lisbon treaty creates the legal framework for the european union's accession to the european convention on human rights (echr), with the eu becoming the 48th signatory to the convention. eu accession to the echr will complement the level of protection established by the lisbon treaty through the charter of fundamental rights, which has binding legal force. the european court of human rights in strasbourg will acquire jurisdiction to exercise judicial review over the acts of eu institutions, bodies and agencies, including judgments of the european court of justice, with regard to compliance with the convention, thus creating additional judicial review in the field of fundamental rights within the eu. following accession, the convention will constitute the minimum standard of protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in europe and will be binding in particular in situations where the protection afforded by the eu is inferior to that afforded under the convention. i believe that both the member states and the commission will have to draw up information programmes containing explanations of all the implications and effects of accession so that the citizens of the union are fully aware of the significance of this process.
in writing. the european union's accession to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms is a logical step following the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon and stimulates deeper integration and the building of a common political space. eu accession to the echr will bring more coherence between the union and the countries belonging to the council of europe and its pan-european human rights system. in my view, the most important consequence of accession to the echr is that it will provide citizens with protection against the actions of the union similar to that which they enjoy against the actions of all the member states. this is a substantial development, given that the member states have transferred important competences to the union. it is logical that there should be the possibility of appealing to the european court of human rights against decisions of the union as a whole. since we are talking about european citizenship, it must also be given a concrete content, including this possibility. i hope that this additional tool put at the disposal of european citizens will be easily accessible, especially as the accession decision will contribute to creating a more coherent human rights framework within the european union.
