author. − madam president, mr simpson apologises for not being present during the discussion on the ash cloud crisis. ironically, in view of this evening’s discussion, he has been caught up in the flight restrictions related to the ash cloud restrictions in the uk and therefore has been unable to travel to strasbourg for the discussion. i will therefore be speaking on his behalf this evening. the oral question on the volcanic ash crisis is just as relevant today, in the context of the ongoing disruption to airspace, as it was at the time of the initial eruption of the icelandic volcano last month, when we saw much of eu airspace closed for six days. we are now dealing not only with the aftermath of that disruption and its financial impact but also with the present ongoing uncertainty of continued and prolonged disruption to european airspace. while i believe that some important lessons have been learned and acted on following the unprecedented scale, duration and cause of the initial airspace shutdown, it is clear that the response at european level needs to be stepped up a gear in the face of ongoing disruptions. faced with the challenges that the unprecedented nature and unspecified duration and the disruption is causing to air travel, i am concerned today to get assurances that the mechanisms we have in place for coping with the disruption are working effectively and that, where gaps have been identified over the last few weeks, these are being adequately addressed. i am pleased to say that the air passengers’ rights regulation has proved vitally important in providing a safety net to ensure that it is not the passengers who bear the brunt of the financial consequences of the disruption and who are not left stranded by the chaos. the airspace closure has, however, raised important questions about airlines fulfilling their obligations when it comes to air passengers’ rights, especially in the light of any compensation afforded to the aviation industry. what feedback is the commission getting on the treatment of passengers, and what assurances can it give that airlines are fulfilling their obligations in line with the legislation? furthermore, the current situation has exposed the vulnerability of those passengers booked on third-country airlines for whom the air passengers’ rights legislation does not apply. how does the commission propose to address this gap in the legislation? we also – very early on in this crisis – recognised the heavy financial losses suffered by the aviation industry during the airspace shutdown. my concern with any compensation package made available to the aviation industry is to ensure that compensation is directed at the different sectors of the aviation industry – not just the airlines – and that the compensation measures are of an eu-wide nature. i know that some member states will be more sympathetic than others when it comes to giving financial aid to their airlines. what assurances is the commission able to give that some conditions will be levelled to avoid any distortions in the compensation handed out at member state level and to ensure a level playing field? i now turn to the most pressing concern today, which is over the procedures in place for defining no-flight zones in the eu. the continued disruption to european airspace has once again put the procedures applied for defining no-flight zones under the spotlight. there are concerns that member states are being over-cautious in their implementation of no-flight zones and that aeroplanes are safe to fly amid higher densities of ash than are currently allowed by eu rules. the ongoing closure and opening of airspace by member states over the last few weeks has very much highlighted the need for a more joined-up approach at eu level, rather than the differentiated approach we are currently seeing. i am also aware that the commission has put renewed emphasis on improving data collection and modelling methodologies to give a more detailed picture of the risks involved for aeroplanes flying through an ash cloud. how does the new information we have impact on the restrictions currently in place and the definition of the no-flight zones? finally, we have seen the value of increased european coordination when it comes to responding to the ash cloud crisis. further areas where we have recognised the importance of greater cooperation include the acceleration of the single european sky initiative and the creation of a mobility action plan to help the eu cope better during such crises.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, i would like to provide an update on the evolution of the icelandic volcano crisis, which of course is linked to aviation. the european union has been heavily affected by the consequences of the eyjafjallajökull volcano eruption in iceland. the volcano eruption laid a cloud of volcanic ash over most of europe. volcanic ash contains many problematic substances that are harmful to aircraft and, in particular, their engines. the presence of this safety threat in the sky forced national authorities to take decisions, in accordance with the relevant procedures developed at international level, to close off all affected airspace. the european union immediately mobilised resources to tackle the most pressing problems. taking into account evolutions in the situation and the need for a more differentiated approach to the model and risk management procedures, the commission took the initiative, over the weekend of 17 and 18 april, with the spanish presidency and eurocontrol, to propose a coordinated european approach. as a result of this work, in full cooperation with member states and the industry, new procedures were defined. at the extraordinary meeting of eu transport ministers that took place on 19 april 2010, this new procedure was endorsed, thereby allowing for a gradual reopening of airspace in a coordinated manner as of 08.00 on 20 april 2010. as a follow-up to this immediate action, the commission produced a report addressing the impact of the volcanic ash cloud crisis on the air transport industry. it received broad support from the council of transport ministers at its extraordinary meeting of 4 may 2010. whereas the focus of the report was to address the current volcano crisis, it has nevertheless sought equally to address the european union’s need to be able to deal effectively with similar crisis situations in the future, should they arise. the events of the past 10 days have shown that the situation is far from being resolved at this stage. the volcano continues to be active, and recurrent closures of airspace continue to take place, depending on the weather conditions affecting the dispersion of the ash cloud. the commission is therefore committed to ensuring a prompt follow-up to the transport council conclusions as adopted on 4 may 2010. i am happy to report the first steps taken as a consequence. the european crisis coordination cell has been agreed with effect from 11 may 2010. the final arrangements for setting it up are being made this week. the nomination of a functional airspace blocks coordinator was endorsed by the single sky committee on 7 may 2010. the designation of eurocontrol’s performance review committee as an ses performance review body was also carried out by the single sky committee on 7 may 2010. the european aviation safety agency (easa) has been given the task of defining binding standards for engine ash tolerance levels. the commission will shortly be calling for the creation of a task force to explore how the current european forecasting and dispersion models can be improved so as to enhance associated risk assessment and risk management in such crisis situations. there is more to come as the commission works towards meeting the council of transport ministers’ expectations, as expressed in their conclusions of 4 may 2010.
on behalf of the epp group. the volcanic eruption in april showed that european air traffic is unprepared to respond adequately to unexpected disruptions. there was no coordination, flexibility or maximum use of flight conditions. the ses ii package was adopted in november 2009 in record time, as also mentioned in the commission's information note. the adoption was achieved despite the resistance of the member states. besides, the translation and publication took longer than the negotiation. the crisis came and the utility of implementing the ses ii package was found. my view is that if the member states were to give up their present reticence, we could have a single european sky in a very short time. this means having a direct route network and effective traffic control that does not take into account national borders. unfortunately, this is not yet desirable and the only solution is to implement the ses ii package very quickly. the commission has proposed emergency measures which are already required by the approved regulations. these are very good measures. the main thing is to have the functional aerospace blocks in place by the end of 2012 at the latest. but this requires the guidance provided for in the regulation, which unfortunately is not mentioned in the council conclusions of 4 may. the absence of the guide may be used by member states as a reason for delay. the guide should also be the instrument by which we can achieve, within the required time, not only coordinated traffic areas but a real single european sky. the guide shall provide for traffic control within the blocks, carried out in coordination with neighbouring blocks, so that there are no overlapping areas. otherwise, we will replace the current national borders with block borders and extend the deadline for the implementation of the single european sky unnecessarily. i do not think we need to think in the future that there will be a need for a ses iii regulation to unite the blocs. this approach also allows the implementation of sesar to take place under optimal conditions and at minimum cost. in 2011, the last remaining member states will join the schengen area. it is unacceptable, i think, that we have no borders on the ground, but we maintain them in the sky.
mr president, i would like to make a point on the situation in those member states that are not members of the eurozone but which still share the same preoccupation. political leaders in our countries have been selling the idea that eu membership should be seen as a guarantee against hard economic times, but reality has now proven differently. the euro is constantly attacked from all sides despite all the efforts made, and we all know that fresh money is only a quick fix for a much deeper problem. this is an exceptionally serious situation and we need exceptional answers. let us face it, there is no escape from deeper economic integration and this therefore implies closer political union. because this imbalance leads to daunting divergences between member states, and to ensure financial discipline at european level, we need good governance, sanctions and compliance mechanisms. we need to find ways to encourage investment, attract capital and boldly cut bureaucratic expenses. we need to see intelligent measures taken by governments. in romania, for example, the government is cutting pensions and salaries instead of reducing bureaucratic expenses or money for political clients. we have in romania more employees of secret services than the fbi has but, instead of cutting here, we are cutting doctors and teachers. i strongly encourage the commission to stand by the proposed measures and not to give up under member states’ pressure, because only a few can be seen as examples these days.
the measures proposed by the commission and the council are very welcome. if these measures had been taken some time ago, they could have prevented much of the effects of the crisis we are experiencing. the lack of economic governance has led to decisions being taken under pressure and without consulting the european parliament. furthermore, there are no mechanisms to follow up on the measures taken. last year, large sums were injected into the banks. it was necessary, but the bailout of the banks did not help to alleviate the crisis afterwards. the crisis continued. the stability and growth pact has not been respected. it's reached unauthorized deficits. states have taken different measures in similar situations. some have decided to tell the citizens the truth and take austerity measures. the lack of common rules creates different effects on european citizens, even though all member states have contributed to the crisis. you can't consume more than you produce, you can't spend more than you can collect. financial stability is needed and therefore proposals to create a new financial stability mechanism or a european monetary fund are absolutely necessary. these measures must, however, be matched by a coherent strategy for economic recovery and control and penalty mechanisms. we can thus say that we will achieve real and effective economic governance for the benefit of all member states.
in this time of economic crisis, the europe 2020 strategy seems a real challenge. on the other hand, it's also an opportunity. it can be an important stimulus to support the long-term economic and social reforms needed. the principles that must underlie it are solidarity and adaptability. i believe that the allocations for the cohesion funds should be maintained, as they play a fundamental role in reducing the differences in economic development between the regions of the union. it is also clear that objectives set at european union level cannot automatically become national objectives. they must be adapted to the possibilities of each country. the government of romania has set up a high-level working group that will set national targets and at the same time play a coordinating role in the development of the national reform plan.
we all know that the europe 2020 strategy was launched to help us get out of the current economic crisis and prepare the eu economy for the new decade. it is important, however, that the european union's 2020 strategy does not provide any clear direction for the revision of one of the most important common policies, namely the reform of the common agricultural policy. this is all the more so as the reference to agriculture as a key political instrument for achieving the objectives of the eu 2020 strategy was made only at the last moment, and it is therefore not surprising that agricultural policies are barely mentioned in this document. in this respect, the eu 2020 strategy includes some ideas for the future cap, but fails to give it its key strategic role in a broader, global approach that takes into account the enormous challenges posed by the prospects of doubling global food demand and climate change.
in writing. if there is one lesson worth learning from the current economic crisis, it must be solidarity. the fact that we live in a globalized world, with economies that are interdependent, is not new. however, states have not been able to break out of the logic of isolation, in which solutions to economic challenges are taken at the national level without considering their wider impact. the lisbon strategy was a failure because it lacked the political commitment of the member states to deliver on its objectives. for strategy 2020 to succeed where the lisbon strategy has failed, more effective monitoring of national reform programmes at european level is needed. equally, social inclusion must be the main objective of good economic governance, and state actors must learn to put people first, not economic profit.
in writing. the economic crisis of recent years has contributed to the failure of the eu's objectives set in the early 2000s. it is therefore important to identify the shortcomings of the lisbon agenda, and to focus on the positive results achieved and to avoid the mistakes made in the past. i think it is important now that we can learn from the failure of the lisbon strategy and have the capacity to act to mitigate these effects in the future. i believe we have the great advantage of knowing the causes of failure and being able to avoid them in the new eu 2020 strategy. i'd focus here specifically on strengthening the multilevel governance. we need to involve local and regional authorities and civil society in the governance process because according to eu statistics, local and regional actors have the highest level of trust among citizens. at the same time, strengthening the regional dimension is one of the priorities of the eu 2020 strategy and in this regard i believe that the role of future cohesion policy is to identify and exploit the specific local potential.
in writing. the report captures in precise terms the important contribution that the structural and cohesion funds make to european economic life and to the achievement of the objectives we set ourselves in the eu 2020 agenda. a few ideas are worth highlighting: the key role played by cities in achieving these goals, and the role played by research and education. i also regret that the report does not cover a wider spectrum by including the role played by rural development funds. by boosting rural economic life, modernising european agriculture, helping to establish young farmers and disseminating best practice, rural development funds make an important and welcome contribution to overall economic progress across the european union.
in writing. reducing the eu poverty rate by at least 25% by 2020 is closely linked to increasing the employment rate and is a priority in social inclusion policy. an ambitious long-term anti-poverty strategy is therefore needed, with far-reaching poverty reduction targets, with the 'centre' being on increasing employment and quality jobs, including for women, young people, the elderly and the working poor. this should include measures to reconcile family and working life, enhanced participation in an open labour market, including the lifting of access restrictions for workers from romania and bulgaria. another poverty reduction target is a minimum income of at least 60% of the nationally equalised average income, a minimum wage of at least 60% of the average wage in the nationally relevant sectors, and a coordinated housing strategy in europe. all these measures must be accompanied by a clear timetable that is easy to implement and monitor.

in writing. − the proposal for a directive on the labelling and standard product information of energy and other resource consumption of energy-related products is part of the energy efficiency package tabled by the commission in november 2008, together with two other proposals on the energy performance of buildings and the labelling of tyres with respect to fuel efficiency. i voted in favour because, by the agreement reached between parliament, the council and the commission, we have achieved the introduction of an improved labelling system. the labels will contain more information on the energy consumption of household and energy-impact products and in the future this labelling will also apply to energy-consuming products for industrial and commercial purposes, which was not possible until now. last but not least, in future any advertising that promotes the price or energy efficiency of product categories will also have to indicate the energy class of the products. the provision of accurate, relevant and comparable information on the energy consumption of energy-related products will enable consumers to make informed and efficient choices in the future, thereby reducing both energy consumption and household expenditure.
in writing. − i voted for this report because the amendment of the energy labelling directive, by including all energy-related products, will generate a €4 million reduction in transposition costs for each updated and newly developed implementing measure (if regulations/decisions are used instead of directives) and will result in an additional reduction of approximately 78 mt of co2 emissions. in future, energy-efficiency labelling will also apply to energy-consuming products for industrial and commercial use, such as refrigerated rooms, display cases, industrial cooking facilities, vending machines (sandwiches, snacks, soft drinks, coffee, etc.), industrial engines, energy products, including construction products, which do not consume energy but have a direct or indirect impact on energy savings, such as door and window heels. an important role in the correct application of this directive is to ensure that every citizen has access to accurate information and to raise consumers' awareness of the impact of the choices they make. the provision of accurate, relevant and comparable information on the specific energy consumption of energy-related products will help end-users to make energy-saving decisions with a view to reducing energy bills in the long term.
in writing. − in recent years, the need for organ transplantation has increased steadily and rapidly in the european union. while the shortage of organs remains the main challenge at present, there are many more difficulties linked to the different transplant systems applicable in the member states. as early as 2008, the european parliament, through its resolution adopted in april, called on the european commission to draw up a directive establishing the legal framework for ensuring the quality and safety of organ donation within the european union. the commission has therefore put forward a proposal for a directive, which is being debated in the european parliament and has three objectives: to ensure quality and safety for patients at eu level, to ensure the protection of donors and to facilitate cooperation between member states. i voted in favour of the compromise reached between parliament, the council and the commission because we need common standards of quality and safety for the collection, transport and use of human organs at union level, which would facilitate organ exchanges, thus bringing benefits every year to the thousands of european patients who need this type of treatment.
in writing. − i voted against the resolution, given that thrombin is an additive that cannot be considered a food safety concern. meat containing thrombin could only be sold in a labelled form, bearing the words 'combined cuts of meat' and all ingredients being indicated on the label, as required by law. citizens could thus make an informed choice, so we cannot claim that they were misled. the use of thrombin could enable many citizens to buy food at much more affordable prices.
in writing. − i fully support this resolution and the efforts to prevent the authorisation of thrombin or ‘meat glue’. it is misleading for consumers because they assume they are buying a single piece of meat, but in fact they are buying many pieces which have been artificially stuck together. industry has argued that use of this substance enables them to create cheap meat for people who cannot afford more expensive products, but the fact is that it enables industry to sell smaller pieces of meat for more money, not less. and there is a health issue here too – many small pieces of meat glued together have a much larger surface area than a single, larger piece, which significantly increases the area on which pathogenic bacteria can thrive. misleading the consumer is contrary to eu law, and there are potentially serious health implications of using this substance in this way. this is why in voted in favour of this resolution.
in writing. − the european commission presented in 2008 an action plan on organ donation and transplantation for 2009-2015, with the aim of improving cooperation between member states in the field of organ donation through the exchange of good practice. the actions provided for in this plan complement the european legal framework provided for in the commission's proposal for a directive on organ donation and transplantation. although there are currently significant differences between member states in terms of practices and outcomes, the exchange of information and good practices will help countries where organ availability is low to improve their availability rate. other actions in the plan are to improve the quality and safety of organ transport, to create a register for the evaluation of post-transplant results, to create a system of organ exchange for special cases such as children or people with special needs. i voted with my colleagues in the european parliament in favour of such a plan, which will facilitate cooperation between member states and combat organ trafficking.
in writing. - organ transplantation is the last chance for life for thousands of people every day. in romania, 13 people on the transplant waiting list die every day from lack of donors. romania faces a dramatic situation with only one donor for every million inhabitants. the romanian parliament tried to introduce the concept of a presumed agreement, but public debates blocked the process each time. the commission and the european parliament are simply trying to put things in order, to make recommendations in a system which is important for saving as many lives as possible. the funding of the health care system is not to be neglected. organ harvesting and transplantation, as well as post-transplant care, are expensive medical operations, but all national states should make efforts to encourage this type of medical procedure. spain is an example, because it has managed to attract the largest number of donors in the european union. no one needs to reinvent the wheel as long as we have a successful example in our own midst. in these circumstances, the encouragement given by this directive to cooperation between member states and the exchange of organs, strictly regulated by quality and safety standards, is welcome.
in writing. − following the ratification of the treaty of lisbon, the charter of fundamental rights of the european union obliges the union to accede to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. i support this because the credibility of the union in the eyes of its citizens will be enhanced by ensuring that rights are respected. by acceding to the convention, citizens will obtain the same protection from the actions of the union and its institutions as they currently enjoy from the actions of the member states. at the same time, we will also achieve closer cooperation between the court of justice of the european union, the european court of human rights and national courts.
in writing. − the organisation of the icc conference in uganda is an important signal for the acceptance of this international institution on the african continent, especially as the first investigations of the court since its establishment in 2002 were launched here. no one can deny the importance of such an international court that investigates serious cases of human rights violations, genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. it is therefore important that more and more states recognize the authority of the international criminal court and that the states signatory to the rome statute urgently ratify the agreement. the idea of an international tribunal to investigate crimes against humanity was first mooted in 1919 at the paris peace conference. it took 83 years to reach an international agreement and establish the icc. now, the states that have ratified the rome statute of the icc must also regulate the court's right to investigate crimes of aggression. and the signatory states must harmonize their national legislation with the provisions of the rome statute, as they have committed themselves to do.
first of all, i would like to congratulate mr cortés lastra on the work he has done in drawing up his report, which once again underlines the importance of cohesion policy in achieving the objectives of the eu 2020 strategy. we need to ensure that the role of cohesion policy focused on regions is recognised as such within this strategy. we all know that the effective implementation of the strategy will depend very much on how it is designed. i therefore believe that local and regional authorities must be involved from the design stage to ensure that they can produce truly effective results at a later stage. better governance at several levels is also a guarantee for the effective implementation of cohesion policy at national, regional and local level. as beneficiaries of this policy, i believe that the member states must retain their key role in the decision-making process on cohesion policy within the council. finally, i would like to welcome the recognition of the role of the structural funds in achieving the objectives of the strategy, but i would like to draw attention once again to the fact that we must not fall into the trap of using these funds in the future as an instrument for sanctioning member states. such a measure would, i believe, be totally at odds with the real objectives of cohesion policy.
europe 2020 must be a europe of the citizens and respond to their needs. this is the approach i believe should underpin this strategy. it is important that in the new european framework we continue the development directions and objectives already set, which must be followed in order to achieve concrete results and to achieve a positive impact. i am referring specifically to investments in infrastructure of all kinds, to become much more economically competitive. the continuation of the policy of economic, social and territorial cohesion is needed to reduce disparities between regions and to lay the foundations for balanced economic development, as stipulated in the treaty of lisbon. europe 2020 must be a europe of global action that can be achieved if there is a common level of development within the european union that increases the capacity of local and regional actors to respond to global challenges. europe 2020 is a europe where regions develop according to their specific potential and use the regional dimension of research, development and innovation for economic growth and job creation.
officer, please! i believe that any plan or strategy for european development must be guided by the idea of building a europe that is truly a single area, at the service of the european citizens. we have talked a lot about the economic and social dimension of the europe 2020 strategy. but the union is now much more than that. the union is not only a community of interests but also a community of values, and its economic strength and political weight are derived from this. if we really want to build a more successful and competitive europe by the end of the decade, we must pay serious attention to properly respecting, strengthening and validating our common values. we must also pay attention to better coordination of member states' education policies, to reducing regional disparities, to the enlargement process, or to guaranteeing fundamental rights and minority rights, to name just a few policies based on european values. economic growth and improvements in the living conditions of citizens are unthinkable without such values-based policies.
european cohesion policy has allowed and is allowing synergies to be created with research and innovation policies and, at the same time, has led to a greater emphasis on the role of the territorial dimension. i believe that the regions should pursue smart and green specialisation, define a set of innovative priorities for themselves, based on the union's objectives and their needs, and focus community resources on these identified priorities. they should also promote successful models in the knowledge triangle, in relations between enterprises, research centres, universities and public authorities, especially those achieved through public-private partnerships. i also believe that the exchange of knowledge within regional groupings can also be facilitated by the structural funds, because european policies are coherently geared towards sustainable development with tangible results at regional level. all these elements are the concrete link to achieving territorial cohesion within the european union.
i congratulate the rapporteurs today, and in particular mr van nistelrooij, on the excellent report they have presented. research and development will be the solutions to be considered in the future to successfully respond to the major challenges we face, whether it is the acute phenomenon of the economic crisis or the achievement of the long-term objectives of strategy 2020. under the impetus of cohesion policy, which aims to encourage innovation and entrepreneurship and develop a knowledge-based economy, research and development must take on two dimensions. in the top-down approach, research and innovation will be the main themes to identify solutions to overcome the problems we face and for sustainable growth and development. it is equally important that innovation should come down from the laboratories and research centres to a level as close as possible to the needs of the european citizen. we need to encourage local and regional economies to increase their capacity to innovate, to identify the most effective solutions in the bottom-up approach, and thus to exploit regional and local potential.
today the union is facing an economic, financial and social crisis. the deindustrialization policy pursued in recent years has led to the loss of millions of jobs, the relocation of european industry to third countries, an unemployment rate of 10% and even 20% among young people, endangering the union's competitiveness. i believe that the union must invest heavily in transport and energy infrastructure, agriculture, health, education and research and, above all, in sustainable economic development. the development of industrial production and, by implication, jobs in the union requires investment in modernising european enterprises to produce more environmentally friendly products. over the next ten years, energy efficiency must be at the top of our agenda. the union's population is also ageing, the birth rate is falling and high unemployment is affecting the sustainability of pension systems. i believe that the time has come for the union to defend its fundamental principles and values, and the greatest value of the union is the 500 million european citizens.
in writing. the principles of the eu 2020 strategy are essential to increasing the competitiveness of the european economy. structural reforms are the key to overcoming the crisis we are in. the solutions so far to the crisis do not address the causes that brought us to this situation. the causes of the crisis can only be eliminated through structural reforms. we need to pay greater attention to the innovation capacity of our economies, because this will be the key to the eu's competitiveness in the period ahead. we need a coordinated use of funds for innovation and regional development. innovation must be a component of regional development. innovation was an objective of the lisbon strategy, but unfortunately it has remained a principle on paper. member states made extremely uneven progress and the overall target was not met. that is why i call on all member states to show responsibility and to respect the commitments they have made. the commission should also play a more active role in coordinating the implementation of this strategy, in order to avoid a disastrous failure like that of the lisbon strategy.
unfortunately, the curriculum places too much emphasis on the theoretical side, and students face problems when entering the job market. their education must be more in the perspective of practice and the real problems encountered in the economic environment. that is why i believe that there is a need to strengthen the links between academia and business. in addition, more openness of universities to the business environment is needed to better adapt university education to the requirements of the labour market. this will enable students to develop the skills and competences required by employers. a number of member states, such as france, germany, italy, the united kingdom and spain, have developed partnerships between universities and business for several years. in romania, a project funded by the european union was implemented last year, whereby twenty faculties benefited from new study programmes adapted to the current requirements of the labour market. one of the important benefits of the project is the reduction of unemployment by increasing the quality of education and reducing the number of graduates with higher education who are unable to adapt to the labour market. such partnerships should not be limited to the level of one member state. in this context, i support the promotion and expansion of the erasmus for young entrepreneurs and erasmus for apprentices programmes.
first of all, i would like to congratulate mr pál schmitt on his coherent and relevant report on the current situation in higher education. we have a big problem, and that is that, at the moment, in all 27 member states of the european union, we are producing unemployed people, not young people who are perfectly suited to the labour market. there is a huge gap between what a young person learns in school and what employers demand in the job market. it is an even bigger problem because we are in an economic crisis, in a financial crisis, and the jobs crisis is also evident. we are talking about many years in which the european union has been a player on the world market with an economy based mainly on knowledge and innovation. if we really want to have a knowledge and innovation economy, we need to go beyond the discussion stage and support more investment and public-private partnerships and encourage partnerships between universities and business so that what is discovered and the results of scientific research in universities can be exploited in the real economy. i was with seán kelly in santiago de compostela, and i visited the university there, and i can tell you that i saw a very clear model of financing for start-ups, for small businesses, for student-run businesses, where the university gives out loans without collateral to students. what students develop at the university is immediately applicable to the local economy. it is a model that we must promote and multiply at union level.
at a time when we need new tools to boost economic growth, i believe it is important to ensure that small and medium-sized enterprises have easier access to the research and development sector. many of these companies suffer from difficult access to finance, so they cannot afford to design and develop new products or redesign existing ones, and face a loss of competitiveness. it would be desirable for universities, especially those funded by public funds, to be more open to the needs of the small and medium-sized enterprises sector. reducing red tape while increasing public funding for research and development programmes that can generate technologies or products that can be transferred to smes could facilitate access to funding for these programmes from the structural funds. universities can also contribute to the training of sme staff as part of the lifelong learning process. the launch of a single european network of business and innovation centres is encouraging. i want to congratulate the reporter.
we have to ask ourselves where we want to go in terms of education and research. there's a lot of talk about the knowledge society, but i wonder if this concept has become just a media-successful catchphrase. i think there's too little talk about competence in this context and too much about the accumulation of knowledge. if you survey students, you'll find that essay writing has become a practice based on some formulas for filling the space required by teachers. they're the ones who will have to engage in an economic environment where the recipes for success are no longer guaranteed. i believe that not only the business environment will be profoundly restructured as a result of the economic and financial crisis, but also universities, which will have to go through transformations to adapt to an ever-changing environment that requires the acquisition of skills, not just knowledge.
i congratulate mr pál schmitt twice: on his new post, but also on the well-structured and complex report which will certainly help to make relations between the business and academic worlds in europe more efficient. since all the strategies we have adopted proclaim the need for well-trained citizens whose skills are in line with the requirements of the labour market, i welcome a concrete approach that ensures a better interconnection between the two areas. i believe that a change of mindset is needed at community level, a business environment that contributes to the adaptation of the university curriculum, just as on the american continent, by initiating and financing specific courses. in this way, students will be familiar with the rigours of entrepreneurship and the european higher education area can become more attractive globally. the practical effect must be to provide added value to society, to transfer knowledge and the results of collaboration between universities and businesses, generating economic growth and, by implication, a better life for our citizens.
i agree with the rapporteur in part. i want to tell you that to achieve the objectives of the eu 2020 strategy, knowledge and innovation are needed, and we are not talking about buying knowledge, we are talking about investing in an education system adapted to the needs of the market. at present, universities in the european union offer less attractive conditions to researchers and students than schools in the united states, and one of the main reasons is that money is lacking. as european commission president josé manuel barroso has pointed out, europeans are fighting to attract the best footballers, but they are losing their researchers to the americans. the modernisation of european universities is therefore imperative if they are to play a decisive role in society and in the knowledge and innovation-based economy. one solution to the complaints of employers that university education fails to take account of labour market requirements and does not prepare students for the current context is to provide opportunities for traineeships in smes in university programmes.

in writing. the eu is 53% dependent on energy imports. to reduce energy dependency, some member states have adopted ambitious strategies for the use of nuclear energy and energy from renewable sources. in the eu, nuclear energy accounts for 28% of total energy consumed and in belgium, france, lithuania, slovakia and sweden it is the most important source of energy. nuclear power generation does not generate carbon dioxide emissions and in member states using nuclear energy, the price per household monthly energy bill is lower. however, the eu is certainly very demanding in the operation of nuclear power plants and in the management of radioactive waste. strong measures and high standards for the safety of nuclear installations, as well as good cooperation between local, regional, national and european authorities, provide the basis for the safe use of nuclear energy in the eu. the commission's proposed regulation ensures fair treatment of bulgaria by granting financial assistance until 2013 for the decommissioning of nuclear power plants, measures laid down in the accession treaties. nuclear decommissioning requires long-term financial planning, continuing until the site has been fully recovered and all radioactive waste and spent fuel has been safely managed.

in writing. − last year, the budget deficit and public debt in the euro area were 6.3% and 78.7% of gdp respectively, well above the level set by the stability and growth pact. the stability and growth pact has proven its limitations in the context of the crisis, as it is not a sufficient instrument for harmonising national economies. i therefore support both a revision of the pact and the search for alternative mechanisms to restore convergence of economies within the union, such as a european public rating agency and closer coordination of budgetary and monetary policies in the member states. so i think the decision taken last week by the european central bank to buy bonds issued by euro area governments is a positive one. i have decided to vote against the final report on the long-term sustainability of public finances because these elements which i consider to be fundamental to ensuring the stability of the european single market and to maintaining a modern welfare state in europe have been removed from the report.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on the need for a european union strategy for the south caucasus. the south caucasus is of strategic importance to the european union. at the same time, the european union can and must help this region, which is struggling to develop economically and commercially. through trade policy we can promote respect for human rights, energy security, democracy and good governance. as the virtual rapporteur of my political group for this resolution, i am calling for the conclusion of free trade agreements with georgia, armenia and azerbaijan. in my view, these will help the economic development of the region by increasing investment and creating new jobs, which will ensure a reduction in poverty.

there are two indisputable facts when we look at the situation in pakistan. the first is that pakistan is a key strategic player in the fight against terrorism. we must do everything we can to ensure that the security of european citizens is not jeopardised. the second is that pakistan has a different attitude towards religious and ethnic minorities than it would have in line with the values that europe and advanced liberal democracies hold. europe cannot remain silent when other states commit serious human rights abuses, and we must therefore raise our concerns, even when it comes to our strategic partners. the union can act credibly vis-à-vis third countries by resolving the problems of religious and national minorities in its own territory in a satisfactory manner. it must be clear to the world that one of the union's fundamental values is a high level of protection of human and minority rights, which the union considers itself primarily obliged to uphold, or should, so to speak, be obliged to uphold. this is the only way to most effectively engage our partners in these achievements or the stops on the way to them.
after nearly nine years of military dictatorship, the 2008 elections in pakistan marked the beginning of a process of democratization in the country. unfortunately, ms. benazir bhutto was assassinated a few weeks before the election. these were won by the pakistan people's party, which she led. although minorities in pakistan face a number of problems, under the current government, a number of positive measures have been initiated. intercultural dialogue was promoted, a 5% quota for minorities in the federal administration was established and some muslim legal holidays were recognized. the pakistani government's commitment to grant minority seats in the senate is commendable. finally, i would like to emphasize the special importance that pakistan has in the fight against terrorism and extremism.

in writing. – reportedly, pakistan has the harshest blasphemy laws in the world. the exercise of the rights to free expression and religion can result in imprisonment and death. section 295b and c of pakistan’s penal code criminalise derogatory remarks regarding the koran and the prophet, providing for punishments of life imprisonment, and death, respectively. section 298 punishes the deliberate wounding of religious feelings, and sections 298a, b and c penalise derogatory remarks of holy figures and places, and outlaw the religious group of ahmadis (who consider themselves muslim). freedom of religion includes the freedom to believe in any religion and the freedom not to believe in any religion. pakistan’s minister for minority affairs announced yesterday that amendments are being prepared to stop the misuse of the blasphemy laws. i believe these laws should be repealed, as any modified text will only be a legacy of the past and allow for continued violence and discrimination.
in writing. in recent years, the government of pakistan has adopted a number of measures which show a certain sensitivity to the situation of national minorities: the appointment of the federal minister for minorities in the person of shahbaz bhatti, the 5% quota for public sector employees, the commitment of a representation in the senate for religious minorities, etc. these efforts should be encouraged, but much more is needed to improve the situation of religious minorities. a crucial element, i think, is the revision of the provisions on religious offences in the so-called blasphemy law. the possibility of abusing the provisions of this law has created an atmosphere of intolerance, which has encouraged religious violence, discrimination, intimidation and persecution of religious minorities. beyond the legal aspect, it is important that the government take decisive action to prevent violence. promoting tolerance is the key to protecting religious minorities in pakistan.

on behalf of the epp group. i would like to start by congratulating the rapporteur, mrs ludford, on all her work and thanking her for the way she has worked with the alternate rapporteurs. the existence of common standards is an essential condition for mutual trust in the legal systems of the member states. the right to a fair trial of suspects or accused persons is a fundamental right, enshrined in article 47 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union and article 6 of the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. however, in the absence of adequate standards of defence, there is a risk of creating imbalances between the means available to the prosecution and the degree of protection of the rights of suspects or accused persons. efforts to strengthen procedural rights in the european union have been long-standing. the first steps were taken in november 2000 when the council, in accordance with the tampere conclusions, adopted a programme of measures to implement the principle of mutual recognition in criminal matters. they followed the commission's proposal for a framework decision on certain procedural rights in criminal proceedings in 2004, which failed to reach agreement and negotiations were abandoned in june 2007; the swedish presidency's roadmap of july 2009, which proposed a gradual approach to procedural rights; the commission's proposal of july 2009 and december 2010, respectively, with the entry into force of the lisbon treaty and the change of legal framework; and finally the initiative of the 13 member states. here we are, after almost seven years, about to adopt the first step in the procedural rights roadmap: the directive on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings. i would like to express my satisfaction with the result of the interinstitutional negotiations, the text we are going to vote on wednesday, which brings important improvements to the member states' proposal. i hope that the three-year implementation period will not set a precedent for subsequent measures under the roadmap and that member states will make every effort to implement all the provisions of the directive as quickly, correctly, consistently and fairly as possible.
when the economic crisis in the european union began, the baltic states were among the worst affected. the baltic tigers were becoming, after a few years of economic boom, the sick men of europe. but now, in record time, estonia is preparing to join the eurozone. but its accession is to strengthen the euro area at a critical moment. estonia's ambition to adopt the single currency is commendable, despite the crisis which did not escape it, but which it has managed to cope with with prompt austerity measures and fiscal discipline. although hard hit by the crisis, the baltic countries have had the advantage of low public debt, which has provided them with a greater degree of flexibility for external borrowing. this is noteworthy given that estonia's debt-to-gdp ratio is 7.2%, well below the 60% reference value. i think it is time to learn from the lessons of the european crisis and the determination of estonia and to find a middle ground between ambition and prudence. however, in this process we cannot afford to neglect the social component of the changeover. the experience of the previous accession states indicates major risks to price increases, so i hope that the estonian authorities will be able to apply balanced fiscal policies so that citizens are not forced to make major sacrifices. in this connection, my colleague mr scicluna draws attention to the risk of inflation. last but not least, estonia's move to the euro has a symbolic dimension, as it sets an example for the eastern european countries, whose momentum and real chances of meeting the deadline for adopting the euro have been diminished by the crisis.
i would first like to congratulate estonia on its particular efforts to meet the convergence criteria by adopting prudent policies. it will thus become the 17th country to adopt the euro. at a difficult time for the european economy, with speculation growing about the exit of some member states from the euro area, estonia is showing that it is ready to move to the single currency. this is also a strong signal for a possible eastward enlargement of the euro area. the other eight countries covered by the 2010 convergence report, including romania, have made uneven progress towards adopting the single currency and do not yet meet all the criteria for joining the euro area. finally, i would like to say that any member state should only adopt the euro when it is fully ready.
in romania and many other eu countries, so-called 'dream shops' have sprung up, selling chemically processed substances as substitutes for drugs. the romanian government has issued an emergency ordinance banning dozens of such substances. however, because of the way these shops operate, the threat of lethal drugs has not been contained and will not be stopped without a general reaction from the european institutions and all the governments of the member states. many have died, and the health of thousands is in jeopardy. numerous ngos in romania warn that there are a huge number of chemically processed substances that can produce such effects and their gradual ban cannot be a realistic solution to combat the problem. romania is a lucky case, because it has seen the rise of this phenomenon in good time, but it could be just as alive in other european countries. that is why i believe that the institutions of the european union must take the lead in ensuring that we have a continuous fight not only against drugs but also against lethal drug surrogates.
in romania, the series of abusive measures that the right-wing power manifests with the attack on the right to free expression continues. a bill on the organization and operation of public radio and television is being discussed in the national parliament. the proposal from the government is a direct attack on freedom of expression in romania and seriously violates both the constitution, minority rights, and international norms in the field. european and romanian organizations have already brought criticism. all media regulations in europe provide for the respect of the right to freedom of expression and information guaranteed by article 10 of the european convention on human rights. i call on the european commission and the romanian authorities to find a fair and democratic solution to a mechanism that will allow public radio and television to operate on equal, ethical and european principles.

according to the italian newspaper la repubblica, may 31 of this year, some insurance companies in italy are charging a so-called nationality risk premium. the consequence of this tax is that citizens from countries with high migration flows, for example romania or bulgaria, are obliged to pay higher taxes when taking out a car insurance policy. according to italian legal experts, national immigration law requires non-discriminatory access to services, regardless of the nationality of the applicant. the question i raise in parliament tonight is whether such a practice can be considered in line with european discrimination law.
over the next nine months, the commission, the member states and the european parliament will define the future ten-t core network and the interconnection nodes with the transport network of the union's neighbouring countries. the development of the ten-t system, both infrastructure and transport services, must be an important part of the eu-2020 strategy. the internal market and the economic and social cohesion of the union depend on an efficient, safe and interoperable transport infrastructure. the union needs high-speed rail infrastructure to serve all eu capitals and all major european cities, as well as modernisation of seaports and river ports. i ask the commission to increase the budget for the development of the transeuropean transport system from 11% of the budget for cohesion policy to at least 20% in the future financial perspective and to reduce the gap in the development of transport infrastructure between the centre and the south-east of the union. in order to encourage member states to invest in ten-t infrastructure, i also ask the commission to increase the co-financing rate from the ten-t budget, in particular for cross-border sections.
the european commission is preparing the green paper on pensions, through which the european executive will seek to stimulate the debate on a european pension strategy. the main lines of this strategy should aim at addressing the demographic and budgetary problems facing the member states. with the ageing population of the european union, the pressures on public finances will increase significantly in the coming years. regardless of the political situation in the member states, the main priority of such a strategy must be to guarantee a decent standard of living for those who have retired from active life. we must not forget that pensioners are a captive social group. they often no longer have the opportunity to opt for an alternative source of income, such as employment, because of their advanced age, and therefore i insist that this priority be the main objective of this document.

in writing. the internet of things is an information architecture consisting of a network of objects interconnected by means of radio frequency identification technology and the internet. the advantage of such innovation is that it facilitates trade in goods and services and transmits information about objects around us in real time. the main points of a regulatory framework in this area are to encourage investment to enable european companies to benefit from the added value of this innovation and to establish a governance system for the information structure, which allows for proper consumer information and respects the personal data of european citizens. i therefore believe that it is the task of the european commission to continue funding projects in the field of the internet of things under the 7th framework programme for competitiveness and innovation and to create a transparent and secure governance system for the internet of things.
in writing. internet of things technology will enable significant advances in health, transport, energy efficiency, the environment, retail and the fight against counterfeiting. the development of new iot applications will depend on the confidence of european consumers in the system. effective security is one of the essential features of any development that risks endangering personal data. the commission should make further efforts to ensure that iot-related technologies meet user requirements (in particular the option to disable traceability) and respect the rights and freedoms of natural persons. this technology should be subject to further evaluations by the european commission in the future, in particular with regard to the impact of radio waves and other means of activating identification technologies on health. the commission will have to ensure the development of a transparent system based on the principle of respect for privacy from the moment of design, which allows the explicit mention of the presence of means of identification and traceability and which guarantees to consumers and delegated authorities the possibility to verify the reliability of the data and the way the system works, and that the data will be accessible only by authorised users.
we have reached a point where the use of the internet is indispensable for both citizens and organisations. the internet, with its wide range of services and facilities, can be seen as a global public good to which everyone should have unconditional access. i am in favour of concrete european funding programmes to facilitate access to this service and develop its communications infrastructure in all regions of europe, especially in rural areas and in developing member states. this will help to bridge the digital, social and cultural gaps between europe and the rest of the world. at the same time, the european union must ensure that the existence and security of its internet infrastructure is well protected against cyberattacks of all kinds. i believe that efforts in this direction should be identified and matched with other protection measures and good practices adopted by the international community.
the european parliament suggests that the commission should create the possibility of real representation of european civil society in international internet governance forums and in internet standardisation organisations or consortia. the protection of the internet infrastructure and its resilience to cyberattacks, as well as the protection of data and privacy, are important to the european union. the commission and the member states should step up their efforts to ensure cybersecurity in the european union and participate in international cooperation in this field. i believe that further measures are needed to achieve a better understanding and awareness of cybercrime and cloud computing jurisdiction on an equal footing and to establish clear obligations and responsibilities for stakeholders. i stress the importance of electronic services and in particular of electronic signatures and the need to create a public key infrastructure at pan-european level to ensure the cross-border interoperability of electronic signatures and to enhance security on the internet. i would like to conclude by drawing attention to the fact that, in order to increase consumer confidence in accessing information and services available on the internet, it is becoming increasingly necessary to certify websites for security reasons.

in writing. − the internet of things is a concept of the future anchored in the present. it is up to us to make sure that it 'works' for the benefit of all citizens in a harmonised and effective way. the new system of integrating technology into everyday life must be implemented with strict respect for consumer privacy rights. the commission should consult the data protection working party on a regular basis and not only when it considers it necessary. we're talking about devices and technologies that are capable of transmitting the position, characteristics and identity of an object. these devices, in addition to the right to silence, should only be integrated at the request of the individual and not as a manufacturing standard. at the same time, the commission must take into account, when deciding on the implementation of projects relating to the internet of things, which network for interconnecting these objects it will choose. right now, we're facing a lot of cyber attacks on the internet. in my view, the use of the world wide web to interconnect the internet of things can pose both a security risk and a substantial burden on the current network. developing a parallel network for interconnecting objects may be the solution in this situation by sharing the spectrum and the digital dividend.

in writing. − less than 1% of the eu budget is currently spent on innovation. and this is happening as europe has become aware that its future lies in the research-innovation-education triangle. the european parliament's request to increase the amount allocated to innovation is perfectly justified in these circumstances. we are approaching the time of the financial projections for the period 2014-2020 and this request must be taken into account. the transformation of the european economy into a sustainable one must lead to a greater competitiveness of european societies and allow new opportunities for national economies to emerge as a result of the economic and environmental challenges facing europe. it is also precisely because of the financial crisis and the credit impasse that increased funding, both at community and national level, and the creation of appropriate funding instruments is decisive for innovation capacity. a fragmentation into a multitude of objectives and a number of specific eu initiatives has not produced satisfactory results so far. the funds must be directed to the areas where the boomerang effect is greatest. in this case, the decisive criterion must be the added value for europe.

the activities of the rating agencies not only led to the current financial crisis, but also contributed to its worsening. the 2009 regulation of the european parliament and of the council on credit rating agencies was designed as a response to regulate the activity of credit rating agencies. the regulation introduces mandatory registration for all credit agencies operating in the european union, focusing on three main aspects: supervision, transparency and conflict of interest. however, we are far from solving the problem of transparency and the oligopolistic structure of the credit rating agency market. it is not right that the economies of the member states, and therefore their companies, should depend on the ratings of only three agencies. speculation in country ratings can push countries, which are in a critical situation anyway, towards bankruptcy, and in these circumstances i believe that the creation of an exclusive european credit rating agency is necessary, which will be a real competitor and an alternative instrument for existing companies.
in the current crisis, the work of rating agencies is increasingly being criticized because they have failed to objectively assess the degree of credit risk of companies and even states. these agencies did not provide early assessments of crisis risk, but downgraded several european countries, thus aggravating the crisis. the major problem is the lack of competition in the market for rating services, because only three american companies control this market. in this respect, i support president barroso's proposal to set up a european credit rating agency. as is well known, last week one of the three agencies changed germany's rating, following an unacceptable error. in conclusion, the european union must ensure that the activity of credit rating agencies is better regulated in the future.
the elimination of double transparency obligations and the reduction of information requirements for companies with a small market capitalisation will generate estimated global savings of eur 110 million per year. the revision of the prospectus directive will thus allow for an increase in the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises in the european union. we must not forget that small and mediumsized enterprises are the engine of the european union's economy. they created 9.4 million jobs in the union between 2002 and 2008 and today provide jobs for 90 million european citizens. there is also a need to harmonise financial transparency requirements across the european union in order to reduce the administrative burden on european companies. the newly created european securities and markets authority will therefore have to seek to coordinate the laws of the member states on the examination and approval of prospectuses.

member of the commission. − mr kelly, the floods directive was adopted in 2007 and the process of implementation is under way. in the last month, new floods have reminded us of the serious consequences of floods and of the importance of flood risk management which focuses on prevention, preparedness and protection. the floods directive requires all member states to prepare comprehensive plans to reduce flood risks. importantly, the public and interested parties need to be consulted on these plans, and member states need to cooperate in transboundary waterways. the first two implementation deadlines have already expired. firstly, the legal transposition into national law was due by november 2009. to date, 12 member states, including ireland, have met this deadline. ten member states have not yet notified their transposition of the directive, and five member states have only notified partial transposition. the commission is pursuing infringement cases to respond to this situation. as regards the notification by the member states to the commission of administrative arrangements, the deadline expires on 26 june of this year. twenty-three member states, including ireland, have notified. the commission is now checking that all relevant information on the responsible authorities and the geographical coverage of the units of management is in compliance with the directive. the main implementation milestones are still some time away. across the european union, member states are preparing these steps, which are: firstly, to carry out a preliminary flood risk assessment in 2011 and to identify areas of potential significant flood risks; secondly, to prepare detailed flood hazard maps and flood risk maps by 2013; and, thirdly, to prepare the first flood risk management plans in 2015. the public and interested parties must also be consulted on these plans before they are adopted. as regards ireland, we understand the implementation is well under way and we have no reason to believe ireland is delayed in implementing the directive. ireland has notified the legislation transposing the directive and has reported administrative arrangements. we furthermore welcome the fact that ireland has already undertaken pilot exercises in the dodder catchment in the dublin area as well as in the lee catchment in the south of ireland – where a draft catchment flood risk management plan was prepared and submitted to public consultation. ireland also takes an active role at the european level in promoting valuable information exchange between the member states on different topics related to the implementation of the directive, such as on how to deal with flash and pluvial floods, flood mapping and development of flood risk management plans.
flood risk prevention and management involves transnational solutions to the eu's hydrological problems and requires massive investment. i would like to ask the commission whether it is considering the development of a common policy on inland waters, as in the case of the common maritime policy, which would deal in an integrated manner with spatial planning, environmental protection, protection of the marine environment, maritime transport, development of areas along inland waters or coastal areas.

in writing. − citizens of the union are now guaranteed full rights of defence if they are involved in criminal proceedings in a member state other than their own. according to the directive on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings, all stages of the investigation or trial will be translated and explained to the suspect or accused involved in the proceedings in their mother tongue. the measure improves the quality of defence for european citizens, building on the unanimously accepted considerations of the right to a fair trial throughout the union. the directive thus complements the legal provisions on cases where european arrest warrants are exercised, with a view to improving the conditions of defence for european citizens accused or suspected in criminal proceedings. translation and interpretation services - provided to the accused in a language he understands - of the investigation or trial proceedings concerning him will be guaranteed in the legislation of each member state within three years. this is the deadline all eu countries have to harmonize their criminal laws. according to the directive, translations and interpretations cover interrogations at police headquarters, dialogue with the lawyer and including the translation of important documents such as detention orders, indictments or indictments.

in writing. − unifying european regulations on the labelling of prepackaged food will enable consumers to make informed choices without causing complications and major financial burdens for producers. the debate on product labelling in the european parliament on wednesday was of great interest to meps because it affects all of us. in a world dominated by unhealthy lifestyles, with obesity and cardiovascular disease reaching epidemic proportions and threatening health across europe, it is important that every consumer makes an informed choice when choosing certain foods. uniform regulations at european level, placing in a visible place the lipid content, saturated fatty acids, sugars and energy content will overcome the language barriers that some consumers might invoke. the european parliament, with its decision this week, demonstrates its understanding of protecting european consumers and recognises the importance of informed decisions. it is up to the consumer, once the new regulations are implemented, to make a choice regarding his own consumption. i hope that these regulations will quickly outgrow the institutional procedures within the union and become binding in the near future.
in writing. − we know that there is a european consumer policy and consumer protection policy, which aims to provide a high level of uniformity throughout the european union, but consumers must have clear and understandable information on the essential nutritional aspects of food in order to make informed choices. i also believe that the need for a new food information regulation arises in the context of a general awareness of the importance of switching to a healthier diet and of european consumers who are increasingly sensitive to the content of food. i believe that this will also provide an incentive for both agricultural producers and industrial groups to take steps to improve labelling in response to consumer demands. the information on the label must not mislead the consumer, when purchasing the products, as to the characteristics of the food and, in particular, its nature, identity, properties, composition, quantity, durability, origin or provenance, and the methods of manufacture or production. as hippocrates said, "let your food be your medicine and your medicine be your food".
in writing. − mandatory country of origin labelling will support european producers by recognising their high quality standards. our citizens want to know where the products they buy come from, whether they are european or imported; at the same time, consumers in other markets trust what is produced and processed in the european union. the commission has also proposed that the eu should be able to use the eu's own resources to support the development of the eu's food industry. the rejection of the amendment on colour codes is welcome, because it would have had the opposite effect: it could have turned consumers away from traditional, healthy and natural european products by simplifying the proposed assessment method.
in writing. − this regulation should provide for a labelling system valid throughout the eu, which - with a few exceptions - applies to all products of the food industry, and not just to certain categories of products. harmonisation of the labelling system is also of particular relevance to the proper functioning of the internal market, as additional national regulations and different interpretations by member states of existing european labelling legislation currently create barriers to trade and competition issues. addressing these problems can help to bring down prices for food producers and traders and, by implication, for consumers. in romania, a survey of 1,000 people aged 18 to 50 shows that romanians are most concerned about product safety (75%), fraudulent clauses (67%) and credit-lending services (51%), and least concerned about tourism services (28%). that is why food labelling is only one of many aspects of food. this form of information can complement, but not replace, efforts to raise public awareness through campaigns and educational measures on relatively healthy lifestyles.
