in writing. − i voted in favour of the ecb's annual report for 2009. the ecb continued its policy since 2008, targeting an inflation rate close to 2%, while increasing liquidity in markets. the ecb therefore adjusted the interest rates to 1% and continued the unconventional measures introduced in 2008 throughout 2009. the five key elements of increased credit support were the full allotment of funds at a fixed rate, the extension of the collateral pool, longer maturities for refinancing operations, the provision of liquidity in foreign currency and the support of the financial market through a controlled but substantial programme of covered bond purchases. rigorous coordination with national governments in eu countries on their own programmes is needed, especially in view of the crises that have hit greece and now ireland, and the bleak prospect of their spreading.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the european central bank annual report 2009, as it proposes a number of measures that could be beneficial for the european union economy. these include a permanent mechanism to defend the euro area against speculative attacks, the supervision of the activities of current credit rating agencies and the consideration of a possible european credit rating agency. as rapporteur for my political group, i also highlighted the limitations of the stability and growth pact in its current form. the pact should be complemented by an alert system to strengthen the coordination of economic policies within the european union.
in writing. − it is becoming clear that internal and external security are increasingly interdependent and, in these circumstances, the development of policies and capacities for crisis management, conflict prevention is, in fact, an investment in the security of the citizens of the european union. the european external action service should be a key factor in developing a truly comprehensive european approach to european-level civil and military crisis management, conflict prevention, and providing the eu with sufficient structures, human and financial resources to meet its global responsibilities. the establishment of the eeas requires the transfer of the csdp structures, including the crisis management and planning directorate, the civilian planning and leadership capability, the eu staff and the situation centre, under the umbrella of the eeas, to the authority and direct responsibility of the high representative for foreign affairs. it is his direct duty to ensure that these structures are integrated and function coherently. to stimulate the development of the eu's comprehensive approach, close collaboration is needed between the eeas and all other relevant units within the commission, in particular those dealing with development, humanitarian aid, civil protection and public health issues.
in writing. − it is desirable that the establishment of the european external action service (eeas) contributes to the development of a truly comprehensive european approach to european civil and military crisis management, conflict prevention and peacebuilding, providing the eu with sufficient structures, human and financial resources to fulfil its global responsibilities under the un charter. as the un security council has the primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security, close cooperation between the eu and the un is needed in the field of civilian and military crisis management, in particular in the field of relief operations, in which the united nations office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs (unocha) has a leading role. it is also desirable to strengthen this cooperation, particularly in those areas where one organisation is to take over the responsibilities of the other, especially in the light of the contradictory experience in kosovo.
in writing. - i voted in favour of mr rapkay's report because i support, among other things, the extension of the deadline for the closure of non-competitive coal mines. in this respect, i believe that efforts will be made to avoid a massive loss of jobs, with romania, spain and germany being the eu countries most affected by the new regulation. i consider that the closure of non-competitive mines must be carried out in accordance with the closure plan, unless they will not become profitable by the deadline set. i would encourage the granting of degressive aid to cover production losses in the context of a well-defined plan for closing mines. as of 1 january 2011, half of the existing mines in romania will be included in a closure plan. in this context, i believe that aid will have to be directed more towards covering social and environmental consequences.
in writing. − i have chosen to vote in favour of the bernhard rapkay report on 'state aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'. it proposes to postpone the closure of uncompetitive coal mines by four years: from 2014, as originally envisaged in the european commission's proposal, to 2018. the report also encourages the european commission to develop a strategy for the retraining of workers affected by these closures. we have to take into account that certain regions of the european union are completely dependent on the mining sector economically and socially, among them the jiu valley in romania. the mining sector provides jobs for 100,000 people in the european union.
in writing. - i voted for this report because i believe that uncompetitive coal mines should be able to benefit from the contribution of state aid, since the absence of such aid would lead to their closure and, therefore, to massive redundancies and very serious social problems. the transitional period granted for the making of these mines profitable or their closure is important and has the role of, on the one hand, achieving the vocational retraining of the population involved in the coal industry and, on the other hand, achieving a gradual transition to less polluting energy sources.
in writing. − the expiry of the coal industry regulation on 31 december 2010 would have forced some member states to close their shale mines. i voted to extend this regulation until 31 december 2030, as opposed to 31 december 2026 as proposed by the european commission. unfortunately, this amendment did not receive the required majority. however, the point that the sharp downward trend in the total amount of closure aid granted by a member state is being reduced was supported. the commission has also concluded that the measures under assessment are in line with the meip and the meip-compliant benchmark. the deadline resulting from the majority vote was 31 december 2018. i would point out that this deadline obtained for subsidy operations is nevertheless an achievement of the european parliament which extends by 4 years the original deadline of 2014 proposed by the european commission.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because the measures contained in it will, if approved by the council, avoid serious social consequences in many of the member states of the european union. the deadline proposed by the european commission is too short and unrealistic, which is why it was necessary to extend the subsidies for the production of pig iron until 2018. romania, my home member state, has experience of the scale of such a social challenge and i believe that the extension of the deadline is necessary and welcome.
in writing. − the ep opinion on the proposed regulation extends the deadline for subsidising coal production until 31 december 2018 (by 4 years more than the commission proposal) and concerns only huila. the coal sector provides jobs for about 100 000 people. the mines relying on operating aid are mainly located in the ruhr area of germany, in north-western spain and in the jiu valley of romania. the commission notes that the romanian authorities have not provided any evidence that the measures in question were necessary to restore the long-term viability of the company. the commission notes that the 2014 date (proposed by the commission) for the closure plan is arbitrary and not justified by the impact assessment carried out by the eu executive itself. the 2018 guidelines provide for the establishment of a european union-wide monitoring and evaluation system for the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance. the rapporteur is in favour of a gradual reduction of the aid, the annual reduction must not be below 10% of the aid granted in the first year and only on the basis of a closure plan which is very well monitored. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because i believe that it is very important that the measures provided for in the stockholm programme are actually implemented in order to improve the area of freedom, security and justice. this can be done by improving judicial cooperation between member states, by promoting a european judicial culture, by addressing the various problems of incompatibility between the various procedural law models that exist at member state level. the commission's action plan for the implementation of the stockholm programme must take account of all these aspects identified in the report.
in writing. − the report addresses a highly important issue, namely how the eu responds to the legal needs of citizens and businesses, in particular crossborder civil and commercial litigation. i regret, however, that i have not found any reference in the report to the actions required to inform citizens or company directors of the possibilities offered by european law for the protection of their interests in judicial proceedings. these possibilities are not sufficiently known and, consequently, not sufficiently exploited. attention to magistrates and lawyers is important, but it does not guarantee full access to this information for citizens.
it is clear that member states are going through a difficult period from a budgetary point of view. on the other hand, it has been very clear that the european budget has made a major contribution to the development of all member states, including the net contributors. it is surprising that the failure of the conciliation was not due to a disagreement on figures but to a refusal to discuss in practice the common future of the member states, the future of europe. parliament does not want to go beyond its powers, it wants to respect the treaty and protect the future interests of the citizens who elected it. what are the talking points that were rejected by the council? the involvement of the european parliament in the preparation of the mff is a treaty provision, it was done in 2006 and i do not think that the 2007-2013 budget was bad for the union, on the contrary. flexibility - a mechanism that has been used effectively so far and benefited all member states. own resources - the budgetary situation of the member states should be the reason for finding stable ways of financing the european budget, which no longer jeopardise the implementation of european policies. the new responsibilities in the treaty and strategy 2020 need funding. it is unacceptable that the same institution, the council, should set targets for 2020 and at the same time not approve the financial means to meet these requirements. i think we're obligated to come to an agreement. we have a responsibility to the citizens - we must not diminish confidence in the european institutions!
in writing. today we are in a stalemate that actually goes beyond the 2011 budgetary procedure and is a watershed moment that will define the future of the union and serve as a precedent for future budgetary procedures and the role of the european parliament. the parliament's grievances are not absurd and in practice we only want the role assigned to parliament by the treaty to be respected. parliament has made many concessions in these negotiations and we are still being asked to make many more. i hope, however, that we will get through this moment and, in the interests of the citizens, that we will be able to vote on the new budget in the december part-session.
president of the commission. − mr president, today i have the honour of presenting the commission work programme for 2011. the presentation marks a beginning and an end. on the one hand, the work programme intervenes and launches a new phase of very important political work. on the other hand, the adoption of the programme is the conclusion of the enhanced structured dialogue, which was opened with the state of the union debate in september here in this parliament. the preparations leading to this year’s commission work programme have indeed been a ‘première’, and in my opinion a very successful one. by advancing the implementation of our revised framework agreement, we have been able to engage in in-depth discussions on the political priorities for the coming years. throughout this fruitful process i have been encouraged by the large degree of convergence on the overall direction and on concrete initiatives. it is a process which has acted to consolidate what i have called ‘a special partnership’. european action must focus on those challenges where the eu can bring a tangible added value. the 40 strategic initiatives which the commission commits to present in 2011 reflect the main political priorities that we have identified together. for the sake of transparency, the programme moreover includes 150 other proposals which the commission is working on. sustaining economic recovery and securing our societies for the future remains the overarching priority in 2011. our efforts will continue along three main tracks: strengthening governance, completing financial sector reform and accelerating our implementation of the europe 2020 strategy for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. long-term growth must be based on a sound macro-economic foundation. through initiating the so-called ‘european semester’, and the follow-up to our proposals of 29 september, we will reinforce the european fiscal framework and broaden macro-economic surveillance to prevent imbalances. an ambitious financial sector reform is already well under way and important legislation has been accomplished. in 2011, the commission will table the remaining pieces of regulation. key priorities, such as transparency and consumer protection, will be pursued, while a bank crisis framework will aim to prevent and tackle future crises. the commission will seek to support parliament and the council in reaching agreement on the complete reform before the end of 2011. europe must keep pace, focusing on our comparative advantages in this 21st century of globalisation. when competitors are cheaper, we must be smarter. as an example of action at european level, we will develop a more integrated european standardisation system as an important platform for sharpening the competitive edge of our companies, particularly smes. for europe to remain competitive and secure more and better jobs, the transition to a low-carbon, resource-efficient society must be carefully planned. therefore, bringing together the policies on climate change, energy, transport and environment will be a priority. a particular focus in 2011 will be on energy efficiency. adapting to a dynamic economic reality also means ensuring a high level of protection of workers’ rights in close cooperation with social partners. key proposals on posting of workers and working time will be developed and tabled in 2011. meanwhile, the revision of the state aid rules applicable to services of general interest will be a tangible step towards establishing a quality framework which takes account of the particular nature of these services. with the single market act, the commission has launched an ambitious process to make the single market deliver on its full potential. our companies should focus on business, not bureaucracy. not least smes are often overburdened or indeed discouraged from pursuing otherwise promising cross-border projects. as a concrete example, by clarifying the rules on collectively managed copyrights we can simplify the current framework conditions, encourage further cross-border activity and release important job-creating potential – not least in the promising digital sector. on the demand side, a priority will be to strengthen consumer confidence with our proposal on alternative dispute resolution as an important instrument to speed up the often much too slow process of resolving consumer problems. whether we act as consumers, as workers, as students, as travellers or in any other of the multiple roles we fulfil in modern, everyday life, it is when we experience new opportunities, a reduction in risks or improvements in the quality of life that the european union makes sense. this is a european union at the service of the citizens. the ambition of making the eu a tangible reality for citizens must go beyond the single market. strengthening security should always be a means of helping citizens to benefit from the opportunities of the european union, never an end in itself. our proposal for ‘smart borders’ will facilitate travelling in and out of the eu while deterring irregular immigration. to keep europe open we will also take action against those that try to exploit our economic system for illegal purposes, while the framework for data protection will respond to a very real concern of citizens in the internet age. the union must play a role in the world that matches its economic weight, so we must ensure coherence in our external action. as such, the work programme announces concrete action to project our 2020 objectives for jobs and growths internationally. we will also modernise our development policy and humanitarian aid. those in the world in need really need a stronger europe in the world. before concluding, i would like to briefly explain what you will not find in the commission work programme and why. as announced, we will submit the proposal for the next multiannual financial framework by mid-2011. the specific financial instruments and programmes will be presented in the second half of 2011 in conjunction with the overall framework. to maintain the political nature of the work programme, implementation work as a rule has not been included. the same applies for international negotiations, as their conclusion depends on third parties. meanwhile, these activities remain an important part of our core business. we will continue to deliver and to pursue our dialogue with you on them. in my introduction i noted that the work programme was not only the conclusion of our fruitful dialogue, but also the beginning of a next step in our concrete efforts to steer the european union out of the crisis and beyond. now is the time to maintain momentum. we need to find ways to collectively accelerate our work. i therefore take this opportunity to encourage parliament and the council to engage in trilateral discussions on how to implement the treaty provisions on union programming. in the commission’s view, this could translate into agreements to move forward quicker in negotiations on selected initiatives of particular importance to attaining our political objectives. such a concerted effort would demonstrate our determination to deliver concrete, timely responses in the face of the crisis which has shaken us all. europe’s citizens would expect this. i believe the european union institutions should respond to citizens’ concerns. thank you for your attention.
on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, times are hard for the european economy and for the european project as a whole. we have been devising big strategies such as the climate package, the energy package and the 2020 strategy: schemes after schemes. we still do not seem to know where we want to go and what we want to be. why am i saying this? because wanting to be the best is not sufficient to be the best. the reality is that we are adopting strategies we do not all believe in. no one – or almost no one – is implementing them and no one is ready to finance them. it seems we have too many strategies and a lack of interest in making them a reality. and this is why i believe it is time to get back to the basics of what made the european project possible and brought us together: simple natural things. the single market should be our big scheme and we should put all our effort into enforcing it, because if we want to be competitive on the world stage, we need more economic integration. the only reasonable way to achieve this is through the single market. i welcome the commission work programme, and specifically your proposal on the single market act. but that is not enough. you have the monetary report. you know what is needed – to encourage investment, attract capital and boldly cut bureaucratic expenses. we should focus on simple things which have an obvious impact on europe’s competitiveness, such as resource efficiency, cutting energy costs, reforming the agriculture policy, and the future of transport. the commission and parliament must work hand in hand and ensure that these means match our will. we are therefore looking forward to an ambitious multiannual financial framework proposal in 2011. do we need more regulation to tackle the financial crisis? yes, but only if the aim is to foster europe’s competitiveness. in any case we should avoid adopting an autistic response to the crisis, hoping that the rest of the world will follow. if the message we are sending to our citizens and to the world is not that the eu is a pragmatic association of ideas, capital and values, we will not become the global player we want to be. instead of influencing policies in the world, we will be affected by them. now a word on the european semester. the commission is best placed to identify our strengths and weaknesses when planning work. but you should be careful, because what you are proposing to eu citizens and member states is that they should believe that brussels knows better, and that politicians in brussels are closer to the citizen’ interests than an mp from their constituency. it is a difficult job, and you will commit on this through policy coordination in 2011. i hope you will succeed in proving this, in boosting growth and jobs – not for some but for all. otherwise, we will witness the rise of real anti-europeanism. i wish you good luck.
european citizens expect the european institutions to focus on job creation and social europe in 2011. as vice-president of the committee on transport and tourism, i regret that you have postponed the white paper on the future of european transport for 2011. this document is essential both for the future financial perspective and for the future of cohesion policy, which we have already begun to discuss. from the 2011 work programme, i stress the importance of legislative initiatives on: the protection of personal data, improving the security of information and networks through standards and recommendations for public procurement, electronic signature and mutual recognition of electronic identification and authentication mechanisms. these initiatives are absolutely necessary for the implementation of the digital agenda and the completion of the internal market, including in the area of services. we also look forward to the legislative initiative on smart energy networks. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules. i would conclude by saying that the digital agenda and energy efficiency, areas that contribute both to job creation and to the competitiveness of the european union, together with social europe, should be our main priorities for 2011.
this debate is particularly timely as the eu's economic recovery has remained fragile and member states still face a deteriorating labour market situation. this is why it is necessary for european society to become a knowledge-based society. the eu must ensure that demand and supply of labour are better matched and that the labour force has the skills to fill the new jobs created. as regards romania, the latest commission monitoring report shows that the labour market has stabilised since the beginning of 2010. however, recovery cannot be accompanied immediately by a reduction in unemployment, and young romanians remain, unfortunately, one of the most affected groups. over 20% of them are out of work. in this respect, i consider the european commission's instrument to be a useful one, with the major objective of increasing the participation of young people in the labour market.
the main concern of european citizens is to keep their jobs. the economic and financial crisis has pushed unemployment to 10 percent and among young people to 20 percent. young people and people over 50 face difficulties in finding a job and are often forced to accept temporary contracts or work below their qualifications. the agenda for new jobs and skills must be linked to the union's industrial and innovation policy. to preserve the union's competitiveness, we must develop the capacity for innovation, but also recreate the capacity for production and, by implication, jobs in the european union. clearly, the eco-efficient economy requires new skills. i'm drawing attention to the high dropout rate. because of the economic crisis, more and more young people are unable to attend high school or college. education guarantees young people a future and that is why we have a duty to guarantee young people access to education.
member of the commission. − i am very happy that the fundamental principles of this flagship initiative to boost and improve employment in europe and finally reach an ambitious target by 2020 have been welcomed. we are, of course, open to discussing the various details now and at a later stage. i would like to address some of the points that have been discussed or perhaps even challenged in the discussion, because some of them need further explanation. first of all, we maintain the concept of flexicurity, but this does not mean that we want to put the emphasis only on flexibility, in which case we would use this concept the way it was used before. i would like to give you some examples where there is clearly a reflection of the current times and a reflection of the new challenges. we are definitely making this initiative more age-conscious, and when we speak about life-long learning, we want to put a greater emphasis on the life-long learning opportunities of older workers, because we have to assume that active working life is becoming longer and people will have to be assisted more with career changes or career developments. we have to have a better focus on young people, which is clearly a key consideration for europe 2020. but a separate flagship initiative – ‘youth on the move’ – already exists, where most of the initiatives and strategies in connection with the young generation are outlined in very concrete terms. youth is the age group where we do not want to push for a greater level of flexibility, because there is already enough. there is more flexibility for young workers in europe than in the united states. we want to facilitate more mobility, because we believe that the young generation is the one that can better take advantage of the integrated european labour market and develop their own skills and improve their competitiveness through taking advantage not only of the market itself but also of the institutions that the european union provides. what i spoke about was better working conditions and quality jobs. i regret that ms schroedter did not understand it perfectly. we want to address segmentation as a major challenge of the current european labour market, and we put forward a very concrete example: the open-ended contract, which can help. it is not about removing people from permanent contracts, it is helping those who so far only had a chance to have a short-term or fixed-term contract to have an open-ended one and build up their rights. this will help, to some extent, to provide more jobs, but it will definitely help to provide more rights. this is also very important if we want to speak about quality jobs. when we speak about investing in human capital, we should not forget that the european social fund is there to support all these initiatives in all member states, and we hope that it will remain a robust instrument of the eu in supporting all these initiatives on employment and social inclusion. these are initiatives for 10 years and for all member states. it is not about addressing short-term emergency financial situations in certain member states. we cannot assume that all the 10 years will be spent amidst financial emergencies. this is obviously not a policy that can be so specific as to address this situation, but it does apply to greece and to ireland. it is clear that greece is one of the countries where more flexibility could help to boost the business investment climate, as is the case with spain. ireland is a country which could rebalance competitiveness factors and have a greater focus on investing in skills and education, as opposed to other sources of competitiveness that have been extensively used recently. we must, of course, pay attention to the very critical situation we are in at this moment, and maybe next year there will be little chance of increasing the level of employment. but we also have to look at the overall picture, which will start to improve from the first half of next year, because the major economies driving the recovery forward are already experiencing job growth. we believe that, despite the disturbances in the financial sector, this process will continue and the european policies which we have put forward, although not being able to micromanage job creation in the member states, will create the right framework and provide guidance for the member states to continue working towards full employment.

member of the commission. − we can disagree on certain principles of taxation, which is always a rather sensitive matter. the biggest support for the ccctb comes from businesses; we have clear evidence of this. i understand this because, when dealing with 27 different member states with 27 different corporate tax systems, it is really a mess for them. concerning foreign direct investment, if we are able to agree on this proposal, we have to do so unanimously. if we are able to agree, this will facilitate foreign direct investment because foreign investors who want to invest, not in one member state but in several, will be able to deal with one corporate tax system instead of several corporate tax systems, and that is a big advantage for foreign investors. throughout bilateral discussions with potential investors, they really emphasise the issue of 27 corporate tax systems as an impediment to facilitating foreign direct investment. finally, when we are talking about the common consolidated corporate tax base, we are not talking about tax rates. it is clear that this has nothing to do with the sovereignty of member states in deciding tax matters because, even within the ccctb environment, they will be able to decide on corporate tax rates, based on their needs, their social systems, public services and so on. so the proposal itself does not reduce the sovereignty of member states in tax matters.

on behalf of the epp group. ten months ago, in this very room, i said that the chinese government's 11-year sentence against liu xiaobo for merely expressing his opinions is a symptom of the intensifying campaign by the chinese authorities against human rights defenders. now, awarding the nobel prize to liu xiaobo is, i think, the appropriate measure to highlight that although china has made great progress in the economic and sometimes social realms, the real mark of progress is respect for human rights. a country can be admired for its economic achievements. but it will not gain the respect of other countries if it restricts freedom instead of protecting it. and the actions by which the chinese government has tried to intimidate the countries invited to attend the ceremony - these actions are absolutely worrying, as is the fact that some countries have given in to this blackmail. we are dealing with an unacceptable situation because a country is positioning itself in international relations against one of its own citizens and, in fact, china would gain, as i said, the respect of others if now instead of these threats to other countries it would allow liu xiaobo to come to oslo to receive his prize. but the chinese authorities' attitude seems to be much tougher than the soviets' attitude, because it's possible that not even a family member or liu xiaobo's lawyer will be able to get to oslo. i therefore welcome lech walesa's initiative to symbolically represent the chinese dissident in oslo, but i hope that at the last moment the chinese authorities will decide to release liu xiaobo.
first of all, i would like to welcome the commitment expressed by the commission in its recent communication to continue the process of simplifying the common agricultural policy. too many rules means less competition, and too much rigidity means less functionality. one of the reasons why the cap is now being reformed is undoubtedly the need to simplify it. i would like to point out some of the very important points in the resolution on simplification of the common agricultural policy adopted by this parliament. my colleague michel dantin referred to those countries which go too far in applying european legislation. i believe it is imperative to reduce bureaucratic red tape to the bare minimum, not only at european level but also at member state level. the commission should consider the possibility of common regulations on the required documentation (i would call such a recommendation: the maximum tolerable level of bureaucracy). it is well known that where the european bureaucracy asks for three signatures for approval, the national bureaucracies come in and add five more. only those rules and conditions which are relevant and absolutely necessary and of undisputed utility should remain in force. simplification is not enough, it is also necessary to extend training and information to potential beneficiaries. a substantial part of rural development funds, for example, should be mandatory for such actions. because simplification is directly linked to transparency, i take advantage of the commissioner's presence in the plenary to ask him a question out of context: in view of the recent decision of the european court of justice on the beneficiaries of the european agricultural funds, what measures does the commission envisage to ensure that information on them is still published?
at european level, there is much talk about simplifying the common agricultural policy, but our farmers still complain about the administrative problems they face when accessing funds or when applying european legislation. not only the commission, but also the member states must take steps to simplify the bureaucracy of the common agricultural policy. i think it is essential that the implementation of european agricultural legislation in the member states be done in such a way that farmers are not discouraged from continuing agricultural practices. many farmers in my country complain that they are not well informed, that it is difficult for them to start a business in this sector, or that it is very difficult to access funds in the agricultural sector. i would like to ask the commission to continue to encourage member states to make more efficient use of technology to provide farmers with better information and to reduce the administrative burden faced by the sector. i also hope that the new common agricultural policy will be simpler, more transparent and fairer.
the united nations food and agriculture organization released a report last week that showed that mankind is dangerously close to another global food crisis. he therefore called on farmers to increase production, especially of wheat and corn, and to replenish food stocks in 2012. global food demand will continue to grow in the future and the union should be able to contribute to meeting global food demand. it is therefore essential that union agriculture maintain and improve its production capacity. small, medium-sized and family farms in particular need simpler and more accessible instruments from both the subsidy and direct payments point of view in order to attract them to the market. the key to long-term food security is to stimulate investment in agriculture, in particular by simplifying the bureaucracy faced by farmers. to this end, it is important to ensure that european farmers have easier access to favourable bank loans and subsidies for farmers. please support us, commissioner, in the revision of the energy taxation directive to achieve a reduced vat rate on electricity used for irrigation.
i would like to start by welcoming, as other colleagues have done, the commission's decision in september to approve the national apiculture programmes of the 27 member states for the period 2011-2013, and in particular the fact that the european union's contribution to the funding of these programmes has increased by 25% compared to the previous period. romania, their home member state, is among the main beneficiaries of these funds with some eur 3.4 million. the commission's decision is therefore extremely important for romanian beekeepers. i also welcome the initiative of the committee on agriculture and rural development to initiate this debate on such an important subject. i fully support the suggestions contained in the motion for a resolution which we shall be voting on thursday. beekeeping provides jobs for many european families, even in areas where other activities are not as well developed. beekeeping also brings economic development to rural areas and in this context i would like to stress that it is important not only for honey producers but also for small processors to be the focus of european support programmes, especially under the current pillar ii of the common agricultural policy. honey processing and packaging lines provide competitive advantages in terms of market access, quality and consumer attractiveness of the products. last but not least, beekeeping products are not only used for food consumption but also become ingredients in products, which is why we need to encourage solutions that allow the creation of high value-added products at local level. i regret that support for small processors is not in the motion for a resolution, because encouraging them is, in effect, encouraging those who are directly involved in the rearing of bees.
i would like to welcome the adoption of the new package of measures on strengthening budgetary discipline and extending economic surveillance. the proposed measures were considered necessary due to the differences in compliance with fiscal and budgetary policies between member states. as a result, the economic crisis has generated a worrying perception in several countries, including romania. i believe that the most important innovation is the creation of a new framework for macroeconomic surveillance. it will allow the detection of emerging imbalances and risks. the adoption of the report on economic governance by the task force chaired by mr van rompuy was an important step. its implementation will thus create a strong new framework for crisis management. i would also like to mention the importance of the regulation on ensuring that national budgets comply with eu tax standards. practically no national budget will be able to escape eu tax rules.
i appreciate that the report on economic governance represents a new starting point in organising a viable system of our functioning in this perspective. the report's recommendation on stronger institutions for more effective economic governance namely the creation at national level of a public institution to provide independent analysis, assessments and forecasts on domestic fiscal policy issues i consider to be the basis for the creation of a transparent system at european level. i appreciate that it is essential that each member state should be able to prove the basis of analysis and estimate for each tax measure proposed internally, so that an approach based on mutual trust and knowledge can be developed. i reaffirm the need for specific measures to enable sound and transparent economic governance, allowing for open debate on any measures taken internally in the member states which can have an impact at eu level.
member of the commission. − mr president, the g20 is definitely a very particular formation, where all decisions should be taken by consensus. but, as our president of the commission and the belgian president emphasised, the process is moving on and i will just address one of the issues, namely the taxation of the financial sector. even if there has not been a breakthrough, it was agreed to undertake further work on innovative financing under the french presidency. the european union stands ready to support work in the g20 to explore and develop a financial transaction tax at global level. as i said, the g20 works by consensus and many g20 partners do not, at this stage, share our view on the issue, but we will continue to work towards a consensus. in the meantime, we need to work on other ways of ensuring that the financial sector makes an equitable contribution through measures such as the financial activities tax. on 7 october 2010, the commission outlined its view on this issue and it will pursue the following objectives. firstly, we must ensure that the financial sector makes a fair contribution to public finances. this is particularly important given the support it received during the crisis. secondly, we must make sure that any tax we put forward offers real benefits and that it will raise substantial revenues without undermining eu competitiveness. thirdly, we must ensure that the patchwork of divergent national financial sector taxes does not create new obstacles to the single market. on this basis, the commission has set out a two-pronged approach to financial sector taxation. a financial activities tax appears the best way to deal with the issue in the eu. taxing the profits and wages of the financial sector could ensure that it is taxed fairly, while also generating much-needed revenues. in addition, a financial activities tax could be less prone to the risks to eu competitiveness that other taxation tools would pose if introduced unilaterally. a financial transaction tax should be promoted at global level. an international transaction tax on the globalised financial sector is the best way to fund international objectives in areas such as development aid and climate change. with the right choice of tax and its proper implementation, we could have an important new source of revenues while still maintaining our competitiveness. the commission aims to continue to work on these options in order to bring forward policy initiatives in 2011. the first step will be an impact assessment on financial sector taxation covering the ideas we have set out. in this respect, we will also take account of member states’ analysis. the assessment of the cumulative impact on the financial sector institutions of new regulation, possible bank levies and taxes will be important before launching any proposal. from my side, i would also mention something that is very important: the g20 very clearly took development policy objectives into its agenda. i believe it is a good sign that the g20 process, with proper determination on the part of the european union, could deliver benefits in the interest of citizens.
acting president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as a conclusion to this debate, first of all in general terms, i would like to say again how clearly we had in mind, on the eve of the g20 meetings, that it was in the union's interest to reach an acceptable result on many issues and that we had to ensure that the g20 remained first and foremost a credible and legitimate forum, capable of producing concrete results, as i said earlier, and of giving a coordinated political impetus to globalisation so that the union, in particular, could make its voice heard in this context. i think, without concealing the difficulties - and many of you have referred to these difficulties - that the union has fulfilled its role and that the work of the european institutions and the countries of the union participating in these g20 discussions can be considered satisfactory. seoul was the fifth summit in two years and many collective commitments were put on the table. many of them have produced positive effects for economic growth, global financial stability even though it's true that the work is far from finished. within the union, and in the light of what the commission has just explained to us on bank withdrawals and the financial transaction tax, it is clear that the conclusions of the european council of 29 october indicate that work on these two issues must continue, both at the internal level of the union and on international issues. on the question of levying, there is a growing consensus on the basis and spirit of such levying. there is still no consensus on the purpose or use of the proceeds. in the meantime, member states are putting in place national systems which differ considerably from each other and therefore, in the short term, it is necessary to introduce a minimum degree of coordination and, in the medium term, to move towards a resolution framework which should harmonise resolution structures much better, in particular on the commission's legislative proposals. on this basis, the october european council concluded that the various existing levy schemes should be further coordinated and the ecofin council was invited to come back with conclusions for the december european council. finally, as regards the financial transaction tax now raised by the commission, the european council asked the council, and therefore ecofin, to examine how the various options for preventing tax havens and tax evasion could be envisaged today, and the ecofin council instructed the council's high level group on taxation to examine these issues.
in writing. – our international institutional economic and financial architecture – dating from the end of the war – is currently under strong pressure. a profoundly changing international system and the world crisis are stretching it to the limit, forcing it to adapt itself to the new circumstances. moreover, new institutions such as the g20 are being created to respond to these. however, this is essentially an intergovernmental organism whose decisions, which affect us all, have to be implemented nationally. this is why it is important that its decisions take into account the interests not only of its members but of us all. from that perspective, it is encouraging to see that the seoul summit stressed cooperation and collaboration between members, thus guaranteeing the implementation of decisions, and that there was an indication of resolution in making fundamental structural alterations and encouragement of growth through job creation, without losing sight of the needs of the developing world. let us hope that the eu as such will benefit from the decisions of a body in which only some of its members are participating and that those which are outside the euro zone will benefit too.

in writing. − increased access by patients to quality information about their treatment increases the chance that they will understand the decisions that affect them directly. so the intention is very good, but it needs to be part of a larger strategy of health education that focuses on the patient and not the drug company. there are many problems in the current legal framework and situation in europe with regard to patients' access to information on prescription-only medicines. different interpretations of the directive by member states provide patients in different parts of europe with different access to high-quality information on pharmaceutical products. in some member states it is difficult to access basic information on the prescribed medicinal product. this creates health inequalities. within seconds, patients have endless access to uncontrolled and often inaccurate information about prescription-only medicines through the internet. but they need access to controlled and secure information to avoid complicating matters further. it is therefore necessary to update the provisions on information on prescribed pharmaceutical products.
in writing. − i believe that patients need to have access to better information on prescription medicines, which requires objective information on the characteristics of the medicines and the diseases for which they are recommended, and the prevention of unsolicited information or disguised advertising.
in writing. − the information provided to patients should meet the following main characteristics: − reliability: the information provided to patients should be based on the latest scientific knowledge and there should be clear references to the sources from which this knowledge has been derived; - independence: it must be clear who provides and who funds the information, so that consumers can identify potential conflicts of interest; - information should be easily accessible to consumers and patient-oriented: it should be easy to understand and available, taking into account the specific needs of consumers (age, cultural differences and availability in all european languages). information on prescription medicines provided to patients should be part of a broader 'patient information' and 'health education' strategy. patients and all interested parties should be able to find accurate and objective information on healthy lifestyles, prevention of specific diseases and illnesses and treatment options. i therefore believe that this proposal should be complemented by a code of conduct on information to patients, drawn up in collaboration with patient organisations. this will help to make 'the voice of the patient' heard.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because health issues are of particular interest to me, in particular equal access for patients to healthcare and information. in europe today, the level of information on medicines available on the market is very varied, i would even say unfair to patients. patients must have the right to accurate and complete information on medicines, and my colleague christofer fjellner's proposals have gone exactly in that direction, giving priority to the patient. the amendments made by the european parliament to the european commission's legislative proposal emphasise that companies that manufacture medicines must provide basic information such as product characteristics, labelling, the package leaflet and a publicly accessible version of the assessment report. however, in order to ensure the reliability of the information, i believe that the national authorities should strictly monitor the specialist websites that provide such details.
in writing. − there are many independent sources of evidence-based information on treatment options available in the european union. these resources take into account the cultural and contextual characteristics of the population, including the determinants of health. greater access to quality information will help to improve patients' health, as a well-informed patient is much more inclined to continue necessary treatment and is much more likely to understand the decisions made about his treatment. therefore, if the proposal is well formulated and implemented, it will create added value. the regulation in question does not take account of technical developments and the possibilities and challenges created by the internet. within seconds, patients in europe already have endless access to uncontrolled and often inaccurate information about prescription-only medicines. however, access to controlled and secure pharmaceutical information via the internet is very limited for most patients. this problem is particularly acute for people who need information in their mother tongue. the aim of the proposal can therefore not only be to harmonise european legislation but also to improve health by improving health-related knowledge.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation (ec) no 726/2004 laying down community procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use and establishing a european medicines agency, as regards the provision of information to the general public on medicinal products for human use which are issued on medical prescription, so as to ensure in the future a community legal framework allowing european citizens equal access to accurate and clear information on medicinal products. the report presented by the commission on 20 december 2007 on 'current practices in the provision of medicinal product information to patients' shows that member states have adopted divergent rules and practices on the provision of medicinal product information, which has resulted in unequal access to this information by patients and the general public. european citizens have the right to accurate and clear information on medicines. i believe it is important that the regulation protects the interests of patients and ensures the use of modern means of communication to provide accurate, accessible and easily understandable information to the general public in a transparent manner and independent of the commercial interests of pharmaceutical companies.
in writing. − annually, about 9.3 million tonnes of electrical and electronic equipment (eee) are sold in the eu alone, the majority of which are large household appliances and it and telecommunications equipment. as the market continues to develop and innovation cycles become shorter, equipment replacement is accelerating, making waste electrical and electronic equipment (weee) the fastest growing complex waste source, with the volume of new weee expected to increase to 12,3 million tonnes by 2020. the essential aspects of this reform of the directive are: - the open scope; - the distinction between rohs and reach; - the modification of the criteria for exemptions; - the criteria for deciding on the length of the exemption/grace periods; - codecision for future restrictions instead of comitology; - specific provisions on nanomaterials. i welcome the agreement on the first reading. i voted for this report because the new proposal for a directive is simpler, will give producers an easier tool to use when classifying their products under the directive and will take account of the socioeconomic impact linked to the protection of health and the environment when amending the criteria for exemptions.
in writing. − electronic equipment produces the fastest growing waste stream in europe, and reducing the carcinogenic and toxic substances from this waste stream must be a top priority. the open scope of the legislation, as recommended by the environment committee, is a much better approach than that proposed by the commission. a definitive list of specific products could exclude new products from the regulation, and we need to ensure that the legislation not only facilitates – but also keeps up with – innovation by industry. it is encouraging to see that several companies are now phasing out the use of some of these potentially harmful substances from their products. but we still need to adopt ambitious legislation which will encourage the rest of industry to follow the lead of others and to innovate in order to ensure better environmental protection.
